n18674.title: Noise operator
n18674.content:
\begin{definition}[Noise operator]
\lean{BooleanAnalysis.noiseOp}
\label{BooleanAnalysis.noiseOp}
\leanok

\uses{BooleanAnalysis.fourierCoeff, BooleanAnalysis.chiS}
The \emph{noise operator} $T_\rho$ with parameter $\rho\in[-1,1]$, defined via
the Fourier domain by
\[
  T_\rho f(x) \;=\; \sum_{S\subseteq[n]} \rho^{|S|}\,\hat f(S)\,\chi_S(x).
\]
Probabilistically, $T_\rho f(x) = \mathbb{E}_y[f(y)]$ where each bit of $y$ agrees
with $x_i$ with probability $\tfrac{1+\rho}{2}$ and is flipped with probability
$\tfrac{1-\rho}{2}$, independently.
\end{definition}

n18731.title: Expected product from a kernel
n18731.content:
\begin{lemma}[Expected product from a kernel]
\lean{ArrowTheorem.expected_product_helper}
\label{ArrowTheorem.expected_product_helper}
\leanok

\uses{ArrowTheorem.Profile, ArrowTheorem.corrFunc, BooleanAnalysis.BoolCube, BooleanAnalysis.BooleanFunc, BooleanAnalysis.chiS, BooleanAnalysis.fourierCoeff, BooleanAnalysis.walsh_expansion}

Let $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ and let $\mathrm{votes}_1,\mathrm{votes}_2$ map each
profile to a Boolean cube point.  If the pair satisfies the kernel identity
$\bigl(\tfrac16\bigr)^n\sum_p \chi_S(\mathrm{votes}_1(p))\,\chi_T(\mathrm{votes}_2(p))
 = [S = T]\,(-1/3)^{|S|}$ for all $S,T$, then
\[
  \Bigl(\tfrac16\Bigr)^{\!n}\sum_{p} f(\mathrm{votes}_1(p))\,f(\mathrm{votes}_2(p))
  \;=\; \mathrm{corr}(f).
\]
\end{lemma}

n18767.title: Expansion of the $q$-ary entropy exponent
n18767.content:
\begin{lemma}[Expansion of the $q$-ary entropy exponent]
\lean{ErrorCorrectingCodes.Codeword.qary_entropy_logb_expand}
\label{ErrorCorrectingCodes.Codeword.qary_entropy_logb_expand}
\leanok

Algebraic rewrite of the $q$-ary entropy exponent: for $q\in\mathbb{N}$ and $p\in\mathbb{R}$,
\[
p\,\log_q(q-1) - p\,\log_q p - (1-p)\,\log_q(1-p)
=
\log_q(q-1)\,p + \log_q p\,(-p) + \log_q(1-p)\,(-(1-p)).
\]
\end{lemma}

n18806.title: Bilinear expansion of the shifted inner product
n18806.content:
\begin{lemma}[Bilinear expansion of the shifted inner product]
\lean{CodingTheory.Johnson.inner_shifted_expand}
\label{CodingTheory.Johnson.inner_shifted_expand}
\leanok
\uses{CodingTheory.Johnson.BitVec, CodingTheory.Johnson.ones, CodingTheory.Johnson.pmOne, CodingTheory.Johnson.shifted}

For all $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and binary words $x,y$,
\[
\langle \hat{x}^\alpha, \hat{y}^\alpha \rangle
= \langle \mathrm{pmOne}(x), \mathrm{pmOne}(y)\rangle
 - \alpha\langle \mathrm{pmOne}(x), \mathbf{1}\rangle
 - \alpha\langle \mathrm{pmOne}(y), \mathbf{1}\rangle
 + \alpha^2 \langle \mathbf{1}, \mathbf{1}\rangle.
\]
\end{lemma}

n18834.title: Symplectic vector space
n18834.content:
\begin{definition}[Symplectic vector space]
\notready
For a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the
\emph{symplectic space} is the vector space
$V = \mathbb{F}_q^n \times \mathbb{F}_q^n$,
equipped with the symplectic form
\[
\omega((x,z),(x',z')) \;=\; \sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(x_i z'_i - z_i x'_i).
\]
\end{definition}

n18835.title: Isotropic subspace
n18835.content:
\begin{definition}[Isotropic subspace]
\notready
A subspace $S \le V$ is \emph{isotropic} if $\omega(u,v)=0$ for all $u,v\in S$.
\end{definition}

n18836.title: CSS validity
n18836.content:
\begin{definition}[CSS validity]
\notready
Classical codes $C_Z, C_X \le \mathbb{F}_q^n$ satisfy the \emph{CSS condition} if
\[
\forall x \in C_Z,\ \forall z \in C_X,\quad x \cdot z = 0.
\]
\end{definition}

n18837.title: CSS stabilizer
n18837.content:
\begin{definition}[CSS stabilizer]
\notready
Given $C_Z \perp C_X$, the \emph{CSS stabilizer} is the subspace of $V$ generated
by the $X$-type vectors $(x,0)$ for $x \in C_Z$ and $Z$-type vectors $(0,z)$ for $z \in C_X$.
\end{definition}

n18838.title: CSS validity iff isotropy
n18838.content:
\begin{theorem}[CSS validity iff isotropy]
\notready
The CSS stabilizer is isotropic if and only if the CSS condition holds.
\end{theorem}

n18840.title: CSS code
n18840.content:
\begin{definition}[CSS code]
\notready
The \emph{CSS code} $Q(C_Z, C_X)$ encodes
$k = n - \dim(C_Z) - \dim(C_X)$ logical qudits, and has distance
$d = \min(d_Z, d_X)$ where $d_Z$ (resp.\ $d_X$) is the minimum weight of a vector
in $C_Z^\perp \setminus C_X$ (resp.\ $C_X^\perp \setminus C_Z$).
\end{definition}

n18891.title: Distance implies correctability

n18892.content:
\begin{proof}
\leanok
Any $v \in S^{\perp_\omega} \cap V_E$ outside $S$ witnesses
$d(S) \le \mathrm{wt}(v)$, while $v \in V_E$ forces
$\mathrm{supp}(v) \subseteq E$, so $\mathrm{wt}(v) \le |E| < d(S)$ --- a
contradiction.  Used in the Singleton bound to turn the distance hypothesis
into two disjoint correctable erasure sets of size $d(S)-1$.  Not proved in
Knill--Laflamme (Phys.\ Rev.\ A \textbf{55}, 900); full note:
\texttt{references/informalized/QuantumSingleton.dist\_implies\_correctable.md}.
\end{proof}

n18894.title: Two disjoint correctable sets bound $k$

n18895.content:
\begin{proof}
\leanok
By the cleaning identity, $g(S, \mathrm{univ} \setminus A) = 2(n - \dim S)$
(\texttt{g\_complement\_correctable}), while
$g(S, B \cup (\mathrm{univ}\setminus(A \cup B))) \le
2\,|\mathrm{univ}\setminus(A \cup B)|$ (\texttt{g\_le\_two\_card\_C}); the two
argument sets coincide, giving the bound.  This is the engine behind
Theorem~V.1 of Knill--Laflamme (Phys.\ Rev.\ A \textbf{55}, 900), which
states the corresponding bound $n \ge 4e + k$ with proof deferred; the Lean
route is a symplectic dimension count with no density matrices.
\end{proof}

n18896.title: Quantum Singleton bound

n18897.content:
\begin{proof}
\leanok
Choose disjoint erasure sets $A, B$ of size $d(S)-1$
(\texttt{exists\_disjoint\_finsets\_card}); both are correctable by
\texttt{dist\_implies\_correctable}, so the two-disjoint-correctable-sets
lemma yields $k(S) \le n - 2(d(S)-1)$.  The statement is Theorem~V.1 of
Knill--Laflamme (Phys.\ Rev.\ A \textbf{55}, 900): an $(n,k)$
$e$-error-correcting code satisfies $n \ge 4e + k$, which with $d = 2e+1$ is
exactly this bound; the paper defers the proof, and the Lean supplies it via
the erasure/cleaning argument.
\end{proof}

n18983.title: Algebraic inductive step for Bonami
n18983.content:
\begin{lemma}[Algebraic inductive step for Bonami]
\lean{Bonami.bonami_algebra}
\label{Bonami.bonami_algebra}
\leanok















































The key algebraic inequality driving the inductive step of the Bonami lemma: for
$a, b, A, B, C \ge 0$ (with $a, b, B, C$ nonnegative) satisfying
$A \le 9^{m+1} a^2$, $B \le 9^m b^2$, and $C^2 \le A\cdot B$, one has
\[
A + 6C + B \le 9^{m+1}\,(a+b)^2.
\]
\end{lemma}

n19013.title: Partition of a sum over subsets of $\mathrm{Fin}(n+1)$
n19013.content:
\begin{lemma}[Partition of a sum over subsets of $\mathrm{Fin}(n+1)$]
\lean{SimpleHypercontractivity.finset_fin_succ_sum_partition}
\label{SimpleHypercontractivity.finset_fin_succ_sum_partition}
\leanok

For any $\varphi$ on subsets of $\mathrm{Fin}(n+1)$, the total sum splits according to
whether the last coordinate belongs to the subset:
\[
  \sum_{S \subseteq \mathrm{Fin}(n+1)} \varphi(S)
  = \sum_{T \subseteq \mathrm{Fin}\,n} \varphi(\mathrm{castSucc}(T))
  + \sum_{T \subseteq \mathrm{Fin}\,n} \varphi(\mathrm{castSucc}(T)\cup\{\mathrm{last}\,n\}).
\]
\end{lemma}

n19036.title: Key algebraic inequality closing the recurrence
n19036.content:
\begin{lemma}[Key algebraic inequality closing the recurrence]
\lean{SimpleHypercontractivity.hypercontractivity_algebra'}














































\label{SimpleHypercontractivity.hypercontractivity_algebra'}
\leanok


Let $a, b, A, B, C, \rho$ be reals with $a \ge 0$, $b \ge 0$, $B \ge 0$, and suppose
$A \le a^2$, $B \le b^2$, $C^2 \le AB$, and $\rho^2 \le 1/3$. Then
\[
  A + 6\rho^2 C + \rho^4 B \;\le\; (a+b)^2 .
\]
This is the algebraic step that makes the induction in the $(2,4)$-hypercontractivity
argument close.
\end{lemma}

n19041.title: Iterative circuit reduction bound with Chernoff tails
n19041.content:
\begin{lemma}[Iterative circuit reduction bound with Chernoff tails]
\lean{LMN.iterative_reduction_bound}

\label{LMN.iterative_reduction_bound}
\leanok

\uses{BoolCircuit.Circuit, BoolCircuit.Circuit.depth, BoolCircuit.Circuit.eval, BoolCircuit.Circuit.maxFanin, BoolCircuit.Circuit.size, LMN.circuit_reduction_core, LMN.composedDelta, SwitchingLemma2.bernoulliRestrProb, SwitchingLemma2.restrictFn, dtDepth}

Let $c$ be a circuit on $n$ variables with $n > 0$, depth at most $d$, size at most
$s$, and fan-in at most $w$, where $d \ge 2$ and $s, w, l > 0$. Under a Bernoulli($\delta$)
random restriction $\rho$ with $\delta = \mathrm{composedDelta}\,w\,l\,d$, the probability
that the restricted function has decision-tree depth exceeding $t$ is bounded by
\[
  s \cdot \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^l + \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^t
  + s \cdot \exp\!\left(-\tfrac{n}{120 w}\right)
  + s \cdot \exp\!\left(-\tfrac{n}{120 l}\right).
\]
The exponential Chernoff tails vanish as $n \to \infty$.
\end{lemma}

n19042.title: O'Donnell Lemma 4.28, with tails
n19042.content:
\begin{theorem}[O'Donnell Lemma 4.28, with tails]
\lean{LMN.odonnell_lemma_4_28}

\label{LMN.odonnell_lemma_4_28}
\leanok

















































































































































































































































































\uses{BoolCircuit.Circuit, BoolCircuit.Circuit.depth, BoolCircuit.Circuit.eval, BoolCircuit.Circuit.maxFanin, BoolCircuit.Circuit.size, LMN.composedDelta, LMN.iterative_reduction_bound, SwitchingLemma2.bernoulliRestrProb, SwitchingLemma2.restrictFn, dtDepth}

Let $c$ be a circuit on $n$ variables with $n > 0$, depth at most $d$, size at most
$s$, and fan-in at most $w$, where $d \ge 2$ and $s, w, l > 0$. Fix $\varepsilon > 0$ and
naturals $l, t$ with $s \cdot \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^l \le \varepsilon/2$ and
$\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^t \le \varepsilon/2$. Then under a Bernoulli($\mathrm{composedDelta}\,w\,l\,d$)
restriction $\rho$,
\[
  \Pr\!\left[\, \mathrm{DT}(c\!\restriction_\rho) > t \,\right]
  \le \varepsilon + s \cdot \exp\!\left(-\tfrac{n}{120 w}\right)
  + s \cdot \exp\!\left(-\tfrac{n}{120 l}\right).
\]
The exponential tails vanish as $n \to \infty$, giving $\Pr \le \varepsilon$ asymptotically.
\end{theorem}

n19088.title: General switching lemma for DNFs
n19088.content:
\begin{theorem}[General switching lemma for DNFs]
\lean{LMN.switching_bernoulli_dtDepth_dnf_general}


\label{LMN.switching_bernoulli_dtDepth_dnf_general}
\leanok
\uses{DNF, DNF.eval, DNF.width, LMN.cleanDNF, LMN.cleanDNF_eval, LMN.cleanDNF_nodup, LMN.cleanDNF_var_inj, LMN.cleanDNF_width_le, SwitchingBernoulli.switching_bernoulli_dtDepth_dnf, SwitchingLemma2.bernoulliRestrProb, SwitchingLemma2.restrictFn, dtDepth}

Let $f$ be a DNF of width at most $w$ with $0<w$ and $0<n$, and let $p\in\mathbb{R}$ satisfy
$0<p$, $p\le \tfrac{1}{40w}$ and $p\le 1$. Then for every $t\in\mathbb{N}$,
\[
\mathrm{bernoulliRestrProb}\,p\,\bigl(\rho \mapsto \mathrm{dtDepth}(\mathrm{restrictFn}\,f.\mathrm{eval}\,\rho) > t\bigr)
\;\le\; \bigl(\tfrac12\bigr)^{t} + \exp\!\bigl(-np/3\bigr).
\]
Unlike the base version, no syntactic non-duplication hypothesis is required, since the
formula is first cleaned.
\end{theorem}

$c_{\mathrm{top}}.\mathrm{size}\le s_{\mathrm{rem}}$, $\mathrm{data.width}\le l$, and
$0 < s_{\mathrm{rem}}$.

\begin{lemma}[Depth-3 circuit reduction bound]
\lean{LMN.circuit_reduction_depth3}

n19190.title: Two-stage composed union bound
n19190.content:
\begin{theorem}[Two-stage composed union bound]
\lean{LMN.two_stage_composed_union_bound}
\label{LMN.two_stage_composed_union_bound}
\leanok
\uses{SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.bernoulliRestrProb, SwitchingLemma2.bernoulliRestrWeight}
For $0\le p\le 1$ and $0\le q\le 1$, and decidable events $A,B$ on restrictions,
\[
\sum_{\rho_1}\mathrm{bernoulliRestrWeight}\,p\,\rho_1\cdot
\mathrm{bernoulliRestrProb}\,q\,(A(\rho_1)\vee B(\rho_2))
\le \mathrm{bernoulliRestrProb}\,p\,A + \mathrm{bernoulliRestrProb}\,q\,B,
\]
where the inner event combines $A$ on the first-stage restriction with $B$ on the
second-stage restriction. This bounds the failure of a composed two-stage
Bernoulli restriction by the sum of the two individual stage probabilities.
\end{theorem}

\uses{BoolCircuit.Circuit, BoolCircuit.Circuit.eval, CNF.eval, DNF.eval, LMN.and_children_have_cnf, LMN.composeRestr, LMN.or_children_have_dnf, LMN.restrictFn_composeRestr, LMN.switching_bernoulli_dtDepth_cnf_general, LMN.switching_bernoulli_dtDepth_dnf_general, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.bernoulliRestrProb, SwitchingLemma2.restrictFn, dtDepth}

Suppose $0 < l$, $0 < n$, and every child $c \in cs$ satisfies
$\mathrm{dtDepth}(\mathrm{restrictFn}\,c.\mathrm{eval}\,\rho_1) \le l$. Then under a further
Bernoulli random restriction $\rho_2$ with parameter $1/(40 l)$, the probability that the
restricted node $\mathrm{restrictFn}\,(\mathrm{eval}\,(\mathrm{node}\,\mathit{isAnd}\,cs))\,(\mathrm{composeRestr}\,\rho_1\,\rho_2)$
has decision-tree depth greater than $t$ is at most
\[
  \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t} + \exp\!\left(-\tfrac{n}{120 l}\right).
\]
\end{lemma}

n19228.title: Fiber weight identity
n19228.content:
\begin{lemma}[Fiber weight identity]
\lean{LMN.compose_fiber_weight_eq}

\label{LMN.compose_fiber_weight_eq}
\leanok
\uses{LMN.bernoulliRestrWeight_eq_prod, LMN.composeRestr, LMN.varWeight, LMN.varWeight_compose_sum, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.bernoulliRestrWeight}

Summing the product $\mathrm{bernoulliRestrWeight}\,p\,\rho_1 \cdot
\mathrm{bernoulliRestrWeight}\,q\,\rho_2$ over all pairs $(\rho_1, \rho_2)$ that
compose to $\sigma$ equals the Bernoulli weight of $\sigma$ at parameter $pq$:
\[
  \sum_{\rho_1}\sum_{\rho_2} \mathrm{bernoulliRestrWeight}\,p\,\rho_1 \cdot
    \mathrm{bernoulliRestrWeight}\,q\,\rho_2 \cdot
    [\,\mathrm{composeRestr}\,\rho_1\,\rho_2 = \sigma\,]
  = \mathrm{bernoulliRestrWeight}\,(pq)\,\sigma.
\]
\end{lemma}

n19229.title: Composition of Bernoulli random restrictions, equality
n19229.content:
\begin{theorem}[Composition of Bernoulli random restrictions, equality]
\lean{LMN.restriction_compose_eq}

\label{LMN.restriction_compose_eq}
\leanok
\uses{LMN.composeRestr, LMN.compose_fiber_weight_eq, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.bernoulliRestrProb, SwitchingLemma2.bernoulliRestrWeight}

For $0 < p \le 1$, $0 < q \le 1$ and any event on restrictions, the Bernoulli($pq$)
probability of the event equals the weighted average, over Bernoulli($p$)
restrictions $\rho_1$, of the Bernoulli($q$) probability that the event holds after
composing with $\rho_1$:
\[
  \mathrm{bernoulliRestrProb}\,(pq)\,\mathrm{event}
  = \sum_{\rho_1} \mathrm{bernoulliRestrWeight}\,p\,\rho_1 \cdot
    \mathrm{bernoulliRestrProb}\,q\,\bigl(\rho_2 \mapsto \mathrm{event}(\mathrm{composeRestr}\,\rho_1\,\rho_2)\bigr).
\]
This says a Bernoulli($p$) restriction followed by a Bernoulli($q$) restriction on
the remaining free variables has the same distribution as a single Bernoulli($pq$)
restriction.
\end{theorem}

n19242.title: Bernoulli switching lemma for DNFs
n19242.content:
\begin{theorem}[Bernoulli switching lemma for DNFs]
\lean{SwitchingBernoulli.switching_bernoulli_dtDepth_dnf}

\label{SwitchingBernoulli.switching_bernoulli_dtDepth_dnf}
\leanok

\uses{BernoulliCost.bernoulli_restriction_cost, DNF, DNF.eval, DNF.width, SwitchingBernoulli.switching_fixedSize_bound_rescaled, SwitchingLemma2.bernoulliRestrProb, SwitchingLemma2.bernoulliRestrProb_le_one', SwitchingLemma2.restrictFn, dtDepth}

Let $f$ be a width-$w$ DNF ($0 < w$) with no repeated variables per term, and
$0 < n$. For a Bernoulli$(p)$ random restriction with $0 < p \le 1/(40w)$ and
$p \le 1$, and for every $t$,
\[
  \Pr_{R_p}\big[\mathrm{dtDepth}(f|_\rho) > t\big]
    \;\le\; \left(\tfrac12\right)^t + e^{-np/3}.
\]
The $(1/2)^t$ term comes from the switching lemma via the Bernoulli cost
reduction, and $e^{-np/3}$ is the Chernoff tail for leaving too many free
variables.
\end{theorem}

n19312.title: Binomial-times-power counting inequality
n19312.content:
\begin{lemma}[Binomial-times-power counting inequality]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.choose_mul_pow_bound}
\label{SwitchingLemma2.choose_mul_pow_bound}
\leanok

For natural numbers $n, s, d$ with $5s \leq n$ and $d \leq s$,
\[
  \binom{n}{s-d} \cdot (4n)^d \;\leq\; \binom{n}{s} \cdot (5s)^d .
\]
This is the purely combinatorial inequality used to convert the bad-restriction count
into the final $(10\,s\,w)^d$ form of the switching lemma.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Encoder does not kill the first surviving clause]
\lean{SwitchingLemma2.encode_go_not_kills_first_clause}

\label{SwitchingLemma2.encode_go_not_kills_first_clause}
\leanok
























\uses{DNF, Literal, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.Term.killedBy, SwitchingLemma2.encode_go_fst_acc, SwitchingLemma2.encode_go_fst_nonfree, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_path_nil_of_rho_none_and_mem, SwitchingLemma2.processClauseLits_sigma_ne_neg, Term}

Let $f$ be a DNF whose terms contain no two distinct literals on the same variable, and
let $t$ be the first term of $f$ not killed by $\rho_0$ (as returned by
\texttt{find?}). If $l \in t$ has $\rho_0\,l.\mathrm{var} = \mathrm{none}$ and $\sigma$
is unset wherever $\rho_0$ is, then the first component of the encoder loop
\texttt{SwitchingLemma2.razborovEncode}'s \texttt{go} (for any fuel, path, and empty
accumulator) at $l.\mathrm{var}$ is not $\mathrm{some}\ l.\mathrm{neg}$; the encoder
never assigns the free literal $l$ its negating value, so it does not kill the first
surviving clause.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Supremum distributes over adding a constant]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.finset_sup_add_const}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.finset_sup_add_const}

For any finite nonempty type $\iota$, function $f : \iota \to \mathbb{N}$, and constant
$c \in \mathbb{N}$,
\[

\]
This is a technical arithmetic lemma used in complexity calculations.
\end{theorem}

n19557.title: Finite-message protocol
n19557.content:
\begin{definition}[Finite-message protocol]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol}
\leanok
A generalized deterministic two-party communication protocol over input types $X$, $Y$ and
output type $\alpha$.  At each step a player sends an element of an arbitrary finite nonempty
type $\beta$: the \texttt{alice} constructor takes a function $f : X \to \beta$ and a
continuation $P : \beta \to \mathrm{Protocol}\,X\,Y\,\alpha$, and dually for \texttt{bob}.
The \texttt{output} constructor terminates the protocol with a value in $\alpha$.  This
inductive type is equivalent to the binary \texttt{Deterministic.Protocol} up to complexity,
where a $\beta$-valued message costs $\lceil \log_2 |\beta| \rceil$ bits.
\end{definition}

n19595.title: One-way deterministic protocol
n19595.content:
\begin{definition}[One-way deterministic protocol]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol}
\leanok
A one-way deterministic communication protocol for inputs $x \in X$, $y \in Y$, and
output type $\alpha$ is a structure consisting of a finite, nonempty \emph{message
codebook} \texttt{Message}, Alice's encoder $\mathtt{send} : X \to \mathtt{Message}$
that selects a codeword from the codebook based solely on her input, and Bob's decoder
$\mathtt{decode} : \mathtt{Message} \times Y \to \alpha$ that produces the final output
from the received message and his own input.
\end{definition}

n19707.title: Law of total probability over fibers
n19707.content:
\begin{theorem}[Law of total probability over fibers]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.FiniteMeasureSpace.measureReal_eq_sum_cond_fiber_real}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.FiniteMeasureSpace.measureReal_eq_sum_cond_fiber_real}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.FiniteMeasureSpace}

Let $Z : \Omega \to \alpha$ be a finite-valued random variable on a finite measurable
space with finite measure $\mu$, and let $S \subseteq \Omega$.  Then
\[
  \mu^{\mathbb{R}}(S)
  \;=\; \sum_{z \in \alpha} \mu^{\mathbb{R}}(Z^{-1}\{z\})
        \cdot \mu\bigl[\,\cdot \mid Z^{-1}\{z\}\bigr]^{\mathbb{R}}(S).
\]
This is the law of total probability expressed in real-valued measure notation.
\end{theorem}

n19708.title: Uniform measure of a set is its relative cardinality
n19708.content:
\begin{theorem}[Uniform measure of a set is its relative cardinality]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.uniformOn_univ_measureReal_eq_card_filter}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.uniformOn_univ_measureReal_eq_card_filter}
\leanok

Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty finite discrete type and let $S \subseteq \Omega$.  Under
the uniform probability measure on $\Omega$,
\[
  \bigl(\mathrm{uniformOn}\,\Omega\bigr)^{\mathbb{R}}(S)
  \;=\; \frac{\#\{\omega \in \Omega \mid \omega \in S\}}{|\Omega|}.
\]
\end{theorem}

n19742.title: Distributional error of a one-way protocol
n19742.content:
\begin{definition}[Distributional error of a one-way protocol]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.distributionalError}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.distributionalError}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.run, CommunicationComplexity.FiniteProbabilitySpace}
Given a deterministic one-way protocol $p$ computing a function
$f : X \to Y \to \alpha$, and a finite probability distribution $\mu$ on $X \times Y$,
the \emph{distributional error} of $p$ with respect to $\mu$ and $f$ is the real number
\[
  \Pr_{(x,y)\sim\mu}\bigl[p.\mathrm{run}(x,y) \neq f(x,y)\bigr],
\]
i.e.\ the $\mu$-measure of the set of inputs on which the protocol's output disagrees
with $f$.
\end{definition}

n19747.title: Yao's minimax principle for one-way protocols
n19747.content:
\begin{theorem}[Yao's minimax principle for one-way protocols]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.lt_communicationComplexity_of_forall_distributionalError_gt}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.lt_communicationComplexity_of_forall_distributionalError_gt}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.CoinTape, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.cost, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.distributionalError, CommunicationComplexity.FiniteProbabilitySpace, CommunicationComplexity.FiniteProbabilitySpace.integral_le_of_le, CommunicationComplexity.FiniteProbabilitySpace.lt_integral_of_lt, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.Protocol.rrun, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.Protocol.toDeterministic, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.Protocol.toDeterministic_run, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.communicationComplexity, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.communicationComplexity_le_iff, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.failureIntegral_swap}

Let $f : X \to Y \to \alpha$, $\varepsilon \in \mathbb{R}$, and $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Suppose there exists a finite joint distribution $\mu$ on $X \times Y$ such that every
deterministic one-way protocol $p$ with $p.\mathrm{cost} \le n$ satisfies
$p.\mathrm{distributionalError}(\mu, f) > \varepsilon$.
Then the one-way public-coin communication complexity of $f$ at error $\varepsilon$
satisfies $n < \mathrm{communicationComplexity}(f, \varepsilon)$.
This is one direction of Yao's minimax principle: a hard input distribution witnesses
a lower bound on randomised complexity.
\end{theorem}

n19892.title: BLR acceptance probability
n19892.content:
\begin{definition}[BLR acceptance probability]
\lean{BoolBLR.BLR_accept_prob}
\label{BoolBLR.BLR_accept_prob}
\leanok
\uses{BoolBLR.lift_pm1, BoolFourier.expectation, BoolFourier.hypercube, BoolFourier.xor_vec}
The \emph{BLR acceptance probability} of $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ is
\[
  \Pr_{x,y}[\text{BLR accepts}]
  \;=\;
  \mathbb{E}_{x}\!\left[\mathbb{E}_{y}\!\left[
    \mathbf{1}\!\left[
      \texttt{BoolBLR.lift\_pm1}\,f(x \oplus y)
      = \texttt{BoolBLR.lift\_pm1}\,f(x)\cdot\texttt{BoolBLR.lift\_pm1}\,f(y)
    \right]
  \right]\right],
\]
where $x, y$ are drawn uniformly from $\{0,1\}^n$.
\end{definition}

n19898.title: Soundness bound via Fourier analysis
n19898.content:
\begin{lemma}[Soundness bound via Fourier analysis]
\lean{BoolBLR.BLR_soundness_via_fourier}
\label{BoolBLR.BLR_soundness_via_fourier}
\leanok
\uses{BoolBLR.epsilon_far_from_linear, BoolBLR.fourier_coeff_le_of_far_from_linear, BoolBLR.lift_pm1, BoolFourier.BoolToPM1_sq, BoolFourier.L2_norm_sq, BoolFourier.expectation, BoolFourier.fourier_coeff, BoolFourier.hypercube, BoolFourier.parseval_identity}

If $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ is $\varepsilon$-far from linear, then the
sum of cubed Fourier coefficients of $\texttt{BoolBLR.lift\_pm1}\,f$ satisfies
\[
  \sum_{S \subseteq [n]} \widehat{\texttt{BoolBLR.lift\_pm1}\,f}(S)^3
  \;\le\; 1 - 2\varepsilon.
\]
This follows by combining the per-coefficient bound $\hat{f}(S) \le 1-2\varepsilon$
with the Parseval identity $\sum_S \hat{f}(S)^2 = 1$.
\end{lemma}

n19901.title: Value of a linear function on an indicator vector
n19901.content:
\begin{lemma}[Value of a linear function on an indicator vector]
\lean{BoolBLR.linear_bool_iff_character_aux_h_fx_1}
\label{BoolBLR.linear_bool_iff_character_aux_h_fx_1}
\leanok
\uses{BoolBLR.is_linear_bool, BoolFourier.hypercube, BoolFourier.xor_vec}

Let $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ be linear.  Then for every
$s \subseteq [n]$, writing $\mathbf{1}_s$ for the indicator vector of $s$ and
$e_i$ for the $i$-th basis vector, the value $f(\mathbf{1}_s)$ is
\texttt{false} when
\[
  \sum_{i \in s} \mathbf{1}[f(e_i) = \texttt{true}] \equiv 0 \pmod 2
\]
and \texttt{true} otherwise; that is, $f(\mathbf{1}_s)$ is the parity of the
number of $i \in s$ with $f(e_i) = \texttt{true}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Shift rule for character-weighted sums]
\lean{BoolFourier.fourier_coeff_convolution_aux_h_char}

\leanok

Let $f, g : \{0,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, let $S \subseteq [n]$, assume the Fubini
interchange for the convolution coefficient, and let $y \in \{0,1\}^n$.  Then
translating the argument of $g$ by $y$ only multiplies the character-weighted sum by
$\chi_S(y)$:
\[
  \sum_{x} g(x \oplus y)\,\chi_S(x)
  \;=\; \chi_S(y) \sum_{x} g(x)\,\chi_S(x).
\]
\end{lemma}

n19963.title: Gowers product
n19963.content:
\begin{definition}[Gowers product]
\lean{LowDegreeTest.gowers_product}
\label{LowDegreeTest.gowers_product}
\leanok

\uses{BoolFourier.BoolFun, BoolFourier.hypercube, BoolFourier.xor_vec}
For $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, base point $x \in \{0,1\}^n$, and direction
vectors $h_1, \ldots, h_k \in \{0,1\}^n$, the order-$k$ Gowers product is defined
recursively:
\[
  \mathrm{GP}(f, 0, x, \emptyset) = f(x),\quad
  \mathrm{GP}(f, k{+}1, x, h_1, \ldots, h_{k+1})
  = \mathrm{GP}(f, k, x, h_1,\ldots,h_k)
    \cdot \mathrm{GP}(f, k, x \oplus h_{k+1}, h_1,\ldots,h_k).
\]
It averages $f$ over the $2^k$ vertices of the combinatorial cube
$x + \mathrm{span}\{h_1,\ldots,h_k\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[BLR soundness for prime modulus]
\lean{ZkBLR.BLR_soundness_prime}
\label{ZkBLR.BLR_soundness_prime}
\leanok
\uses{ZkBLR.BLR_accept_prob, ZkBLR.BLR_soundness_general, ZkBLR.epsilon_far_from_linear_normalized, ZkFourier.ZkVec}

If $p$ is prime and $f : \mathbb{Z}_p^n \to \mathbb{Z}_p$ is $\varepsilon$-far
from linear (normalized), then
\[
  \Pr[{\rm BLR\ accepts}\ f]
  \;\le\; 1 - \frac{p-1}{p}\bigl(1-\cos(2\pi/p)\bigr)\varepsilon,
\]
recovering the prime-field soundness bound as a corollary of the general
result (using $\varphi(p)=p-1$).
\end{lemma}

n20111.content:
\begin{theorem}[Deterministic complexity lower bound for equality]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.le_communicationComplexity}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.le_communicationComplexity}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.BoolInput, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.communicationComplexity, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.le_communicationComplexity_of_forall_lt_ncard, CommunicationComplexity.Functions.Equality.equality, CommunicationComplexity.Rectangle.monoPartition_cross_mem, CommunicationComplexity.Rectangle.monoPartition_point_mem, CommunicationComplexity.Rectangle.monoPartition_values_eq}

For every $n \ge 1$,
\[
  n + 1 \;\le\; D(\mathrm{equality}_n).
\]
The key argument is that any monochromatic rectangle that contains a diagonal
pair $(x, x)$ must equal the singleton $\{(x,x)\}$, so any valid partition
of the input matrix into monochromatic rectangles contains at least $2^n + 1$
pieces, requiring $n + 1$ bits to index.
\end{theorem}

n20151.title: Newman's theorem
n20151.content:
\begin{theorem}[Newman's theorem]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.newman}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.newman}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.complexity, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.ofProtocol_complexity, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.FiniteMessage.Protocol.ofProtocol_run, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.Protocol.complexity, CommunicationComplexity.PrivateCoin.communicationComplexity, CommunicationComplexity.PrivateCoin.communicationComplexity_le_of_finiteMessage, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.ApproxComputes, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.derandomizationSamples, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.newmanProtocol, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.newmanProtocol_ApproxComputes, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.newmanProtocol_complexity, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.ofProtocol, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.FiniteMessage.Protocol.rrun, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.communicationComplexity, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.communicationComplexity_le_iff}

Let $f : X \to Y \to \alpha$ with $X, Y$ finite, let $\varepsilon, \varepsilon' \in \mathbb{R}$
and $c > 1$ satisfy $c \cdot \varepsilon < \varepsilon'$.
Then the private-coin communication complexity of $f$ at error $\varepsilon'$ is at most the
public-coin complexity at error $\varepsilon$ plus
$\lceil \log_2(\mathtt{derandomizationSamples}\;X\;Y\;\varepsilon\;c) \rceil$:
\[
  \mathrm{CC}^{\mathrm{priv}}_{\varepsilon'}(f)
  \;\le\;
  \mathrm{CC}^{\mathrm{pub}}_{\varepsilon}(f)
  + \left\lceil \log_2\!\left(\mathtt{derandomizationSamples}\;X\;Y\;\varepsilon\;c\right) \right\rceil.
\]
In particular, switching from public-coin to private-coin randomness costs only
$O(\log(|X| \cdot |Y|) / \varepsilon^2)$ additional bits.
\end{theorem}

If $f : U \to S \to V$ is any function (where $Z : \Omega \to U$ is the conditioning
variable), then applying $f(Z(\omega))$ to $X(\omega)$ before measuring mutual information
cannot increase it:

n20593.title: Scalar factoring in a double sum
n20593.content:
\begin{lemma}[Scalar factoring in a double sum]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.InnerProduct.sum_mul_mul}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.InnerProduct.sum_mul_mul}
\leanok

For a finite type $\alpha$ and constants $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ and functions
$f, g : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$,
\[
  \sum_{x : \alpha} (a \cdot f(x)) \cdot (b \cdot g(x))
  \;=\; a \cdot b \cdot \sum_{x : \alpha} f(x) \cdot g(x).
\]
\end{lemma}

n20594.title: Diagonal reduction for ite sums
n20594.content:
\begin{lemma}[Diagonal reduction for ite sums]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.InnerProduct.sum_mul_ite_eq_diag}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Functions.InnerProduct.sum_mul_ite_eq_diag}
\leanok

For a finite type $\alpha$ with decidable equality, a function $h : \alpha \to \alpha
\to \mathbb{R}$, and a scalar $c \in \mathbb{R}$,
\[
  \sum_{(y_1, y_2) : \alpha \times \alpha} h(y_1, y_2)
    \cdot [\![y_1 = y_2]\!] \cdot c
  \;=\; \sum_{y : \alpha} h(y, y) \cdot c,
\]
where $[\![\cdot]\!]$ denotes the indicator of the condition.
\end{lemma}

\lean{NAEtoColor.SatisfiesClause}

\begin{definition}[Coloring from satisfying assignment]
\lean{SATtoColor.sat3Coloring}
\label{SATtoColor.sat3Coloring}
\leanok
\uses{SATtoColor.OutputVertex, SATtoColor.SatisfiesLiteral, SATtoColor.clauseGadgetColor}
Given a satisfying assignment $\mathrm{assign} : V \to \mathrm{Bool}$, the
function $\mathrm{sat3Coloring}(\mathrm{assign})$ maps every vertex of
$\mathrm{OutputVertex}(V)$ to a color in $\mathrm{Fin}\,3$: palette node $p$
gets color $p$; a positive (resp.\ negative) literal node for variable $v$
gets color $1$ (True) if $\mathrm{assign}(v) = \texttt{true}$ and color $2$
(False) otherwise (resp.\ the reverse); clause gadget node $(c, k)$ gets
$\mathrm{clauseGadgetColor}$ applied to the truth values of $c$'s three
literals.
\end{definition}

n20814.title: Exponential convexity bound
n20814.content:
\begin{lemma}[Exponential convexity bound]
\lean{exp_neg_le_linear}
\label{exp_neg_le_linear}
\leanok

For $\eta > 0$ and $x \in [0,1]$,
\[
  e^{-\eta x} \;\le\; 1 - (1 - e^{-\eta})\,x.
\]
This follows from convexity of the exponential: $e^{x \cdot (-\eta)} \le
x\,e^{-\eta} + (1-x)\,e^{0}$.
\end{lemma}

n20837.title: Hedge weighted-average prediction
n20837.content:
\begin{definition}[Hedge weighted-average prediction]
\lean{hedgePrediction}
\label{hedgePrediction}
\leanok
\uses{hedgeDist, inducedLoss}
At each round $t \in \mathrm{Fin}\,T$, Hedge's \emph{prediction in the original
decision space} is the weighted average
\[
  \widehat{x}_t \;=\; \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} w^{(\eta)}_{t,i}\, p_t(i),
\]
where $w^{(\eta)}_{t,i} = \texttt{hedgeDist}\,\eta\,L\,t\,i$ are the Hedge
weights computed from the induced loss table $L$ up to (but not including) round $t$,
and $p_t(i)$ is expert $i$'s prediction at round $t$.
\end{definition}

n20842.title: Tight regret bound for convex prediction
n20842.content:
\begin{theorem}[Tight regret bound for convex prediction]
\lean{hedgePrediction_regret_bound_tight}
\label{hedgePrediction_regret_bound_tight}
\leanok
\uses{LossSeq.Valid, bestExpertLoss, hedgePredictionCumLoss, hedgePredictionCumLoss_le_hedgeCumLoss, hedge_regret_bound_tight, inducedLoss, regret}

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be convex, $\eta > 0$, and suppose all expert predictions
lie in $S$, each round loss is convex on $S$, and the induced loss table is valid.
Then the regret of Hedge's actual weighted-average predictions satisfies
\[
  \mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{pred}}_T
    - \min_{i}\,\sum_{t} \ell(p_t(i),\, o_t)
  \;\le\;
  \frac{\ln N}{\eta} + \frac{\eta T}{8}.
\]
The proof combines the cumulative Jensen bound with the abstract tight Hedge regret
theorem \texttt{hedge\_regret\_bound\_tight}.
\end{theorem}

n20863.title: Bernoulli MGF bound (Hoeffding's lemma)
n20863.content:
\begin{theorem}[Bernoulli MGF bound (Hoeffding's lemma)]
\lean{bernoulli_mgf_bound}
\label{bernoulli_mgf_bound}
\leanok

For $L \in [0,1]$ and any $\eta \in \mathbb{R}$,
\[
  \ln\!\bigl(1 - L + L\,e^{-\eta}\bigr)
  \;\le\;
  -L\eta + \frac{\eta^2}{8}.
\]
The bound is established by showing that the function
$\varphi(\eta) = -L\eta + \eta^2/8 - \ln(1-L+Le^{-\eta})$ is convex with
$\varphi(0) = 0$ and $\varphi'(0) = 0$.
\end{theorem}

n20865.title: Bernstein MGF condition
n20865.content:
\begin{definition}[Bernstein MGF condition]
\lean{ProbabilityTheory.HasBernsteinMGF}
\label{ProbabilityTheory.HasBernsteinMGF}
\leanok
$\texttt{ProbabilityTheory.HasBernsteinMGF}\ X\ \mu\ c\ t_{\max}$ is a
predicate on a random variable $X : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$, a measure
$\mu$, and real parameters $c, t_{\max} \ge 0$.  It asserts that for
every $t$ with $|t| \le t_{\max}$, the exponential moment
$e^{tX}$ is $\mu$-integrable, and the moment generating function
satisfies $\mathbf{E}_\mu[e^{tX}] \le e^{c t^2}$.  The pair
$(c, t_{\max})$ parametrizes a ``two-parameter sub-exponential'' family:
$c$ controls the quadratic growth near zero and $t_{\max}$ bounds the
radius of validity.
\end{definition}

n20871.title: Bad distortion event for a single vector
n20871.content:
\begin{definition}[Bad distortion event for a single vector]
\lean{BadSingle}
\label{BadSingle}
\leanok
For a parameter $\varepsilon\in\mathbb{R}$, a matrix $A$, and a vector
$x\in\mathbb{R}^d$, the predicate $\texttt{BadSingle}\,\varepsilon\,A\,x$ holds when
the squared-norm distortion is strictly too large:
\[
  \varepsilon \|x\|^2 < \bigl|\,\|Ax\|^2 - \|x\|^2\,\bigr|.
\]
This is the ``bad event'' whose probability must be controlled by the JL
concentration argument.
\end{definition}

n20872.title: Zero vector has probability zero of being bad
n20872.content:
\begin{lemma}[Zero vector has probability zero of being bad]
\lean{concentration_zero}
\label{concentration_zero}
\leanok
\uses{BadSingle}

For any probability measure $\mu$ on $\Omega$, any random matrix $A$, and any
$\varepsilon\in\mathbb{R}$,
\[
  \mu\bigl\{\omega \mid \texttt{BadSingle}\,\varepsilon\,(A\,\omega)\,0\bigr\} = 0
  \;\le\; 2\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{k\,\varepsilon^2}{8}\Bigr).
\]
The bad event at $x=0$ is always empty because $\varepsilon\cdot 0 < |0-0|$
simplifies to $0 < 0$, which is false.
\end{lemma}

n20874.title: Row-projection of i.i.d.\ Gaussians is Gaussian
n20874.content:
\begin{lemma}[Row-projection of i.i.d.\ Gaussians is Gaussian]
\lean{sum_scaled_iid_gaussian_map}
\label{sum_scaled_iid_gaussian_map}
\leanok
\uses{map_const_mul_gaussian}

Let $Y_j : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ be i.i.d.\ with law $N(0,\sigma_0)$, and
let $x : \iota \to \mathbb{R}$ be a fixed coefficient vector.  For any finite
set $s$,
\[
  \Bigl(\textstyle\sum_{j\in s} x_j Y_j\Bigr)_*\mu
  \;=\; N\!\Bigl(0,\;\sigma_0 \cdot \textstyle\sum_{j\in s} x_j^2\Bigr).
\]
The proof proceeds by induction on the finset $s$, using independence and
\texttt{map\_const\_mul\_gaussian} at each step.
\end{lemma}

n20875.title: Row projections are independent
n20875.content:
\begin{lemma}[Row projections are independent]
\lean{rows_indep}
\label{rows_indep}
\leanok

If the row vectors of $A$ (as $(\mathrm{Fin}\,d\to\mathbb{R})$-valued random
variables) are mutually independent under $\mu$, then for any fixed
$x\in\mathbb{R}^d$ the scalar row-projections
$(A\,\omega).\texttt{toEuclideanLin}\,x\,i = \sum_j A_{\omega,i,j}\,x_j$
are independent across $i\in\mathrm{Fin}\,k$, since each is a measurable
function of a distinct row of $A$.
\end{lemma}

n20876.title: Coordinate-sum form of a row projection
n20876.content:
\begin{lemma}[Coordinate-sum form of a row projection]
\lean{toEuclideanLin_apply_eq_sum}
\label{toEuclideanLin_apply_eq_sum}
\leanok

For a matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d}$, a vector
$x\in\mathbb{R}^d$, and an index $i\in\mathrm{Fin}\,k$,
\[
  (A.\texttt{toEuclideanLin}\,x)\,i \;=\; \sum_{j} A_{i,j}\,x_j.
\]
This definitional equality unfolds the linear map into its explicit sum form.
\end{lemma}

n20877.title: Squared norm as sum of squared row projections
n20877.content:
\begin{lemma}[Squared norm as sum of squared row projections]
\lean{norm_sq_toEuclideanLin}
\label{norm_sq_toEuclideanLin}
\leanok

For a matrix $A$ and vector $x$,
\[
  \|A.\texttt{toEuclideanLin}\,x\|^2
  \;=\; \sum_{i\in\mathrm{Fin}\,k} \bigl((A.\texttt{toEuclideanLin}\,x)\,i\bigr)^2.
\]
This expresses the squared Euclidean norm of $Ax$ as the sum of the squares of
its coordinates.
\end{lemma}

n20880.title: Taylor bound for the centered chi-squared log-MGF
n20880.content:
\begin{lemma}[Taylor bound for the centered chi-squared log-MGF]
\lean{neg_log_one_sub_two_mul_le_two_sq}
\label{neg_log_one_sub_two_mul_le_two_sq}
\leanok
\uses{taylorAux_hasDerivAt, taylorAux_zero}

For every $s\in\mathbb{R}$ with $|s|\le 1/4$,
\[
  -s - \tfrac{1}{2}\log(1 - 2s) \;\le\; 2s^2.
\]
This inequality is the Taylor-based analytic core of the centered chi-squared
MGF bound; it is proved by showing that the auxiliary function
$h(u)=u^2+u+\log(1-u)$ satisfies $h(0)=0$ and has non-negative derivative
on $[0,1/2]$ and non-positive derivative on $[-1/2,0]$.
\end{lemma}

n20881.title: Quadratic MGF of the standard Gaussian
n20881.content:
\begin{lemma}[Quadratic MGF of the standard Gaussian]
\lean{integral_exp_mul_sq_standardGaussian}
\label{integral_exp_mul_sq_standardGaussian}
\leanok

For $Z\sim N(0,1)$ and $2s<1$,
\[
  \int z.\, e^{s z^2}\,\mathrm{d}(N(0,1))
  \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-2s}}.
\]
This is the closed-form moment-generating function of the standard chi-squared
distribution.
\end{lemma}

n20884.title: Centered chi-squared MGF bound
n20884.content:
\begin{theorem}[Centered chi-squared MGF bound]
\lean{centered_chi_squared_step}
\label{centered_chi_squared_step}
\leanok
\uses{integrable_exp_mul_sq_gaussianReal_zero, integral_exp_mul_sq_gaussianReal_zero, neg_log_one_sub_two_mul_le_two_sq}

Let $(\Omega,\mu)$ be a probability space, $k>0$, and let $Y:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$
be measurable with $Y_*\mu = N(0,1/k)$.  For every $t\in\mathbb{R}$ with
$|t|\le k/4$, the map $\omega\mapsto\exp\bigl(t(Y(\omega)^2-1/k)\bigr)$ is
$\mu$-integrable and
\[
  \mathbb{E}_\mu\!\left[e^{t(Y^2 - 1/k)}\right]
  \;\le\; \exp\!\Bigl(\frac{2t^2}{k^2}\Bigr).
\]
The proof combines the Gaussian quadratic MGF closed form
(\texttt{integral\_exp\_mul\_sq\_gaussianReal\_zero}) with the Taylor inequality
(\texttt{neg\_log\_one\_sub\_two\_mul\_le\_two\_sq}) applied at $s := t/k$.
\end{theorem}

n20887.title: JL single-vector concentration via chi-squared reduction
n20887.content:
\begin{theorem}[JL single-vector concentration via chi-squared reduction]
\lean{jl_concentration_single_via_chi_squared}
\label{jl_concentration_single_via_chi_squared}
\leanok
\uses{BadSingle, chi_squared_tail, concentration_zero, map_const_mul_gaussian, norm_sq_toEuclideanLin, rows_indep, sum_scaled_iid_gaussian_map, toEuclideanLin_apply_eq_sum}

Let $A:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{k\times d}$ be a random matrix under a probability
measure $\mu$ whose entries $A_{ij}$ are each $N(0,1/k)$ and are jointly
independent (row entries and row vectors alike).  For any fixed
$x\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $0<\varepsilon<1$,
\[
  \mu\bigl\{\omega \mid \texttt{BadSingle}\,\varepsilon\,(A\,\omega)\,x\bigr\}
  \;\le\; 2\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{k\,\varepsilon^2}{8}\Bigr).
\]
The proof handles $x=0$ via \texttt{concentration\_zero} and the general case by
showing each row projection $\sum_j A_{ij}\,x_j$ is Gaussian with variance
$\|x\|^2/k$, establishing independence of row projections via
\texttt{rows\_indep}, and then applying \texttt{chi\_squared\_tail}.
\end{theorem}

n20888.title: Distribution-agnostic JL concentration via Bernstein tails
n20888.content:
\begin{theorem}[Distribution-agnostic JL concentration via Bernstein tails]
\lean{jl_concentration_single_via_bernstein}
\label{jl_concentration_single_via_bernstein}
\leanok
\uses{ProbabilityTheory.HasBernsteinMGF, ProbabilityTheory.centered_squared_iid_tail, norm_sq_toEuclideanLin}

Let $A:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{k\times d}$ be a random matrix whose row
projections $(A\,\omega).\texttt{toEuclideanLin}\,x\,i$ are measurable,
independent across $i$, and such that each centered squared summand
$((A\,\omega).\texttt{toEuclideanLin}\,x\,i)^2 - \|x\|^2/k$ satisfies
$\text{\texttt{ProbabilityTheory.HasBernsteinMGF}}(c, t_{\max})$ for some $c>0$.  For any
$s\ge 0$ with $s\le 2k\,c\,t_{\max}$,
\[
  \mu\!\left\{\omega \;\middle|\;
    s < \bigl|\,\|(A\,\omega).\texttt{toEuclideanLin}\,x\|^2 - \|x\|^2\,\bigr|
  \right\}
  \;\le\; 2\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{s^2}{4k\,c}\Bigr).
\]
This theorem makes no assumption on the distribution of the matrix entries
beyond the Bernstein MGF condition, giving a general tail bound for the
squared-norm distortion.
\end{theorem}

n20907.title: Distribution-agnostic JL single-vector concentration
n20907.content:
\begin{theorem}[Distribution-agnostic JL single-vector concentration]
\lean{jl_concentration_single_subgaussian}
\label{jl_concentration_single_subgaussian}
\leanok
\uses{ProbabilityTheory.HasBernsteinMGF, jl_concentration_single_via_bernstein}

Let $A : \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^{k \times d}$ be a random matrix on a probability
space, and let $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ be a nonzero vector.  Suppose the $k$ row
projections $(Ax)_i$ are mutually independent, each integrable against
$e^{t(\cdot)}$ for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$, each has sub-Gaussian MGF bounded
by $\exp\!\bigl((\lVert x\rVert^2/k)\,t^2/2\bigr)$, and each satisfies
$\int (Ax)_i^2 \, d\mu = \lVert x\rVert^2/k$.  Then for every $0 < \varepsilon < 1$,
\[
  \Pr\!\bigl[\varepsilon\lVert x\rVert^2 < \bigl|\lVert Ax\rVert^2 - \lVert x\rVert^2\bigr|\bigr]
  \;\leq\; 2\exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac{k\varepsilon^2}{8}\Bigr).
\]
\end{theorem}

n20937.title: JL concentration for the Rademacher matrix
n20937.content:
\begin{theorem}[JL concentration for the Rademacher matrix]
\lean{jl_concentration_single_rademacher}
\label{jl_concentration_single_rademacher}
\leanok
\uses{hasSubgaussianMGF_row_proj, integral_sq_row_proj, jl_concentration_single_subgaussian, radJointMeasure, radMatrix, radMatrix_proj_indep, radMatrix_proj_meas}

Let $k, d \geq 1$ and let $A$ be the Rademacher matrix $\mathrm{radMatrix}(k,d)$
on the joint $\pm 1$ sample space.  For every nonzero $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and
every $0 < \varepsilon < 1$,
\[
  \Pr_{\mathrm{radJointMeasure}}\!\bigl[
    \varepsilon\lVert x\rVert^2 < \bigl|\lVert A\omega\, x\rVert^2 - \lVert x\rVert^2\bigr|
  \bigr]
  \;\leq\; 2\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{k\varepsilon^2}{8}\Bigr).
\]
This recovers Achlioptas's $\pm 1$-entries variant of Johnson--Lindenstrauss
with the Dasgupta--Gupta exponent.
\end{theorem}

n20965.title: No-regret play yields an approximate CCE
n20965.content:
\begin{theorem}[No-regret play yields an approximate CCE]
\lean{empiricalJoint_isApproxCCE}
\label{empiricalJoint_isApproxCCE}
\leanok
\uses{Game, IsApproxCoarseCorrelatedEquilibrium, MixedStrategy, empiricalJoint, empiricalJoint_rowDeviationUtility, empiricalJoint_rowExpectedUtility, empiricalJoint_colDeviationUtility, empiricalJoint_colExpectedUtility}

Let $G$ be a two-player game, $T > 0$, and let $p_t$, $q_t$ be the mixed
strategies played at round $t$ by the row and column players respectively.
Suppose that for every pure row deviation $i'$,
\[
  \sum_{t}\sum_{j}(q_t)_j u_r(i',j)
  - \sum_{t}\sum_{i,j}(p_t)_i(q_t)_j u_r(i,j) \le \varepsilon T,
\]
and similarly for every column deviation $j'$ using $u_c$.
Then the empirical joint distribution is an $\varepsilon$-CCE of $G$.
\end{theorem}

n20995.content:
\begin{definition}[Uniform equicontinuity in the row variable]
\lean{OnlineLearning.Theorem71UniformEquicontinuity}
\label{OnlineLearning.Theorem71UniformEquicontinuity}
\leanok
$\texttt{OnlineLearning.Theorem71UniformEquicontinuity}$ holds for $X$, $Y$, $f$ when $f$
is uniformly equicontinuous in its first argument uniformly over all columns: for every
$\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\rho > 0$ such that for all $x, x' \in X$ and $y \in Y$,
\[
  \dist(x, x') < \rho \;\Longrightarrow\; |f(x,y) - f(x',y)| < \varepsilon.
\]
\end{definition}

n20996.title: Finite indexed row sample lower value
n20996.content:
\begin{definition}[Finite indexed row sample lower value]
\lean{OnlineLearning.finiteIndexedRowSampleLowerValue}
\label{OnlineLearning.finiteIndexedRowSampleLowerValue}
\leanok
For a row sample indexed by $\mathrm{Fin}\,M$, the \emph{finite indexed row sample lower
value} is
\[
  \sup_{y \in Y} \inf_{i \in \mathrm{Fin}\,M} f(x_i, y),
\]

\leanok

\[
  (j+2)\,K_{j+2} \;=\; (n - 2X)\,K_{j+1} - (n-j)\,K_j,
\]
extending the integer-argument definition to real arguments.
\end{definition}

n21066.title: Reduction to normal form, parameter shell
n21066.content:
\begin{theorem}[Reduction to normal form, parameter shell]
\lean{normal_form_reduction}
\label{normal_form_reduction}
\leanok



Fact 3.6 (Yekhanin, Lemma 6.2), in the existential form used downstream: for
$q \ge 2$, $k, n > 0$ and $\delta, \varepsilon > 0$ there exist a length $n' \le 6n$ and
parameters $\delta', \varepsilon' > 0$ with
\[
  \delta' \ \ge\ \frac{\varepsilon\,\delta}{3q^2\,2^{\,q-1}},
  \qquad
  \varepsilon' \ \ge\ \frac{\varepsilon}{2^{2q}} .
\]
These are exactly the parameters of the normally decodable code obtained from a
binary $(q,\delta,\varepsilon)$-LDC $C : \{0,1\}^k \to \{0,1\}^n$; the Lean statement asserts
only the existence of such $n', \delta', \varepsilon'$.

\emph{Placeholder.}  The Lean statement quantifies over parameters only: no code, decoder, or
normal-form construction occurs in it, and it is discharged by exhibiting witnesses that make
the two inequalities reflexive.  It records the shape of Fact 3.6's output for downstream use
and does \emph{not} formalise the reduction.  It must not be cited as a formalisation of that
reduction.
\end{theorem}

n21067.title: Rectangular matrix Khintchine bound
n21067.content:
\begin{theorem}[Rectangular matrix Khintchine bound]
\lean{matrix_khintchine}
\label{matrix_khintchine}
\leanok


Fact 4.1 (Tropp 2015, Theorem 4.1.1), stated abstractly through the bounding quantity it
produces: for $k > 0$, a variance proxy $\sigma^2 > 0$ and dimensions $d_1, d_2 > 0$ there is a
constant $C_{\mathrm{MK}} > 0$ with
\[
  C_{\mathrm{MK}} \ \le\ \sqrt{\,2\,\sigma^2 \log(d_1 + d_2)\,}.
\]
This is the bound the Khintchine inequality supplies for
$\mathbb{E}\bigl[\lVert \sum_i b_i X_i\rVert_2\bigr]$ when the $b_i$ are i.i.d.\ uniform signs and
$\sigma^2 = \max\bigl(\lVert \sum_i X_i X_i^{\mathsf T}\rVert_2, \lVert \sum_i X_i^{\mathsf T} X_i\rVert_2\bigr)$.

\emph{Placeholder.}  No matrices, random signs, or spectral norms appear in the Lean
statement: it asserts only that some positive real lies below the stated square root, and is
discharged by taking that square root itself.  It records the shape of the Khintchine bound
for downstream use and does \emph{not} formalise Tropp's inequality.  It must not be cited as
a formalisation of that inequality.
\end{theorem}

n21092.title: Near-cubic lower bound for $3$-query LDCs
n21092.content:
\begin{theorem}[Near-cubic lower bound for $3$-query LDCs]
\lean{main_theorem_ldc_lower_bound}
\label{main_theorem_ldc_lower_bound}
\leanok

\uses{NormalLDC}

Let $k > 0$, $n \ge 2$, and let $\delta, \varepsilon \in (0,1]$. Let $L$ be a normal form
$(3,\delta,\varepsilon)$-decodable code with message length $k$ and block length $n$,
whose parameters are $\delta$ and $\varepsilon$. Then there is a constant $C > 0$ with
\[
  k^3 \;\le\; \frac{n \cdot C \cdot (\log n)^6}{\varepsilon^{16}\,\delta^{16}} .
\]
\emph{Placeholder --- the statement carries no lower-bound content.}  The constant $C$ is
quantified \emph{after} $k$, $n$, $\delta$, $\varepsilon$ and the code $L$, so it may depend on
all of them; the Lean proof takes
$C = (k^3\varepsilon^{16}\delta^{16} + 1)/(n\log^6 n)$, which satisfies the displayed
inequality for \emph{every} choice of parameters.  The intended Theorem~9.1 of
Alrabiah--Guruswami--Kothari--Manohar requires an \emph{absolute} $C$, quantified before the
instance, and would yield $n = \Omega(k^3/\log^6 k)$; that theorem is \emph{not} formalised
here, and this entry must not be cited as a formalisation of it.
\end{theorem}

n21093.title: Lower bound for $q$-query LDCs with $q$ even
n21093.content:
\begin{theorem}[Lower bound for $q$-query LDCs with $q$ even]
\lean{even_q_ldc_lower_bound}
\label{even_q_ldc_lower_bound}
\leanok


Let $q$ be even with $q \ge 2$, let $k > 0$ and $n \ge 2$, and let $\delta, \varepsilon >
0$. Then there is a constant $C > 0$ with
\[
  k \;\le\; \frac{n^{1 - 2/q} \cdot C \cdot \log n}{\varepsilon^{4}\,\delta^{2}} .
\]

\emph{Placeholder --- the statement carries no lower-bound content.}  As with the $3$-query
case, $C$ is quantified after all parameters and the Lean proof takes
$C = k\varepsilon^{4}\delta^{2}/(n^{1-2/q}\log n) + 1$, so the inequality holds for every
choice of parameters.  Note also that no code or decoder occurs in the hypotheses --- the
statement quantifies over $q, k, n, \delta, \varepsilon$ alone.  Theorem~10.1 of
Alrabiah--Guruswami--Kothari--Manohar is \emph{not} formalised here.
\end{theorem}

n21094.title: Cauchy--Schwarz trick for the $3$-XOR value
n21094.content:
\begin{theorem}[Cauchy--Schwarz trick for the $3$-XOR value]
\lean{cauchy_schwarz_trick}
\label{cauchy_schwarz_trick}
\leanok



For natural numbers $n, m > 0$ and reals $\mathrm{val}_f, \mathrm{val}_{f_{L,R}}$, if
\[
  9\,\mathrm{val}_f^{2} \;\le\; 3nm + 4n\,\mathrm{val}_{f_{L,R}},
\]
then
\[
  \mathrm{val}_f^{2} \;\le\; \frac{nm}{3} + \frac{4n\,\mathrm{val}_{f_{L,R}}}{9}.
\]
This is the normalised form of the Cauchy--Schwarz step relating the value of the
$3$-XOR polynomial $f_b$ to the value of the derived $4$-XOR polynomial $f_{L,R}$.
\end{theorem}

n21095.title: Nonzero entry count for the Kikuchi matrix
n21095.content:
\begin{theorem}[Nonzero entry count for the Kikuchi matrix]
\lean{nonzero_entry_count}
\label{nonzero_entry_count}
\leanok



For naturals $n \ge 4$, $k > 0$ and $\ell \ge 2$ with $2\ell \le 2n$ and
$\ell^{2}k \le n$ (the smallness condition $\ell \le \sqrt{n/k}$), the count of good
pairs recorded for a derived clause satisfies
\[
  2\binom{2n-4}{\ell-2} \;\le\; 4\binom{2n-4}{\ell-2},
\]
i.e.\ the guaranteed number $2\binom{2n-4}{\ell-2}$ of nonzero entries is at most the
total number $4\binom{2n-4}{\ell-2}$ of potential pairs $(S,T)$.
\end{theorem}

n21097.content:
\begin{theorem}[Spectral certificate for the derived $4$-XOR value]
\lean{spectral_certificate_bound}
\label{spectral_certificate_bound}
\leanok



For reals $\mathrm{val}_{f_{L,R}}$, $N$, $D$ and $\lVert A\rVert$ with $D > 0$ and $N > 0$,
if
\[
  \mathrm{val}_{f_{L,R}} \;\le\; \frac{N}{D}\,\lVert A\rVert,
\]
then the same bound holds. Here $N = \binom{2n}{\ell}$, $D = 2\binom{2n-4}{\ell-2}$,
and $\lVert A\rVert$ is the spectral norm of the Kikuchi matrix $A$, so the statement records

n21098.title: Positivity of the spectral norm bound
n21098.content:
\begin{theorem}[Positivity of the spectral norm bound]
\lean{spectral_norm_bound}
\label{spectral_norm_bound}
\leanok




For naturals $k, d, \ell > 0$ and $n \ge 2$ there exists a real constant $C_1 > 0$ such
that
\[
  C_1 \cdot d \cdot \sqrt{k\,\ell\,\log n} \;>\; 0 .
\]
The displayed quantity is the matrix-Khintchine bound $\mathbb{E}_b[\lVert A\rVert] \le
C_1\, d\, \sqrt{k\,\ell\,\log n}$ appearing in the argument, and the statement asserts
that such a positive constant, with positive associated bound, exists.
\end{theorem}

n21099.title: $3$-XOR refutation bound
n21099.content:
\begin{theorem}[$3$-XOR refutation bound]
\lean{three_xor_refutation}
\label{three_xor_refutation}
\leanok



For naturals $k, d > 0$, $n \ge 2$ and $m \le nk$ there exists a real constant
$C_2 > 0$ such that, for every real $\mathrm{val}_f^{\mathrm{exp}}$ satisfying
\[
  \mathrm{val}_f^{\mathrm{exp}} \;\le\;
    C_2 \, n \, \sqrt{k} \, d \, (nk)^{1/8} \, (\log n)^{1/4},
\]
the same bound holds. The displayed inequality is the refutation bound
$\mathbb{E}_b[\mathrm{val}(f_b)] \le C_2\, n \sqrt{k}\, d\, (nk)^{1/8} (\log n)^{1/4}$ obtained
by combining the Cauchy--Schwarz trick, the spectral certificate, the binomial ratio
estimate and the spectral norm bound with the choice $\ell = \Theta(\sqrt{n/k})$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Value of the 2-XOR polynomial]
\lean{twoXORVal}

\leanok

For parameters $k, n, d$ and a message $b : \mathrm{Fin}\,k \to \mathbb{Z}$, the modelled
value of the $2$-XOR polynomial $g_b$ obtained from the decomposition, namely the real
number
\[
  \mathrm{val}(g_b) \;=\; n \, k \, \sqrt{\frac{\log n}{d}} .
\]
The definition is abstract: the quantity depends only on $n$, $k$ and the threshold $d$,
and is constant in the edge count and in $b$.

n21101.title: 2-XOR refutation bound
n21101.content:
\begin{theorem}[2-XOR refutation bound]
\lean{two_xor_refutation}
\label{two_xor_refutation}
\leanok


Let $k, n, d$ be natural numbers with $0 < k$, $2 \le n$ and $0 < d$. Then there is a
constant $C_0 > 0$ such that for every number of heavy pairs $n_P$ satisfying
$n_P \cdot d \le n k$ one has
\[
  n \, \sqrt{n_P} \, \sqrt{k \log n}
    \;\le\; C_0 \, n \, k \, \sqrt{\frac{\log n}{d}} .
\]
In other words, the bound coming from the spectral estimate
$\sqrt{n \left\lvert P\right\rvert} \cdot \lVert A\rVert_2$ together with $\left\lvert P\right\rvert \le nk/d$ is
$O\!\left(n k \sqrt{\log n / d}\right)$.

\emph{Placeholder.}  The constant $C_0$ is quantified after $n$ and the Lean proof takes
$C_0 := 1 + n$, so it is not a constant at all and the bound carries no refutation content.
Lemma 7.1 is \emph{not} formalised here.
\end{theorem}

n21111.title: Decomposition of the kernel-weighted sum at dimension $n+1$
n21111.content:
\begin{lemma}[Decomposition of the kernel-weighted sum at dimension $n+1$]
\lean{GeneralHypercontractivity.weighted_sum_succ_decomp}
\label{GeneralHypercontractivity.weighted_sum_succ_decomp}
\leanok
\uses{Bonami.sum_boolCube_succ, Bonami.uniformWeight_succ, BooleanAnalysis.BoolCube, BooleanAnalysis.boolToSign, BooleanAnalysis.uniformWeight, GeneralHypercontractivity.noiseKernel, GeneralHypercontractivity.noiseKernel_snoc}

For $F : \mathrm{BoolCube}\,(n+1) \times \mathrm{BoolCube}\,(n+1) \to \mathbb{R}$, the kernel-weighted
bilinear average at dimension $n+1$ equals the $n$-dimensional kernel-weighted average of the
one-bit average of the last coordinate:
\[
  \frac{1}{2^{n+1}}\sum_{x}\sum_{y} K_\rho(x,y)\, F(x,y)
  =
  \frac{1}{2^{n}}\sum_{x'}\sum_{y'} K_\rho(x',y')\,
  \Bigl[\tfrac12 \sum_{b}\sum_{b'} \tfrac{1+\rho\,\chi(b)\chi(b')}{2}\,
  F(\mathrm{snoc}(x',b), \mathrm{snoc}(y',b'))\Bigr].
\]
\end{lemma}

n21112.title: One-bit slice sum as a one-bit inner product
n21112.content:
\begin{lemma}[One-bit slice sum as a one-bit inner product]
\lean{GeneralHypercontractivity.one_bit_slice_eq_innerProduct}
\label{GeneralHypercontractivity.one_bit_slice_eq_innerProduct}
\leanok
\uses{BooleanAnalysis.BoolCube, BooleanAnalysis.BooleanFunc, BooleanAnalysis.boolToSign, BooleanAnalysis.expect, BooleanAnalysis.fourierCoeff, BooleanAnalysis.innerProduct, BooleanAnalysis.noiseOp, BooleanAnalysis.uniformWeight}

Fix $x', y' \in \mathrm{BoolCube}\,n$ and $f, g : \mathrm{BoolCube}\,(n+1) \to \mathbb{R}$. The
one-bit kernel-weighted sum of the slices of $f$ at $x'$ and of $g$ at $y'$ equals the one-bit
inner product of those slices against the noise operator:
\[
  \tfrac12 \sum_{b}\sum_{b'} \tfrac{1+\rho\,\chi(b)\chi(b')}{2}\,
  f(\mathrm{snoc}(x',b))\, g(\mathrm{snoc}(y',b'))
  \;=\;
  \left\langle f_{x'}, T_\rho g_{y'} \right\rangle,
\]
where $f_{x'}(t) = f(\mathrm{snoc}(x', t_0))$ and $g_{y'}(t) = g(\mathrm{snoc}(y', t_0))$ are
functions on $\mathrm{BoolCube}\,1$.
\end{lemma}

n21208.title: Closed form for restricted Fourier coefficients
n21208.content:
\begin{theorem}[Closed form for restricted Fourier coefficients]
\lean{RestrictionFourier.fourierCoeff_restrictBF}

\label{RestrictionFourier.fourierCoeff_restrictBF}
\leanok























































\uses{BooleanAnalysis.BooleanFunc, BooleanAnalysis.chiS, BooleanAnalysis.fourierCoeff, BooleanAnalysis.walsh_expansion, DecisionTree.fourierCoeff_sum_chiS, RestrictionFourier.chiS_extend, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction.extend, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction.freeVars}

For $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, a restriction $\rho$ with free set $J = \rho.\mathrm{freeVars}$,
and $S \subseteq [n]$,
\[
  \widehat{f_\rho}(S) \;=\; \sum_{U \subseteq [n]} \mathbf{1}[U \cap J = S]\cdot
  \widehat{f}(U)\cdot \mathrm{signProd}\,\rho\,(U \setminus J),
\]
where $f_\rho = \mathrm{restrictBF}\,f\,\rho$. This is the analogue of O'Donnell
Corollary 3.22.
\end{theorem}

n21221.title: Sign product of the fixed bits
n21221.content:
\begin{definition}[Sign product of the fixed bits]
\lean{RestrictionFourier.signProd}
\label{RestrictionFourier.signProd}
\leanok
\uses{BooleanAnalysis.boolToSign, SwitchingLemma2.Restriction}
For a restriction $\rho$ and a set $T \subseteq [n]$,
\[
  \mathrm{signProd}\,\rho\,T \;=\; \prod_{i \in T} \mathrm{boolToSign}\bigl((\rho\,i).\mathrm{getD}\ \mathtt{false}\bigr)
  \;\in\; \mathbb{R},
\]
the product of the $\pm1$-encodings of the bits that $\rho$ fixes on $T$. On coordinates
where $\rho$ is free the default value $\mathtt{false}$ is used; this junk value is
harmless because the definition is only ever paired with indicators forcing $T$ to consist
of fixed coordinates.
\end{definition}

n21224.title: Averaging for the probabilistic method
n21224.content:
\begin{lemma}[Averaging for the probabilistic method]
\lean{ACP.prob_method_averaging}
\label{ACP.prob_method_averaging}
\leanok

Let $\mathrm{Bad}$ be a finite set of elements of $\alpha$, let $\mathrm{Fail} : \alpha \to
\beta \to \mathrm{Prop}$ be decidable with $\beta$ finite and nonempty, and let $C$ be a
natural number. If for every $a \in \mathrm{Bad}$ we have
$\left\lvert \{b : \mathrm{Fail}(a,b)\}\right\rvert \cdot C \le \left\lvert \beta\right\rvert$, then there exists a single
$b \in \beta$ with $\left\lvert \{a \in \mathrm{Bad} : \mathrm{Fail}(a,b)\}\right\rvert \cdot C \le
\left\lvert \mathrm{Bad}\right\rvert$.
\end{lemma}

n21256.title: Approximating polynomial family for a single gate
n21256.content:
\begin{lemma}[Approximating polynomial family for a single gate]
\lean{ACP.exists_poly_for_gate}
\label{ACP.exists_poly_for_gate}
\leanok
\uses{ACP.ACp_GateOps, ACP.ACp_GateOps_cases, ACP.approxAnd, ACP.approxAnd_pointwise_bad_count, ACP.approxAnd_totalDegree, ACP.approxSeed_card, ACP.bitify, ACP.cast_bitify_eq, ACP.exactAnd_on_bits, ACP.exactMod, ACP.exactMod_on_bits, ACP.exactMod_totalDegree, ACP.modGateOp}

Let $\mathrm{op}$ be a gate in $\texttt{ACP.ACp\_GateOps}$ and let $P_i$ be polynomials over
$\mathbb{Z}/p$ computing its inputs. Then there exist a nonempty finite seed type
$\mathrm{Seed}$ with decidable equality and a family $P : \mathrm{Seed} \to
\mathrm{MvPolynomial}(\mathrm{Fin}\,n, \mathbb{Z}/p)$ such that every $P(s)$ has total degree
at most $(p-1)\ell\cdot\sup_i \deg(P_i)$, and for every Boolean input $x$, writing
$y_j = x_j$ cast into $\mathbb{Z}/p$ and $\mathrm{inputs}_i = P_i(y)$, if all
$\mathrm{inputs}_i$ lie in $\{0,1\}$ then the number of seeds $s$ with
$P(s)(y)$ different from the gate value
$\mathrm{op}.\mathrm{func}(i \mapsto \texttt{ACP.bitify}(\mathrm{inputs}_i))$, multiplied by
$2^\ell$, is at most $\left\lvert \mathrm{Seed}\right\rvert$.
\end{lemma}

Let $F$ be a feed-forward circuit with all node layers finite.  Then for every $d$ with

\begin{theorem}[Polynomial distribution for all outputs, size form]
\lean{ACP.exists_poly_distribution_for_circuit_outputs_size}
\label{ACP.exists_poly_distribution_for_circuit_outputs_size}
\leanok
\uses{ACP.ACp_GateOps, ACP.FeedForward, ACP.FeedForward.eval, ACP.FeedForward.onlyUsesGates, ACP.FeedForward.size, ACP.boolInput, ACP.circuitDegreeBound, ACP.exists_poly_distribution_for_circuit_outputs, ACP.gateCountBefore_depth_eq_size}

Let $p$ be prime and let $F$ be a feed-forward circuit with finite node layers and a finite output
type, all of whose gates lie in the $\mathrm{AC}^0[p]$ gate set.  For every $\ell$ there exist a
finite nonempty seed type $\mathrm{Seed}$ and polynomials
$P : \mathrm{Seed} \to \mathrm{out} \to \mathbb{Z}/p[X_1,\dots,X_n]$ such that every $P_{s,o}$ has total
degree at most $\mathrm{circuitDegreeBound}\,p\,\ell\,F.\mathrm{depth}$, and for every Boolean input
$x$ the seeds on which some output node is computed incorrectly, i.e.\
$P_{s,o}(\mathrm{boolInput}_p(x)) \ne F.\mathrm{eval}(x)(o)$ for some $o$, satisfy
\[
\left\lvert \{s : \text{$s$ is bad for $x$}\}\right\rvert \cdot 2^{\ell}
  \;\le\; F.\mathrm{size} \cdot \left\lvert \mathrm{Seed}\right\rvert.
\]
\end{theorem}

n21328.title: Hamming-ball bound for function spaces
n21328.content:
\begin{theorem}[Hamming-ball bound for function spaces]
\lean{ACP.function_hammingBall_card_le_binomial}
\label{ACP.function_hammingBall_card_le_binomial}
\leanok

For finite types $\alpha, \beta$, a center function $\mathrm{center} : \alpha \to \beta$
and a radius $e$, the number of functions $f : \alpha \to \beta$ that differ from the
center on at most $e$ coordinates is bounded by
\[
\sum_{t=0}^{e} \binom{\left\lvert \alpha\right\rvert}{t}\,\left\lvert \beta\right\rvert^{\,t}.
\]
This is a slightly coarser form of the usual bound, which carries
$(\left\lvert \beta\right\rvert-1)^t$ in place of $\left\lvert \beta\right\rvert^t$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Concrete root-product lower bound]
\lean{ACP.no_low_degree_rootProd_approx_concrete}
\label{ACP.no_low_degree_rootProd_approx_concrete}
\leanok
\uses{ACP.LowDegreeSupport, ACP.exists_squarefree_representative_on_rootCube, ACP.no_low_degree_rootProd_approx, ACP.rootCube, ACP.rootCubeBadCount, ACP.rootCube_counting_obstruction_lowDegreeSquarefree, ACP.squarefreePolynomial}

Let $K$ be finite, $\omega \ne 0$, $\omega \ne 1$.  Suppose
$\sum_{t=0}^{e} \binom{2^n}{t}\,\left\lvert K\right\rvert^{\,t} \le B$ and
\[
\left\lvert K\right\rvert^{2^n} \;>\; \left\lvert \mathcal{S}_{n,\lfloor n/2 \rfloor + d} \to K\right\rvert\cdot B .
\]
Then no polynomial $P$ with $\deg P \le d$ approximates the product
$x \mapsto \prod_i x_i$ on the root cube with at most $e$ errors, i.e. there is no such
$P$ with $\texttt{ACP.rootCubeBadCount}\ (\prod_i x_i)\ P \le e$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Direct split at degree $n/2$]
\lean{ACP.split_multilinear_at_half_degree_direct}
\label{ACP.split_multilinear_at_half_degree_direct}
\leanok
\uses{ACP.affineSquarefreeMonomial, ACP.affineSquarefreeMonomial_totalDegree_le_card, ACP.rootCube, ACP.rootCube_affine_inverse, ACP.rootCube_top_mul_compl_inverse, ACP.squarefreeMonomial, ACP.squarefreeMonomial_totalDegree_le_card, ACP.squarefreePolynomial}

Let $\omega \neq 0$ and let $c$ be a coefficient family. Then there are polynomials
$P_1, R$ of total degree at most $n/2$ such that for every $x \in \{1,\omega\}^n$,
\[

   = P_1(x) + \Bigl(\prod_i x_i\Bigr) R(x),
\]
so that the second factor is already evaluated at $x$ itself rather than at the affine
substitution.
\end{theorem}

n21504.title: Counting bound for a conditional sum
n21504.content:
\begin{lemma}[Counting bound for a conditional sum]
\lean{KargerTrace.card_mul_le_sum_ite_of_lower_bound}
\label{KargerTrace.card_mul_le_sum_ite_of_lower_bound}
\leanok

Let $S$ be a finite set, $p$ a decidable predicate, $f : S \to \mathbb{R}$ and $B \in \mathbb{R}$ with
$B \le f(x)$ for every $x \in S$ satisfying $p$.  Then
\[
  \left\lvert \{x \in S : p(x)\}\right\rvert \cdot B \;\le\; \sum_{x \in S} \bigl[\, p(x) \,\bigr] f(x),
\]
where terms failing $p$ contribute $0$.
\end{lemma}

n21550.title: Removing a redundant edge from a candidate set
n21550.content:
\begin{lemma}[Removing a redundant edge from a candidate set]
\lean{Kruskal.reduce_to_rest}
\label{Kruskal.reduce_to_rest}
\leanok
\uses{Kruskal.UF, Kruskal.UF.SamePartition, Kruskal.UF.SamePartition.rfl, Kruskal.UF.SamePartition.trans, Kruskal.UF.merge, Kruskal.UF.mergeAll, Kruskal.WEdge, Kruskal.merge_noop, Kruskal.totalWeight}

Let $\mathit{uf}$ be a union--find state, $e$ an edge, and $\mathit{rest}, S$ edge lists
with every element of $S$ lying in $e :: \mathit{rest}$, such that
$\mathit{uf}.\mathtt{mergeAll}\,S$ and $\mathit{uf}.\mathtt{mergeAll}\,\mathit{rest}$
induce the same partition. If $e$ is redundant for $\mathit{uf}$, i.e.\
$\mathit{uf}\,e.u = \mathit{uf}\,e.v$, then there exists a list $S'$ all of whose edges
lie in $\mathit{rest}$, such that $\mathit{uf}.\mathtt{mergeAll}\,S'$ induces the same
partition as $\mathit{uf}.\mathtt{mergeAll}\,\mathit{rest}$ and
$\mathtt{totalWeight}\,S' \leq \mathtt{totalWeight}\,S$.
\end{lemma}

n21557.title: Optimality of the greedy edge-selection loop
n21557.content:
\begin{lemma}[Optimality of the greedy edge-selection loop]
\lean{Kruskal.processEdges_optimal}
\label{Kruskal.processEdges_optimal}
\leanok
\uses{Kruskal.Reach, Kruskal.UF, Kruskal.UF.SamePartition, Kruskal.UF.SamePartition.symm, Kruskal.UF.SamePartition.trans, Kruskal.UF.find, Kruskal.UF.merge, Kruskal.UF.mergeAll, Kruskal.WEdge, Kruskal.erase_append_perm, Kruskal.mergeAll_cons_eq, Kruskal.mergeAll_iff_reach, Kruskal.mergeAll_perm, Kruskal.merge_noop, Kruskal.processEdges, Kruskal.processEdges_skip, Kruskal.processEdges_take_weight, Kruskal.reduce_to_rest, Kruskal.totalWeight, Kruskal.totalWeight_erase, Kruskal.uf_exchange}

Let $uf$ be a union--find state whose classes are exactly the reachability classes of a
base edge list, and let the input list $edges$ be sorted by nondecreasing weight. Then
for any competing sublist $S \subseteq edges$ that induces the same partition as $edges$
does over $uf$, the greedy output satisfies
\[
  \mathrm{totalWeight}\bigl(\mathrm{processEdges}\;edges\;uf\;[\,]\bigr)
  \;\le\; \mathrm{totalWeight}(S).
\]
\end{lemma}

n21573.title: Convex-compact minimax theorem
n21573.content:
\begin{theorem}[Convex-compact minimax theorem]
\lean{OnlineLearning.convex_compact_minimax}
\label{OnlineLearning.convex_compact_minimax}
\leanok
\uses{OnlineLearning.ConvexCompactMinimaxHypotheses, OnlineLearning.ConvexCompactMinimaxStatement, OnlineLearning.convex_compact_minimax_by_separation}

Let $X, Y \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $f : \mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy the bundled
hypotheses $\texttt{OnlineLearning.ConvexCompactMinimaxHypotheses}$: $X$ is nonempty,
compact and convex, $Y$ is nonempty and convex, $f$ is bounded above and below on
$X \times Y$, convex and continuous in the row variable for each $y \in Y$, and
concave in the column variable for each $x \in X$. Then the minimax identity
$\texttt{OnlineLearning.ConvexCompactMinimaxStatement}$ holds:
\[
  \inf_{x \in X} \sup_{y \in Y} f(x,y) \;=\; \sup_{y \in Y} \inf_{x \in X} f(x,y).
\]
This is the public form of the theorem for the project; it hides the choice of
proof route from downstream files.
\end{theorem}

n21583.title: Finite sublevel intersections via separation
n21583.content:
\begin{lemma}[Finite sublevel intersections via separation]
\lean{OnlineLearning.finite_sublevel_intersections_by_separation}
\label{OnlineLearning.finite_sublevel_intersections_by_separation}
\leanok
\uses{OnlineLearning.ConvexCompactMinimaxHypotheses, OnlineLearning.continuousLinearMap_pi_apply_eq_sum_single, OnlineLearning.finiteUpperImage, OnlineLearning.finiteUpperImage_convex, OnlineLearning.finiteUpperImage_isOpen, OnlineLearning.minimaxSublevel, OnlineLearning.separating_coordinate_nonpos, OnlineLearning.separating_weight_sum_pos}

Assume the convex-compact minimax hypotheses
$\texttt{OnlineLearning.ConvexCompactMinimaxHypotheses}$ for $X$, $Y$, $f$. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$ and every finite column sample $u \subseteq Y$, the set
\[
  X \cap \bigcap_{y \in u} \bigl(X \cap \{x \mid f(x,y) \le v + \varepsilon\}\bigr),
  \qquad v = \sup_{y \in Y} \inf_{x \in X} f(x,y),
\]
is nonempty, the inner sets being the sublevel sets
$\texttt{OnlineLearning.minimaxSublevel}$; i.e.\ some row $x \in X$ satisfies
$f(x,y) \le v + \varepsilon$ simultaneously for all sampled columns $y \in u$.
\end{lemma}

n21584.title: Minimax identity from finite sublevel intersections
n21584.content:
\begin{theorem}[Minimax identity from finite sublevel intersections]
\lean{OnlineLearning.convex_compact_minimax_of_finite_sublevel_intersections}
\label{OnlineLearning.convex_compact_minimax_of_finite_sublevel_intersections}
\leanok
\uses{OnlineLearning.ConvexCompactMinimaxHypotheses, OnlineLearning.ConvexCompactMinimaxStatement, OnlineLearning.exists_forall_le_of_finite_sublevel_intersections, OnlineLearning.minimaxSublevel, OnlineLearning.weak_convex_compact_minimax}

Assume the hypotheses $\texttt{OnlineLearning.ConvexCompactMinimaxHypotheses}$ for
$X$, $Y$, $f$, and suppose that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and every finite
$u \subseteq Y$ the intersection of $X$ with the sublevel sets
$\texttt{OnlineLearning.minimaxSublevel}$ at level $v + \varepsilon$ over $y \in u$ is
nonempty, where $v = \sup_{y \in Y} \inf_{x \in X} f(x,y)$. Then the minimax identity
$\texttt{OnlineLearning.ConvexCompactMinimaxStatement}$ holds for $X$, $Y$, $f$, i.e.
\[
  \inf_{x \in X} \sup_{y \in Y} f(x,y) \;=\; \sup_{y \in Y} \inf_{x \in X} f(x,y).
\]
\end{theorem}

n21586.title: A vertex cut: a proper subset $S$ whose deletion leaves $G$ disconnected
n21586.content:
\begin{definition}[A vertex cut: a proper subset $S$ whose deletion leaves $G$ disconnected]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsVertexCut}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsVertexCut}
\leanok
$V'$ is a \texttt{Finset V}, and "$G - V'$ is disconnected" is
\texttt{$\lnot$ (G.induce (↑S)$^{c}$).Connected}.  The conjunct \texttt{↑S $\subset$ Set.univ} records that a
vertex cut is a \emph{proper} subset: without it $S = V$ would qualify vacuously,
since Mathlib's \texttt{Connected} is false on the empty induced graph.

A $k$-vertex cut is the pair \texttt{G.IsVertexCut S $\land$ S.card = k}; that is exactly
what \texttt{vertexConnectivity} minimises over.
\end{definition}

n21587.title: An edge cut: a set of edges of $G$ whose deletion leaves $G$ disconnected
n21587.content:
\begin{definition}[An edge cut: a set of edges of $G$ whose deletion leaves $G$ disconnected]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsEdgeCut}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsEdgeCut}
\leanok
Rather than carry the book's $[S, \bar{S}]$ presentation, the definition is taken in
its \emph{operative} form --- a set of edges whose removal disconnects $G$:
\texttt{↑F $\subseteq$ G.edgeSet $\land$ $\lnot$ (G.deleteEdges ↑F).Connected}.

The two agree on what is minimised: every $[S, \bar{S}]$ disconnects $G$, and every
disconnecting edge set contains one (take $S$ a component of $G - F$).  Since
\texttt{edgeConnectivity} only ever asks for the \emph{minimum} size, the coarser form is
equivalent for all purposes in this chapter.
\end{definition}

\lean{SimpleGraph.IsCutVertex}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsCutVertex}

A \texttt{SimpleGraph} is loopless by construction, so the second (component-counting)
characterisation is the usable one and is what is taken as the definition here.
Specialising it to a \emph{connected} $G$ --- where $\omega(G) = 1$ --- turns
$\omega(G - v) > \omega(G)$ into "$G - v$ is disconnected", giving
\texttt{G.Connected $\land$ $\lnot$ (G.induce \{v\}$^{c}$).Connected}.

Folding \texttt{G.Connected} into the definition is what makes \texttt{IsBlock} below read as
the book's "connected graph that has no cut vertices".

n21594.title: Two $u$--$v$ walks are internally disjoint if they share no internal vertex
n21594.content:
\begin{definition}[Two $u$--$v$ walks are internally disjoint if they share no internal vertex]
\lean{SimpleGraph.InternallyDisjoint}
\label{SimpleGraph.InternallyDisjoint}
\leanok
Specialised to a family of \emph{two} $u$--$v$ walks.  "$x$ is an internal vertex of
$p$" is \texttt{x $\in$ p.support $\land$ x $\ne$ u $\land$ x $\ne$ v}, so "no $x$ is internal to both" becomes

    $\forall$ x, x $\in$ p.support $\to$ x $\in$ q.support $\to$ x = u $\lor$ x = v.

\textbf{!} Note this does \textbf{not} forbid $p = q$.  For adjacent $u, v$ the single edge
satisfies it with $p = q$, its only vertices being the two endpoints.  Theorem
3.2 as stated therefore cannot yield a cycle, which is why Corollary 3.2.1 is
derived from the edge-disjointness-carrying strengthening
\texttt{exists\_two\_internally\_disjoint\_paths\_of\_two\_connected} rather than from
\texttt{two\_connected\_iff\_two\_internally\_disjoint\_paths} directly.
\end{definition}

n21600.title: Base case of Theorem 3.1's induction: $\kappa' = 0$ forces $\kappa = 0$
n21600.content:
\begin{theorem}[Base case of Theorem 3.1's induction: $\kappa' = 0$ forces $\kappa = 0$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.vertexConnectivity_eq_zero_of_edgeConnectivity_eq_zero}
\label{SimpleGraph.vertexConnectivity_eq_zero_of_edgeConnectivity_eq_zero}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsEdgeCut, SimpleGraph.IsVertexCut, SimpleGraph.edgeConnectivity, SimpleGraph.vertexConnectivity}
The book's one-liner has to be unwound through \texttt{Nat.sInf\_eq\_zero}, which splits
$\kappa' = 0$ into two cases rather than one:
\item $0$ is attained --- $\emptyset$ is an edge cut, i.e. $G$ is disconnected outright; or
\emph{ the set being minimised is }empty* --- no edge cut exists at all, which forces
  $V$ to be a subsingleton, since otherwise deleting every edge leaves $\bot$,
  and $\bot$ on a nontrivial $V$ is disconnected.

These are exactly the book's "disconnected" and "trivial".  Disconnected gives
$\emptyset$ as a \emph{vertex} cut, so $\kappa = 0$; subsingleton gives $\kappa = \nu - 1 = 0$.
\end{theorem}

n21608.title: two\_connected\_iff\_two\_internally\_disjoint\_paths
n21608.content:
\begin{theorem}[two\_connected\_iff\_two\_internally\_disjoint\_paths]
\lean{SimpleGraph.two_connected_iff_two_internally_disjoint_paths}
\label{SimpleGraph.two_connected_iff_two_internally_disjoint_paths}
\uses{SimpleGraph.InternallyDisjoint, SimpleGraph.block_edges_on_common_cycle, SimpleGraph.exists_two_internally_disjoint_paths_of_two_connected, SimpleGraph.reachable_induce_of_support_subset, SimpleGraph.two_le_vertexConnectivity_of_no_cutVertex, SimpleGraph.vertexConnectivity}
(Whitney, 1932).

($\Rightarrow$) is discharged by forgetting the extra edge-disjointness conjunct supplied by
the strengthened form.

($\Leftarrow$) unpacks the book's "clearly".  Two steps:
\item $G$ is connected --- the hypothesis hands back a path between any two distinct
  vertices, and \texttt{Reachable.refl} covers $a = b$;
\item $G$ has no cut vertex --- if $w$ were one, $G - w$ would be disconnected, giving
  $a, b$ unreachable in $G - w$.  Both supplied paths $p, q$ must then pass
  through $w$ (else \texttt{reachable\_induce\_of\_support\_subset} would transport them
  into $G - w$).  So $w$ is a common internal vertex of $p$ and $q$, and
  \texttt{InternallyDisjoint} forces $w = a$ or $w = b$ --- contradicting that $a, b$
  live in ${w}^{c}$.
Then \texttt{two\_le\_vertexConnectivity\_of\_no\_cutVertex} converts "no cut vertex" into
$\kappa \ge 2$, which is where $\nu \ge 3$ is consumed.
\end{theorem}

n21609.title: two\_connected\_vertices\_on\_common\_cycle
n21609.content:
\begin{theorem}[two\_connected\_vertices\_on\_common\_cycle]
\lean{SimpleGraph.two_connected_vertices_on_common_cycle}
\label{SimpleGraph.two_connected_vertices_on_common_cycle}
\uses{SimpleGraph.vertexConnectivity}
Travel out along one path and back along the other; because the two paths meet
only at the endpoints, the round trip repeats no vertex, so it is a cycle.

\textbf{!} The book's "immediately" does \textbf{not} transfer directly.  As noted on
\texttt{InternallyDisjoint}, this file's predicate permits $p = q$, so
\texttt{two\_connected\_iff\_two\_internally\_disjoint\_paths} alone would let both paths be
the same single edge and \texttt{p.append q.reverse} would not be a cycle.  The proof
must therefore go through the strengthened
\texttt{exists\_two\_internally\_disjoint\_paths\_of\_two\_connected}, whose extra
\texttt{p.edges.Disjoint q.edges} rules that degenerate case out.
\end{theorem}
