n21615.title: edgeCard\_ge\_of\_kEdgeConnected
n21615.content:
\begin{theorem}[edgeCard\_ge\_of\_kEdgeConnected]
\lean{SimpleGraph.edgeCard_ge_of_kEdgeConnected}
\label{SimpleGraph.edgeCard_ge_of_kEdgeConnected}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.edgeConnectivity, SimpleGraph.edgeConnectivity_le_minDegree}
a $k$-edge-connected graph satisfies $k\nu \le 2\varepsilon$.

Stated multiplicatively as $k\nu \le 2\varepsilon$ to stay in the natural numbers and avoid
division.

By Theorem 3.1, $k \le \kappa' \le \delta$, so every vertex has degree at least $k$.  Summing
over all $\nu$ vertices gives $\sum_v d(v) \ge k\nu$, and handshaking (Theorem 1.1) says
that sum equals $2\varepsilon$.  Hence $2\varepsilon \ge k\nu$.

A network that survives any $k$ link failures must give every station at least
$k$ links, so it cannot be sparse --- this is exactly the lower bound
$f(m, n) \ge \lceil mn/2\rceil$ of (3.1), which \S{}3.3 shows the Harary graphs attain.
\end{theorem}

n21617.title: vertexConn\_eq\_edgeConn\_of\_threeRegular
n21617.content:
\begin{theorem}[vertexConn\_eq\_edgeConn\_of\_threeRegular]
\lean{SimpleGraph.vertexConn_eq_edgeConn_of_threeRegular}
\label{SimpleGraph.vertexConn_eq_edgeConn_of_threeRegular}
\uses{SimpleGraph.edgeConnectivity, SimpleGraph.vertexConnectivity}
a simple 3-regular graph has $\kappa = \kappa'$.

Theorem 3.1 gives $\kappa \le \kappa' \le \delta = 3$, so both parameters lie in ${0, 1, 2, 3}$ and
only $\kappa' \le \kappa$ needs argument.  Given a minimum vertex cut $S$ of size $\kappa$, one
converts it into an edge cut of the same size by choosing, for each $v \in S$, a
single suitable incident edge --- possible precisely because every vertex of a
cubic graph has just three neighbours, so the local structure around a cut
vertex is tightly constrained.

Cubic graphs are the smallest interesting regular case, and this exercise records
that for them the vertex and edge measures of reliability agree --- unlike the
general situation, where figure 3.2 has $\kappa = 2 < \kappa' = 3$.
\end{theorem}

n21619.title: B\&M's unimodular (Thm 12.3, p. 226): every \emph{full} square submatrix (order $\nu- 1$, selected by an\dots
n21619.content:
\begin{definition}[B\&M's unimodular (Thm 12.3, p. 226): every \emph{full} square submatrix (order $\nu- 1$, selected by an\dots]
\lean{Matrix.IsUnimodular}
\label{Matrix.IsUnimodular}
\leanok
"Full" means as large as the matrix allows --- for a $(\nu-1) \times \varepsilon$ basis
matrix of the bond space, the square submatrices of order $\nu - 1$.  Theorem 12.3
says such a basis matrix is unimodular, and that is exactly what makes theorem
12.4's determinant count the spanning trees: each nonsingular full submatrix
contributes $(\pm 1)^{2} = 1$.

\textbf{!} \textbf{Not} \texttt{Matrix.IsTotallyUnimodular}, which quantifies over
\emph{all} square submatrices --- that is B\&M's strictly stronger \emph{totally} unimodular of
exercise 12.2.3, stated separately below.  "Full square submatrix" is rendered as
\texttt{M.submatrix id g} for an injective $g : n \to m$: all rows, and \texttt{card n} columns
chosen injectively.  Placed in the \texttt{Matrix} namespace so it reads
\texttt{B.IsUnimodular}.
\end{definition}

n21620.title: B\&M's oriented incidence matrix $M$ (p. 222)
n21620.content:
\begin{definition}[B\&M's oriented incidence matrix $M$ (p. 222)]
\lean{CycleSpace.orientedIncMatrix}
\label{CycleSpace.orientedIncMatrix}
\leanok
Record, for each vertex and each arc, whether the arc leaves the
vertex ($+1$), enters it ($-1$), or misses it ($0$).  The signs make this the
\emph{oriented} incidence matrix, distinct from the $0/1$ matrix of \S{}1.3, and they encode
the conservation condition exactly: $M *_{v} f = 0$ says inflow balances outflow at
every vertex.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib: \texttt{SimpleGraph.incMatrix} is the
\emph{unoriented} $0/1$ matrix, and the oriented version is one of Mathlib's own open
TODOs.  B\&M's "if $a$ is a link" clause (i.e. loops map to $0$) is \textbf{automatic} in
this encoding: a loop has \texttt{tail a = head a = v}, so the two indicators cancel to
$1 - 1 = 0$.  Stated over a general \texttt{[Ring R]} so the same definition serves the
$F$-valued \S{}12.1 and the $\mathbb{Z}$-valued \S{}12.2.
\end{definition}

n21623.title: The standard dot-product bilinear form on $K \to K$ (here $A \to F$)
n21623.content:
\begin{definition}[The standard dot-product bilinear form on $K \to K$ (here $A \to F$)]
\lean{CycleSpace.dotForm}
\label{CycleSpace.dotForm}
\leanok
$f$ and $g$ are orthogonal when $\sum_{a \in A} f(a)g(a) = 0$.  For real
coefficients this is the usual inner product; but the chapter also needs it over
fields of characteristic $p$ (exercise 12.2.4), where the form is \textbf{degenerate} and
a vector can be orthogonal to itself.  That degeneracy is precisely why Shank's
result --- \texttt{dim($\mathcal{B}$\_F $\cap$ $\mathcal{C}$\_F) > 0} iff $p \mid \tau(G)$ --- is possible at all: over $\mathbb{R}$ the two
spaces meet only in zero.

\textbf{!} \textbf{Not} an inner product, and deliberately so.  Used with
\texttt{LinearMap.BilinForm.orthogonal}, which works over every field --- in particular
\texttt{ZMod p} --- unlike \texttt{Submodule.orthogonal}/$^{\perp}$, which needs \texttt{RCLike} and would make
exercise 12.2.4 unstateable.  The four $mk_{2}$ obligations are bilinearity, all
discharged by \texttt{simp} on sums.
\end{definition}

n21624.title: $G$ is the underlying (simple) graph of the digraph \texttt{(tail, head)}
n21624.content:
\begin{definition}[$G$ is the underlying (simple) graph of the digraph \texttt{(tail, head)}]
\lean{CycleSpace.IsUnderlyingGraph}
\label{CycleSpace.IsUnderlyingGraph}
\leanok
$u$ and $v$ are adjacent in $G$ exactly when some arc runs between them
in one direction or the other.  The chapter's counting results --- \texttt{dim $\mathcal{B}$ = $\nu$ - $\omega$},
\texttt{dim $\mathcal{C}$ = $\varepsilon$ - $\nu$ + $\omega$}, $\tau(G)$ --- are all statements about this underlying graph, the
orientation being an auxiliary device that cancels out.

\textbf{!} A \texttt{SimpleGraph} underlying graph loses information the arc
carrier has: loops (\texttt{tail a = head a}) and parallel arcs both vanish.  That is
harmless for the \emph{counting} results, which are about $G$, but means $G$ does not
determine \texttt{(tail, head)} --- hence this is a relation, not a function.
\end{definition}

n21625.title: \texttt{(tail, head)} is an orientation of the simple graph $G$
n21625.content:
\begin{definition}[\texttt{(tail, head)} is an orientation of the simple graph $G$]
\lean{CycleSpace.IsOrientationOf}
\label{CycleSpace.IsOrientationOf}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.IsUnderlyingGraph}
$G$ is recovered by forgetting directions.  The point of \S{}12.2 is that
$\tau(G)$ is an invariant of $G$ alone, yet is most easily computed through the
\emph{oriented} incidence matrix of an arbitrarily chosen orientation --- the signs cancel
in the determinant, which is exactly what exercise 12.2.2(a) makes precise.

\textbf{!} Definitionally equal to \texttt{IsUnderlyingGraph}, so "orientation
of $G$" here means only "has $G$ as underlying graph" --- it does \textbf{not} forbid $D$
from having both $(u,v)$ and $(v,u)$, which chapter 10's \texttt{IsOrientationOf} does.
For this chapter that is deliberate and harmless: the results are about $M$ and
\texttt{MM$^{T}$}, which tolerate digons and loops.
\end{definition}

n21626.title: An arc-level cycle in the digraph, as a nonempty closed arc-sequence
n21626.content:
\begin{definition}[An arc-level cycle in the digraph, as a nonempty closed arc-sequence]
\lean{CycleSpace.ArcCycle}
\label{CycleSpace.ArcCycle}
A cycle of the \emph{underlying} graph, traversed in one of its two
directions; some arcs point along the direction of travel and some against it,
which is what the sign in $f_C$ records.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: this structure is degenerate.}  It carries only a nonempty list of
arcs, with \textbf{no} closed-walk condition and \textbf{no} distinctness condition --- the
docstring's "the closed/interior-distinct invariants are elided" understates the
cost.  As a result \emph{any} nonempty list of arcs is an \texttt{ArcCycle}, and the derived
predicate collapses:

    IsArcAcyclic tail head S  $\leftrightarrow$  S = $\emptyset$

(for nonempty $S$, pick $a \in S$ and take the one-element list $[a]$).  Downstream,
theorem 12.2(i) then reads \emph{"the columns of $B | S$ are independent iff $S = \emptyset$"} ---
false --- and lemma 12.2.1 becomes trivially true for the wrong reason.  This is not
\texttt{sorry}, which makes it more dangerous: the definition \emph{looks} honest.

\emph{The repair} needs three fields beyond \texttt{arcs} and \texttt{nonempty}:
\item \textbf{closed walk} --- a vertex sequence \texttt{verts : List V} with \texttt{verts.length = arcs.length}
  such that consecutive arcs meet head-to-tail, cyclically: for each $i$,
  \texttt{\{tail arcs[i], head arcs[i]\} = \{verts[i], verts[i+1 mod n]\}} (the set form allows
  an arc to be traversed against its direction, which is exactly what $C^{+}$ records);
\item \textbf{interior distinctness} --- \texttt{verts.Nodup};
\item optionally \textbf{no repeated arc} --- \texttt{arcs.Nodup}.

\textbf{!} \texttt{SimpleGraph.Walk.IsCycle} genuinely cannot serve, as the note says: the chapter's
digraphs admit loops (\texttt{tail a = head a}) and parallel arcs, which a \texttt{SimpleGraph}
cannot express.  But that argues for building the structure properly, not for
omitting its invariants.
\end{definition}

n21627.title: $S \subseteq A$ is acyclic: it contains no arc-cycle

n21628.title: $f_C$: the circulation of an oriented cycle ($\pm 1$ on $C^{+} / C^{-}$, $0$ off $C$)
n21628.content:
\begin{definition}[$f_C$: the circulation of an oriented cycle ($\pm 1$ on $C^{+} / C^{-}$, $0$ off $C$)]
\lean{CycleSpace.cycleCirculation}
\label{CycleSpace.cycleCirculation}
\uses{CycleSpace.ArcCycle}
Send one unit of current round the cycle in the chosen direction; arcs
pointing with the flow carry $+1$, those against it $-1$, everything else nothing.
Conservation holds at every vertex because the cycle enters and leaves each of its
vertices exactly once.  These are the elementary circulations from which all others
are built, and they give the cycle space its name.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: \texttt{sorry} body.}  $f_C$ is an opaque function, so
\texttt{isBasisMatrix\_cycleSpace\_of\_maximalForest} --- whose rows are these --- asserts nothing.

\emph{The repair} depends on repairing \texttt{ArcCycle} first: once a cycle carries its vertex
sequence, $C^{+}$ is definable (arc $i$ is in $C^{+}$ when \texttt{tail arcs[i] = verts[i]}, i.e.
it is traversed forwards), and

    f\_C a = if a $\notin$ arcs then 0 else if a $\in$ C$^{+}$ then 1 else -1

\textbf{!} With \texttt{arcs} a \texttt{List}, $a \in C^{+}$ needs the \emph{position}, not just membership --- an arc
could in principle occur twice.  Adding \texttt{arcs.Nodup} to \texttt{ArcCycle} removes that
ambiguity and is the cleaner route.
\end{definition}

n21629.title: B\&M's edge cut $(S, \bar{S})$: the arcs with exactly one end in $S$
n21629.content:
\begin{definition}[B\&M's edge cut $(S, \bar{S})$: the arcs with exactly one end in $S$]
\lean{CycleSpace.edgeCutSet}
\label{CycleSpace.edgeCutSet}
\leanok
The arcs crossing the boundary of $S$, in either direction.  The
\emph{direction} matters for the associated potential difference $g_B$, which takes $+1$
on arcs leaving $S$ and $-1$ on those entering it --- the edge cut is undirected, its
potential difference is not.

A \texttt{Set A}, not a \texttt{Finset}, matching \texttt{IsBond}'s quantification
over arbitrary \texttt{S : Set V}.
\end{definition}

n21630.title: A bond: a MINIMAL nonempty edge cut. \textbf{!} MISSING from Mathlib
n21630.content:
\begin{definition}[A bond: a MINIMAL nonempty edge cut. \textbf{!} MISSING from Mathlib]
\lean{CycleSpace.IsBond}
\label{CycleSpace.IsBond}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.edgeCutSet}
An edge cut with nothing to spare.  Bonds are dual to cycles: lemma
12.2.2 says the support of a nonzero potential difference contains a bond, exactly
as lemma 12.2.1 says the support of a nonzero circulation contains a cycle.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib --- and beware two false friends.
\texttt{Dart.lean} uses "bond" for an unrelated half-edge notion, and the repo's
\texttt{IsEdgeCut} is a \emph{cut} without the minimality clause, on a different carrier.

\textbf{!} The minimality clause here quantifies over subsets $B' \subseteq B$ that are \textbf{themselves
edge cuts} (\texttt{$\exists$ S', B' = edgeCutSet S'}).  That is the right reading of "minimal
nonempty edge cut" and is stronger than minimality among arbitrary subsets; check it
against use sites, since lemma 12.2.2 only produces an edge cut inside the support
and then needs a \emph{bond} inside that.
\end{definition}

n21631.title: $g_B$: the potential difference of a bond, $p =$ indicator of $S$ (B\&M give it, p. 221)
n21631.content:
\begin{definition}[$g_B$: the potential difference of a bond, $p =$ indicator of $S$ (B\&M give it, p. 221)]
\lean{CycleSpace.bondPotentialDiff}
\label{CycleSpace.bondPotentialDiff}
\leanok
Put every vertex of $S$ at voltage $1$ and every other at $0$; the
drops are $+1$ on arcs leaving $S$, $-1$ on arcs entering, $0$ on arcs with both
ends on one side.  These are the elementary potential differences, and they give the
bond space its name.

Defined directly by the book's $\delta p$ formula with $p$ the
indicator of $S$, rather than by the three-case rule --- that makes membership in $\mathcal{B}$
immediate and turns the book's "it can be verified" into \texttt{rfl}.  Note the definition
takes an arbitrary \texttt{S : Set V}, not a bond, so $g_B$ exists for any vertex set; the
bond condition matters only for the \emph{basis} claims.
\end{definition}

n21632.title: A basis matrix of a submodule $W \le (A \to F)$: its rows are a basis of $W$
n21632.content:
\begin{definition}[A basis matrix of a submodule $W \le (A \to F)$: its rows are a basis of $W$]
\lean{CycleSpace.IsBasisMatrix}
\label{CycleSpace.IsBasisMatrix}
\leanok
Package a basis as the rows of a matrix, so questions about the space
become questions about the matrix.  This is what lets theorem 12.2 phrase acyclicity
as linear independence of \emph{columns}, and theorem 12.4 count spanning trees by a
determinant.

"Rows form a basis" is unfolded into its two halves ---
\texttt{LinearIndependent F M} and \texttt{span (range M) = W} --- rather than using \texttt{Basis}, which
would require a chosen index equivalence.  The row index $n$ is a free \texttt{Fintype},
so the same predicate serves matrices indexed by $T$, by $T^{c}$, or by ${v // v \ne y}$.
\end{definition}

n21634.title: A spanning tree of the digraph
n21634.content:
\begin{definition}[A spanning tree of the digraph]
\lean{CycleSpace.IsSpanningTree}
\label{CycleSpace.IsSpanningTree}
A maximal acyclic set of arcs touching every vertex.  By theorem 12.2,
spanning trees are exactly the $(\nu-1)$-element subsets $S$ for which $B | S$ is
nonsingular --- which is what makes \S{}12.2's determinant formula count them.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: \texttt{sorry} body --- the most damaging one in the file.}  \texttt{tau} counts the
\texttt{Finset}s satisfying this predicate, so \textbf{$\tau(G)$ is an opaque natural number}, and
every \S{}12.2 statement about it is vacuous: theorem 12.4, (12.8), corollary 12.4, the
matrix-tree theorem, and exercises 12.2.1(b), 12.2.2(b), 12.2.4(a), (b).

\emph{The repair}, once \texttt{ArcCycle} is fixed:

    IsSpanningTree tail head T := IsArcAcyclic tail head T $\land$ T.card + 1 = Fintype.card V
                                  $\land$ (the underlying subgraph on T is connected)

or equivalently "acyclic and spanning", using the connectivity notion suggested for
\texttt{IsConnectedDigraph}.  Acyclic plus $|T| = \nu - 1$ already forces connectivity for a
graph on $\nu$ vertices, so the middle clause plus acyclicity suffices --- but only once
\texttt{IsArcAcyclic} is genuine.
\end{definition}

n21635.title: A maximal forest of the digraph
n21635.content:
\begin{definition}[A maximal forest of the digraph]
\lean{CycleSpace.IsMaximalForest}
\label{CycleSpace.IsMaximalForest}
A maximal acyclic set of arcs --- a spanning tree of each component.
Its size $\nu - \omega$ is exactly the rank of the bond space, which is how corollary 12.2
computes \texttt{dim $\mathcal{B}$}.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: \texttt{sorry} body.}  Makes both tree-basis theorems
(\texttt{isBasisMatrix\_cycleSpace\_of\_maximalForest},
\texttt{isBasisMatrix\_bondSpace\_of\_maximalForest}) vacuous, and is a hypothesis of
\texttt{fundamentalCycle}.

\emph{The repair:} \texttt{IsArcAcyclic tail head T $\land$ $\forall$ a $\notin$ T, $\lnot$ IsArcAcyclic tail head (insert a T)}
--- acyclic and maximally so.  Note this is the \emph{forest} notion, weaker than
\texttt{IsSpanningTree}: it does not require connectivity, which is exactly why corollary
12.2 gets $\nu - \omega$ rather than $\nu - 1$.
\end{definition}

n21636.title: The fundamental cycle of $a \notin T$ ($T + a$ contains a unique cycle)
n21636.content:
\begin{definition}[The fundamental cycle of $a \notin T$ ($T + a$ contains a unique cycle)]
\lean{CycleSpace.fundamentalCycle}
\label{CycleSpace.fundamentalCycle}
\uses{CycleSpace.ArcCycle, CycleSpace.IsMaximalForest}
The tree already provides a unique route between the ends of $a$
(theorem 2.1), and adding $a$ closes exactly one cycle.  The $\varepsilon - \nu + \omega$ fundamental
cycles, one per non-tree arc, give the tree-basis of the cycle space --- the matrix
$C$ is a basis matrix because $C | \bar{T}$ is an identity matrix, so its rank is full.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: \texttt{sorry} body.}  An opaque \texttt{ArcCycle}, so
\texttt{isBasisMatrix\_cycleSpace\_of\_maximalForest} asserts nothing about it.

\emph{The repair.}  The lever noted in the source comment is right: \texttt{IsAcyclic.path\_unique}
gives the unique $T$-path between $a$'s ends, and the cycle is that path closed by
$a$.  \textbf{!} But it is stated for \texttt{SimpleGraph}, while this chapter's carrier is
\texttt{tail, head : A $\to$ V} with loops and parallel arcs --- so either transfer along the
underlying graph (losing the multi-arc case) or redo the uniqueness argument on the
arc carrier.  The \texttt{hT} hypothesis is what makes "unique" true, and $ha : a \notin T$ what
makes the cycle exist.
\end{definition}

n21637.title: The vertex set $S$ of the fundamental bond of $a \in T$ ($\bar{T} + a$ contains a unique bond, B\&M's\dots

n21638.title: $B$ is the tree-$T$ basis matrix of the bond space (rows indexed by $T$)
n21638.content:
\begin{definition}[$B$ is the tree-$T$ basis matrix of the bond space (rows indexed by $T$)]
\lean{CycleSpace.IsBasisMatrixOfTree}
\label{CycleSpace.IsBasisMatrixOfTree}
Its defining feature is that $B | T$ is an identity matrix --- the
fundamental bond of $a$ contains $a$ itself with coefficient $1$ and no other tree
arc.  That is what pins down \texttt{det(B | T) = 1} in the proof of theorem 12.3, and
what makes exercise 12.1.2(b)'s change-of-basis identity readable.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: \texttt{sorry} body.}  This predicate is a hypothesis of theorems 12.3,
12.4, corollary 12.4 and exercises 12.2.1(b), 12.2.3(a), 12.2.4(a) --- all of which
therefore constrain nothing.

\emph{The repair:} $B$ is the tree-$T$ basis matrix when its rows are the fundamental-bond
potential differences, i.e.

    B = fun a : {a // a $\in$ T} => bondPotentialDiff tail head (fundamentalBondVertexSet tail head T a.1)

--- exactly the matrix appearing in \texttt{isBasisMatrix\_bondSpace\_of\_maximalForest}.  \textbf{!}
Alternatively, characterise it axiomatically as *"a basis matrix of $\mathcal{B}$ whose
restriction $B | T$ is the identity"*, which is weaker to state, enough for theorem
12.3, and does not depend on \texttt{fundamentalBondVertexSet} --- probably the better
choice, since it is the property every proof actually uses.
\end{definition}

n21639.title: $C$ is the tree-$T$ basis matrix of the cycle space (rows indexed by $\bar{T}$)
n21639.content:
\begin{definition}[$C$ is the tree-$T$ basis matrix of the cycle space (rows indexed by $\bar{T}$)]
\lean{CycleSpace.IsBasisMatrixOfTree'}
\label{CycleSpace.IsBasisMatrixOfTree'}
The cycle-side mirror of \texttt{IsBasisMatrixOfTree}: $C | \bar{T}$ is the
identity, because the fundamental cycle of $a$ is the only one using $a$.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: \texttt{sorry} body.}  Hypothesis of (12.8), corollary 12.4 and exercises
12.2.1(b), 12.2.4(a) --- all vacuous as a result.

\emph{The repair:} as for \texttt{IsBasisMatrixOfTree}, either concretely (rows are the
fundamental-cycle circulations) or axiomatically (*a basis matrix of $\mathcal{C}$ with
$C | \bar{T}$ the identity*).  The axiomatic form is again preferable and is what the
determinant arguments actually consume.
\end{definition}

n21640.title: $\tau(G)$: the number of spanning trees

n21641.title: bondSpace\_eq\_rowSpace
n21641.content:
\begin{theorem}[bondSpace\_eq\_rowSpace]
\lean{CycleSpace.bondSpace_eq_rowSpace}
\label{CycleSpace.bondSpace_eq_rowSpace}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.bondSpace, CycleSpace.orientedIncMatrix}
, first half.  *Let $M$ be the incidence matrix of a digraph
$D$.  Then $\mathcal{B}$ is the row space of $M$.*

The drop across $a$ is the signed combination of the vertex potentials,
with $m_v$ picking out the sign.  So the bond space is \emph{exactly} the row space of
$M$, and \texttt{dim $\mathcal{B}$ = rank M}.

\texttt{Submodule.span F (Set.range M)} is the row space, $M$ being read
as a family of rows indexed by $V$.  Step 3's identity is the only real content and
is worth extracting, since theorem 12.1's second half needs it too.
\end{theorem}

n21643.title: exists\_arcCycle\_subset\_support\_of\_isCirculation
n21643.content:
\begin{theorem}[exists\_arcCycle\_subset\_support\_of\_isCirculation]

\label{CycleSpace.exists_arcCycle_subset_support_of_isCirculation}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.ArcCycle, CycleSpace.cycleSpace}
*If $f$ is a nonzero circulation, then $\| f\|$ contains a
cycle.*

Current cannot enter a dead end: anything that flows must flow round in
a loop.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Currently trivial for the wrong reason.}  Since \texttt{ArcCycle} has no closure
condition, the goal is satisfied by the one-element list $[a]$ for any $a \in \| f\|$ ---
so this is provable in two lines and means nothing.  Repair \texttt{ArcCycle} before
filling; the skeleton above is for the repaired statement.
\end{theorem}

n21645.title: basisMatrix\_bondSpace\_cols\_linearIndependent\_iff
n21645.content:
\begin{theorem}[basisMatrix\_bondSpace\_cols\_linearIndependent\_iff]
\lean{CycleSpace.basisMatrix_bondSpace_cols_linearIndependent_iff}
\label{CycleSpace.basisMatrix_bondSpace_cols_linearIndependent_iff}
\uses{CycleSpace.IsArcAcyclic, CycleSpace.IsBasisMatrix, CycleSpace.bondSpace, CycleSpace.restrictCols}
*Let $B$ be a basis matrix of $\mathcal{B}$.  Then for any $S \subseteq A$,
the columns of $B | S$ are linearly independent if and only if $S$ is acyclic.*

The theorem converting a combinatorial question into a linear-algebraic
one --- and it holds over \textbf{any} field, which is why exercise 12.1.5 is subsumed by
stating \S{}12.1 over \texttt{[Field F]}.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Currently false.}  With \texttt{ArcCycle} degenerate, \texttt{IsArcAcyclic S $\leftrightarrow$ S = $\emptyset$}, so the
right-hand side says $S = \emptyset$ while the left is true for any independent column set.
Repair \texttt{ArcCycle} first.  Step 4 additionally needs \texttt{cycleCirculation}, also
\texttt{sorry}-bodied.
\end{theorem}

n21651.title: isUnimodular\_basisMatrix\_bondSpace
n21651.content:
\begin{theorem}[isUnimodular\_basisMatrix\_bondSpace]
\lean{CycleSpace.isUnimodular_basisMatrix_bondSpace}
\label{CycleSpace.isUnimodular_basisMatrix_bondSpace}
\uses{CycleSpace.IsBasisMatrixOfTree, CycleSpace.IsSpanningTree, Matrix.IsUnimodular}
(proof due to Tutte, 1965b).  *The basis matrix $B$ is
unimodular.*

Exactly what theorem 12.4 needs: every full submatrix contributes $0$
or a determinant of absolute value $1$, so squaring and summing counts the spanning
trees.  The proof is due to Tutte (1965b).

\textbf{\textbf{!} Currently vacuous} --- \texttt{IsSpanningTree} and \texttt{IsBasisMatrixOfTree} both have
\texttt{sorry} bodies.  Note step 4 is where the \emph{axiomatic} reading of
\texttt{IsBasisMatrixOfTree} (\emph{"basis matrix with $B | T$ the identity"}) would pay off
directly.
\end{theorem}

n21655.title: tau\_eq\_det\_fromBlocks
n21655.content:
\begin{theorem}[tau\_eq\_det\_fromBlocks]
\lean{CycleSpace.tau_eq_det_fromBlocks}
\label{CycleSpace.tau_eq_det_fromBlocks}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.IsBasisMatrixOfTree, CycleSpace.IsBasisMatrixOfTree', CycleSpace.IsSpanningTree, CycleSpace.tau}
\emph{\texttt{$\tau$(G) = $\pm$ det [B; C]}}, the determinant of the square
matrix obtained by stacking a tree-basis matrix of $\mathcal{B}$ on top of one of $\mathcal{C}$.

The stacked matrix is square because
\texttt{dim $\mathcal{B}$ + dim $\mathcal{C}$ = ($\nu$ - $\omega$) + ($\varepsilon$ - $\nu$ + $\omega$) = $\varepsilon$} --- the two spaces are complementary,
which is theorem 12.1's orthogonality counted dimensionally.

The $\lor$ in the conclusion is the book's $\pm$.  The row index is
${a // a \in T} \oplus {a // a \notin T}$, reindexed to $A$ by \texttt{Equiv.sumCompl} --- that equiv is
canonical here, unlike in exercise 12.2.1(b) where one must be supplied.
\textbf{!} Currently vacuous, resting on \texttt{tau} and both \texttt{IsBasisMatrixOfTree} predicates.
\end{theorem}

n21656.title: matrix\_tree\_theorem
n21656.content:
\begin{theorem}[matrix\_tree\_theorem]
\lean{CycleSpace.matrix_tree_theorem}
\label{CycleSpace.matrix_tree_theorem}
\uses{CycleSpace.orientedIncMatrix, CycleSpace.tau}
(implicit in Kirchhoff, 1847).  *\texttt{$\tau$(G) = det KK'},
where $K$ is obtained from the incidence matrix $M$ by deleting any one row.*

The rows of $M$ sum to zero --- every arc contributes $+1$ at its tail
and $-1$ at its head --- so exactly one row is redundant, and discarding it leaves an
independent spanning set of $\mathcal{B}$.  By exercise 12.2.2(a) the product \texttt{MM'} is the

(B\&M's \emph{conductance matrix}), so this says every cofactor of the
Laplacian equals $\tau(G)$ --- the form in which the matrix-tree theorem is usually
quoted, and the closed formula for $\tau(G)$ promised back in \S{}2.4.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Currently vacuous} --- \texttt{tau} and \texttt{IsConnectedDigraph} both rest on \texttt{sorry} bodies.
Step 3 is a genuine restructuring worth doing before any of \S{}12.2 is filled.
\end{theorem}

n21657.title: isUnimodular\_deleteRow
n21657.content:
\begin{theorem}[isUnimodular\_deleteRow]
\lean{CycleSpace.isUnimodular_deleteRow}
\label{CycleSpace.isUnimodular_deleteRow}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.orientedIncMatrix, Matrix.IsUnimodular}
\emph{.  }A matrix $K$ obtained from $M$ by deleting any one row
is unimodular.*

The incidence-matrix counterpart of theorem 12.3, and what upgrades
exercise 12.1.3 into the matrix-tree theorem \texttt{$\tau$(G) = det KK'}.  Note it is proved
\emph{directly}, not via theorem 12.3 --- $K$ is not a tree-basis matrix.

\textbf{!} Step 3's leaf induction is the real work and has no counterpart
in theorem 12.3's slick change-of-basis argument.  \textbf{!} The statement lacks a
connectivity hypothesis, unlike \texttt{isBasisMatrix\_deleteRow}; step 2 uses that $K$ is a
basis matrix, which \emph{does} need \texttt{hconn} --- so either add it or find a route through
step 3 alone.
\end{theorem}

n21658.title: lapMatrix\_eq\_orientedIncMatrix\_mul\_transpose
n21658.content:
\begin{theorem}[lapMatrix\_eq\_orientedIncMatrix\_mul\_transpose]
\lean{CycleSpace.lapMatrix_eq_orientedIncMatrix_mul_transpose}
\label{CycleSpace.lapMatrix_eq_orientedIncMatrix_mul_transpose}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.IsOrientationOf, CycleSpace.orientedIncMatrix}
*The conductance matrix $C$ of a loopless graph $G$
satisfies \texttt{C = MM'}, where $M$ is the incidence matrix of any orientation of $G$.*

\textbf{*} \textbf{The cheapest win in the file} --- a direct computation, no dependency
on the defective definitions.  This is what Mathlib calls the \textbf{Laplacian}; B\&M call
it the \emph{conductance matrix}.  Notably the \emph{orientation drops out} --- the signs cancel
--- so it is an invariant of the undirected graph, as it must be.

Step 3's parallel-arc caveat is the one thing to pin down before
starting; everything else is \texttt{Finset.sum} manipulation.
\end{theorem}

n21659.title: tau\_eq\_det\_lapMatrix\_deleteRowCol
n21659.content:
\begin{theorem}[tau\_eq\_det\_lapMatrix\_deleteRowCol]
\lean{CycleSpace.tau_eq_det_lapMatrix_deleteRowCol}
\label{CycleSpace.tau_eq_det_lapMatrix_deleteRowCol}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.IsOrientationOf, CycleSpace.tau}
*All cofactors of the conductance matrix $C$ are equal
to $\tau(G)$.*

The form in which the matrix-tree theorem is normally stated: *the
number of spanning trees is any cofactor of the Laplacian*.  It finally delivers, in
full generality, the closed formula for $\tau(G)$ that \S{}2.4 promised and that theorem
2.9 gave only for complete graphs.

This states the \emph{principal} $(y,y)$-minor, which is what the
matrix-tree theorem gives directly and what every application uses.  B\&M claim
\textbf{all} cofactors equal $\tau(G)$, including the non-principal ones; that full statement
is \texttt{tau\_eq\_lapMatrix\_cofactor} directly below, and this principal case is the one to
prove first.
\end{theorem}

n21660.title: tau\_eq\_lapMatrix\_cofactor
n21660.content:
\begin{theorem}[tau\_eq\_lapMatrix\_cofactor]
\lean{CycleSpace.tau_eq_lapMatrix_cofactor}
\label{CycleSpace.tau_eq_lapMatrix_cofactor}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.IsOrientationOf, CycleSpace.tau}
, full form.  *All cofactors of the conductance matrix $C$
are equal to $\tau(G)$.*

\texttt{tau\_eq\_det\_lapMatrix\_deleteRowCol} above states only the
principal $(y,y)$-minor.  The triage (\texttt{log/graphtheory-EXERCISE\_TRIAGE.md} \S{}A.11)
recorded this as a fidelity gap and recommended stating the exercise as written.  The
general form is the one usually cited, because it is what licenses deleting \emph{any} row
and \emph{any} column --- the principal case alone does not.

\textbf{!} Deleting row $i$ and column $j$ for $i \ne j$ leaves a matrix whose
row and column index types are the \emph{different} subtypes ${v // v \ne i}$ and
${v // v \ne j}$, so \texttt{Matrix.det} does not apply to it.  A reindexing equiv $e$ between
the two is therefore threaded through explicitly --- the same device
\texttt{tau\_eq\_det\_fromBlocks\_K} uses further down this file for the same reason.  Because $e$
is not canonical it fixes the column order only up to a permutation, so the conclusion
is stated up to sign, absorbing $(-1)^(i+j)$ and \texttt{sign e} together.  Taking $i = j$ and
\texttt{e = Equiv.refl} recovers the principal case above.

\textbf{!} Currently vacuous via \texttt{tau} and \texttt{IsConnectedDigraph}, exactly as the principal case
is.
\end{theorem}

n21661.title: incMatrix\_isTotallyUnimodular\_iff\_isBipartite
n21661.content:
\begin{theorem}[incMatrix\_isTotallyUnimodular\_iff\_isBipartite]
\lean{CycleSpace.incMatrix_isTotallyUnimodular_iff_isBipartite}
\label{CycleSpace.incMatrix_isTotallyUnimodular_iff_isBipartite}
\leanok
*The incidence matrix of a simple graph $G$ is totally
unimodular if and only if $G$ is bipartite.*

\textbf{!} Note this is the \emph{unoriented} $0/1$ incidence matrix of \S{}1.3, \textbf{not}
the signed one of this chapter --- the signed version is always totally unimodular, for
every graph.  The classical characterisation underlying the integrality of bipartite
matching linear programs, and it links back to theorem 1.2: bipartite means no odd
cycle.

\textbf{*} Independent of every defective definition in this file --- it
mentions only \texttt{SimpleGraph.incMatrix} and \texttt{IsBipartite}, both Mathlib.  Together with
exercise 12.2.2(a), one of the two items that can be filled today.  Step 2's
determinant computation is the concrete part.
\end{theorem}

n21662.title: finrank\_inf\_pos\_iff\_dvd\_tau
n21662.content:
\begin{theorem}[finrank\_inf\_pos\_iff\_dvd\_tau]
\lean{CycleSpace.finrank_inf_pos_iff_dvd_tau}
\label{CycleSpace.finrank_inf_pos_iff_dvd_tau}
\leanok
\uses{CycleSpace.bondSpace, CycleSpace.cycleSpace, CycleSpace.tau}
(H. Shank).  *Let $F$ be a field of characteristic $p$.
Then \texttt{dim($\mathcal{B}$\_F $\cap$ $\mathcal{C}$\_F) > 0} if and only if $p \mid \tau(G)$.*

Over $\mathbb{R}$ the two spaces are orthogonal complements and meet only in
zero.  In characteristic $p$ the dot form is \textbf{degenerate} --- a vector can be
orthogonal to itself --- so they may genuinely overlap, and Shank's result says the
overlap is nontrivial exactly when $p \mid \tau(G)$.  A purely arithmetic property of
$\tau(G)$ detected by a linear-algebraic degeneracy --- a striking illustration of the
chapter's theme.

\textbf{!} Step 1 must \textbf{not} be derived from orthogonality (\texttt{dim $\mathcal{C}$ =
$\varepsilon$ - dim $\mathcal{B}$}), which is exactly what fails here; use the rank--nullity argument
recorded under \texttt{finrank\_cycleSpace}.  Getting this wrong would make the proof
circular --- the whole point is that the two spaces are \emph{not} complementary.
\end{theorem}

n21663.title: Edge connectivity $\kappa'(G)$
n21663.content:
\begin{definition}[Edge connectivity $\kappa'(G)$]
\lean{edgeConnectivity}
\label{edgeConnectivity}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsEdgeCut}
The least number of edges one must cut to break $G$ apart.  "$G$ is
$k$-edge-connected" is spelled \texttt{k $\le$ edgeConnectivity G} throughout this file --- see
\texttt{robbins\_orientation} ($k = 2$) and \texttt{exists\_kArcConnected\_orientation\_of\_eulerian}.

Mathlib has no edge-connectivity, so this is the repo's notion
restated locally.  \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} in $\mathbb{N}$ reproduces the book's trivial-graph
convention automatically --- but it also means a graph with \emph{no} edge cut (a
one-vertex graph) gets $\kappa' = 0$, which is the source of the \texttt{[Nontrivial V]} gap in
\texttt{associatedDigraph\_isKArcConnected\_iff} below.
\end{definition}

n21664.title: The bridge \texttt{Digraph $\to$ Quiver}: \texttt{Quiver.\{0\} V} has \texttt{Hom : V $\to$ V $\to$ Prop},\dots
n21664.content:
\begin{definition}[The bridge \texttt{Digraph $\to$ Quiver}: \texttt{Quiver.\{0\} V} has \texttt{Hom : V $\to$ V $\to$ Prop},\dots]
\lean{Digraph.toQuiver}
\label{Digraph.toQuiver}
\leanok
A quiver is a vertex set together with, for each ordered pair, a
\emph{type} of arrows.  Taking that type to be a \texttt{Prop} --- arrow or no arrow --- recovers
exactly a digraph, and Mathlib's \texttt{Quiver.Path} then supplies directed walks for
free, which \texttt{Digraph} (a bare \texttt{Adj} with a lattice API) does not.

\textbf{!} Deliberately \textbf{not} an \texttt{instance}.  The chapter routinely
handles several digraphs on one vertex type at once --- $D$ and its converse $\breve{D}$,
$D$ and a reorientation of one arc (exercise 10.2.1) --- and a global instance would
make \texttt{Quiver.Path} ambiguous between them.  The cost is that every use site must
write \texttt{@Quiver.Path V D.toQuiver u v} explicitly, which is why the statements below
are visually heavy.
\end{definition}

n21665.title: A directed path: a \texttt{Quiver.Path} with no repeated vertex
n21665.content:
\begin{definition}[A directed path: a \texttt{Quiver.Path} with no repeated vertex]
\lean{Digraph.IsDirectedPath}
\label{Digraph.IsDirectedPath}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.toQuiver}
Follow the arrows, never against them; a directed path additionally
never revisits a vertex.  The book stresses (figure 10.3) that there is *no close
relationship between the lengths of paths and directed paths in a digraph* --- the
digraph there has arbitrarily long paths but no directed path of length above one.
Theorem 10.1 is remarkable precisely because it recovers control of directed-path
length from the chromatic number.

\textbf{!} \texttt{Quiver.Path} \textbf{is} the directed walk, so a directed path is
a \texttt{Quiver.Path} with \texttt{Nodup} vertices.  Note the book's directed walks are
\emph{non-null}, whereas \texttt{Quiver.Path.nil} is available here; that mismatch is harmless
for paths but bites for Euler tours (see \texttt{IsDirectedEulerTour}).
\end{definition}

n21666.title: A directed cycle: a positive-length closed walk whose vertices (bar the repeated endpoint) are distinct
n21666.content:
\begin{definition}[A directed cycle: a positive-length closed walk whose vertices (bar the repeated endpoint) are distinct]
\lean{Digraph.IsDirectedCycle}
\label{Digraph.IsDirectedCycle}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.toQuiver}
Follow the arrows all the way round and return to where you started,
never repeating a vertex en route.  Directed cycles are the subject of \S{}10.3: Moon
(theorem 10.3) finds them of every length in a diconnected tournament, and
Ghouila-Houri (theorem 10.4) finds a spanning one under a degree condition.

\texttt{0 < length} excludes \texttt{nil}; \texttt{vertices.tail.Nodup} allows the
repeated basepoint at the two ends while forbidding any other repeat.  Note a
\textbf{loop} \texttt{D.Adj v v} counts as a directed cycle of length $1$ under this
definition, which is what makes the acyclicity hypotheses below (\texttt{hacyc})
automatically exclude loops --- relied on by \texttt{exists\_topological\_ordering}.
\end{definition}

n21667.title: $v$ is reachable from $u$
n21667.content:
\begin{definition}[$v$ is reachable from $u$]
\lean{Digraph.Reachable}
\label{Digraph.Reachable}
\leanok
You can get from $u$ to $v$ travelling only along arrows in their
given direction.  Reachability is \emph{not} symmetric --- that asymmetry is the whole
point of directing a graph, and is what makes diconnection a strictly stronger
condition than connection.

\texttt{Relation.ReflTransGen D.Adj} rather than an existential over
\texttt{Quiver.Path}.  The two agree (a path witnesses reachability and conversely), but
\texttt{ReflTransGen} comes with induction principles and is \emph{reflexive}, matching the
book's convention that every vertex reaches itself.  Being defined directly from
\texttt{Adj}, it needs no \texttt{Quiver} instance, so $D$ and \texttt{D.converse} coexist freely ---
which \texttt{converse\_reachable} relies on.
\end{definition}

n21668.title: $D$ is diconnected: every vertex reaches every other
n21668.content:
\begin{definition}[$D$ is diconnected: every vertex reaches every other]
\lean{Digraph.Diconnected}
\label{Digraph.Diconnected}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.Reachable}
Wherever you start and wherever you want to go, some route respecting
the arrows exists.  In the road-network reading of \S{}10.6 this is exactly the
condition that a one-way system lets traffic flow freely --- every junction remains
reachable from every other, and Robbins' theorem 10.5 says $2$-edge-connectivity is
precisely what makes it achievable.

Stated directly as "every ordered pair is reachable" rather
than via dicomponents, which avoids constructing the quotient.  The two agree: one
dicomponent means the equivalence relation is total.  Note this is \emph{not} symmetric
by fiat --- \texttt{$\forall$ u v, Reachable u v} quantifies over ordered pairs, so both directions
are demanded.
\end{definition}

n21669.title: $d^{-}(v)$, the indegree
n21669.content:
\begin{definition}[$d^{-}(v)$, the indegree]
\lean{Digraph.indegree}
\label{Digraph.indegree}
\leanok
How many arrows point \emph{into} $v$.  Exercise 10.1.2 gives the directed
handshake lemma $\sum d^{-}(v) = \varepsilon = \sum d^{+}(v)$ --- each arc is counted once by its head and
once by its tail, which is why the directed sum is $\varepsilon$ and not $2\varepsilon$.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib (0 hits).  Counts \emph{vertices} $u$ with
\texttt{D.Adj u v}, not arcs --- the same thing here, since \texttt{Digraph} is a bare relation and
admits no parallel arcs.  Needs \texttt{[DecidableRel D.Adj]} for the \texttt{filter}.
\end{definition}

n21670.title: $d^{+}(v)$, the outdegree
n21670.content:
\begin{definition}[$d^{+}(v)$, the outdegree]
\lean{Digraph.outdegree}
\label{Digraph.outdegree}
\leanok
How many arrows point \emph{out of} $v$.  Together with the indegree this
refines the single degree of an undirected graph into two numbers, and their
interplay drives most of the chapter: Euler tours need them equal (exercise
10.3.2), Ghouila-Houri's theorem 10.4 needs both large, and exercise 10.1.10 asks
for an orientation making them nearly equal everywhere.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  The exact mirror of \texttt{indegree} under
\texttt{converse}, which is the content of exercise 10.1.5(a)(ii).
\end{definition}

n21671.title: $\varepsilon$, the number of arcs
n21671.content:
\begin{definition}[$\varepsilon$, the number of arcs]
\lean{Digraph.arcCount}
\label{Digraph.arcCount}
\leanok
Count the ordered pairs $(u, v)$ for which an arc runs from $u$ to
$v$.  This is the $\varepsilon$ of exercise 10.1.2's handshake lemma and of exercise 10.1.1's
$2^\varepsilon$ orientation count.

Since \texttt{Digraph} allows no parallel arcs in the same direction,
$\varepsilon$ is simply the size of the adjacency relation, counted as a \texttt{Finset (V $\times$ V)}.
Note this differs from the book for multi-digraphs, which B\&M permit --- a point that
also forces the restatement of \texttt{adjMatrix} below.
\end{definition}

n21672.title: $\delta^{-}$, the minimum indegree
n21672.content:
\begin{definition}[$\delta^{-}$, the minimum indegree]
\lean{Digraph.minIndegree}
\label{Digraph.minIndegree}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.indegree}
The least number of arrows pointing into any one vertex.  Exercise
10.1.3(a) says an acyclic digraph must have $\delta^{-} = 0$, which is what makes
topological ordering possible; exercises 10.1.6--10.1.7 turn a large $\delta^{-}$ into long
directed paths and cycles.

\textbf{!} $\bigsqcap$ over $\mathbb{N}$ is \texttt{Nat.sInf}, and \texttt{Nat.sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}, so on an
empty carrier this silently returns $0$ rather than being undefined.  Every use
site below carries \texttt{[Nonempty V]} for that reason.  Only the \emph{minima} are defined
here; $\Delta^{-}$, $\Delta^{+}$ are never needed by a surviving statement.
\end{definition}

n21673.title: $\delta^{+}$, the minimum outdegree

n21674.title: The converse $\breve{D}$: reverse every arc
n21674.content:
\begin{definition}[The converse $\breve{D}$: reverse every arc]
\lean{Digraph.converse}
\label{Digraph.converse}
\leanok
Turn every arrow around.  It is an involution ($\breve{\breve{D}} = D$), it swaps
indegree with outdegree, and it reverses reachability --- so every theorem about
digraphs comes with a free dual, obtained by applying it to the converse.  Exercise
10.1.5(a) records exactly these three facts and (b) puts them to work.

A one-line \texttt{Digraph.mk} with the arguments of \texttt{Adj} swapped, so
\texttt{converse\_converse} should be \texttt{rfl}-adjacent.  Because \texttt{Reachable} is defined from
\texttt{Adj} and not through a \texttt{Quiver} instance, $D$ and \texttt{D.converse} can appear in the
same statement without ambiguity --- see \texttt{converse\_reachable}.
\end{definition}

n21675.title: $D$ is strict: loopless (\texttt{Digraph} already forbids parallel same-direction arcs)
n21675.content:
\begin{definition}[$D$ is strict: loopless (\texttt{Digraph} already forbids parallel same-direction arcs)]
\lean{Digraph.IsStrict}
\label{Digraph.IsStrict}
\leanok
The directed analogue of "simple".  Note a strict digraph \emph{may} have
both $(u,v)$ and $(v,u)$ --- forbidding that is what makes an orientation, which is a
strictly stronger condition.  Strictness is the standing hypothesis of exercises
10.1.6, 10.1.7 and theorem 10.4, where it guarantees that $\delta^{+}$ out-neighbours are
$\delta^{+}$ genuinely \emph{distinct} vertices.

Since \texttt{Digraph} is a bare relation it already forbids repeated
arcs in the same direction, so the book's second clause is automatic and strictness
reduces to looplessness --- \texttt{Irreflexive D.Adj}.
\end{definition}

n21676.title: $D$ is an orientation of $G$ --- the chapter's keystone gap
n21676.content:
\begin{definition}[$D$ is an orientation of $G$ --- the chapter's keystone gap]
\lean{Digraph.IsOrientationOf}
\label{Digraph.IsOrientationOf}
\leanok
Make every edge one-way, choosing a direction for each.  Orientations
are the chapter's central object: exercise 10.1.1 counts them ($2^\varepsilon$), the remark
after theorem 10.1 builds one whose directed paths are short, exercise 10.1.10 one
that is degree-balanced, and \S{}10.6 asks which graphs admit \emph{diconnected} ones ---
Robbins' theorem 10.5.

Two clauses.  The first, \texttt{D.toSimpleGraphInclusive = G}, says
the underlying graph comes back out as $G$.  The second,
\texttt{$\forall$ u v, $\lnot$(D.Adj u v $\land$ D.Adj v u)}, forbids making an edge two-way --- without it the
associated digraph $D(G)$ would count as an orientation of $G$, which it is not.
Taking $u = v$ in the second clause also forces looplessness, so an orientation is
automatically strict.
\end{definition}

n21677.title: $D$ is a tournament: an orientation of the complete graph
n21677.content:
\begin{definition}[$D$ is a tournament: an orientation of the complete graph]
\lean{Digraph.IsTournament}
\label{Digraph.IsTournament}
\leanok
Every pair of players meets exactly once and the arrow points from
winner to loser.  Tournaments are remarkably well behaved: every one has a directed
Hamilton path (R\'edei, corollary 10.1) and a "king" reaching everyone in at most two
steps (corollary 10.2); diconnected ones are vertex-pancyclic (Moon, theorem 10.3)
and hence have directed Hamilton cycles (Camion).  \S{}10.7 uses them to rank players.

Unfolded rather than defined as "\texttt{IsOrientationOf} some
complete graph": \texttt{Irreflexive D.Adj} plus, for distinct $u$, $v$, exactly one of
\texttt{D.Adj u v}, \texttt{D.Adj v u}.  The $\leftrightarrow \lnot$ phrasing packs both "at least one" (from
completeness of the underlying graph) and "at most one" (from being an orientation)
into a single clause.
\end{definition}

n21678.title: B\&M's $(S, T)$: arcs with tail in $S$, head in $T$
n21678.content:
\begin{definition}[B\&M's $(S, T)$: arcs with tail in $S$, head in $T$]
\lean{Digraph.arcsBetween}
\label{Digraph.arcsBetween}
\leanok
The arcs crossing from $S$ into $T$, counted with their direction.
Unlike the undirected edge cut $[S, \bar{S}]$, the directed version splits into two
generally \emph{unequal} halves $(S, \bar{S})$ and $(\bar{S}, S)$ --- which is precisely what
$k$-arc-connectivity measures, and what theorem 10.6 has to balance.

A \texttt{Finset (V $\times$ V)} obtained by filtering the product $S \times^{s} T$,
so $|(S, T)|$ is its \texttt{card}.  Used in \texttt{IsKArcConnected} and in Moon's theorem 10.3,
where the book's "$(S, T)$ must be nonempty" becomes a cardinality claim.
\end{definition}

n21679.title: $D$ is $k$-arc-connected: every nonempty proper cut has $\ge k$ outgoing arcs
n21679.content:
\begin{definition}[$D$ is $k$-arc-connected: every nonempty proper cut has $\ge k$ outgoing arcs]
\lean{Digraph.IsKArcConnected}
\label{Digraph.IsKArcConnected}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.arcsBetween}
However you split the vertices in two, at least $k$ arrows point from
the first part to the second.  Exercise 10.3.5 says $1$-arc-connected is the same
as diconnected, and exercise 10.3.6(b) that $D(G)$ is $k$-arc-connected exactly when
$G$ is $k$-edge-connected.  Nash-Williams' theorem --- of which theorem 10.6 is the
easy special case --- says every $2k$-edge-connected graph has a $k$-arc-connected
orientation.

\textbf{!} The book says \textbf{nontrivial} digraph, and this definition
drops that.  On a one-vertex carrier there is no nonempty proper $S$, so the
condition is vacuously true for \emph{every} $k$ --- which is why statements consuming it
must supply \texttt{[Nontrivial V]} themselves.  \texttt{diconnected\_iff\_isKArcConnected\_one}
does; \texttt{associatedDigraph\_isKArcConnected\_iff} does not, and is false in consequence
(see its docstring).
\end{definition}

n21680.title: The induced subdigraph on $S$ (kept on the same carrier to avoid subtype juggling)
n21680.content:
\begin{definition}[The induced subdigraph on $S$ (kept on the same carrier to avoid subtype juggling)]
\lean{Digraph.induce}
\label{Digraph.induce}
\leanok
Keep only the vertices in $S$ and the arcs with both ends there.  The
dicomponents of $D$ are the induced subdigraphs $D[V_{i}]$ on the diconnection classes,
and theorem 10.2's induction removes ${v} \cup N^{+}(v)$ this way.

Kept on the \textbf{same carrier} $V$, with membership in $S$ folded
into \texttt{Adj}, rather than moving to a subtype.  This avoids subtype juggling across
the many statements that induce, at the cost that \texttt{induce D S} has isolated
vertices outside $S$ --- harmless, since every consumer only asks about arcs.
\end{definition}

n21681.title: The list of arcs traversed by a directed walk
n21681.content:
\begin{definition}[The list of arcs traversed by a directed walk]
\lean{Digraph.arcsOf}
\label{Digraph.arcsOf}
\uses{Digraph.toQuiver}
Reading off the arrows a directed walk uses, in order.  This is what a
\emph{trail} condition quantifies over --- a directed trail repeats no arc --- and what a
directed Euler tour must exhaust.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: this definition has a \texttt{sorry} body.}  It is declared
\texttt{List (V $\times$ V) := sorry}, so \texttt{arcsOf} is an \emph{opaque, unspecified} function, not the
arc list of anything.  This is the most damaging defect in the file, because the
opacity propagates:
\item \texttt{IsDirectedTrail} and \texttt{IsDirectedEulerTour} are defined from it, so both are
  meaningless as stated;
\item and therefore \texttt{exists\_directedEulerTour\_iff} (exercise 10.3.2),
  \texttt{deBruijnDigraph\_exists\_directedEulerTour} and \texttt{exists\_arcDisjoint\_directedPaths}
  (exercise 10.3.3) say nothing --- which is the entire \S{}10.5 computer-drum
  application plus the flow precursor to chapter 11.
\emph{ It also violates the project convention (\texttt{.claude/CLAUDE.md}): }never \texttt{sorry} in
  a \texttt{def}* --- a \texttt{sorry}-ed proof is an honest debt, a \texttt{sorry}-ed definition is a
  silent change of meaning.

\emph{The repair} is a routine structural recursion on \texttt{Quiver.Path}, whose two
constructors are \texttt{nil : Path a a} and \texttt{cons : Path a b $\to$ (b ⟶ c) $\to$ Path a c}:

    arcsOf nil        = []
    arcsOf (cons p e) = arcsOf p ++ [(b, c)]

with $b$, $c$ the source and target of the arrow $e$.  Nothing about it is
delicate; the outline simply left it unspecified.  This is a change of \emph{meaning},
not of annotation, so it has been flagged rather than made here.
\end{definition}

n21682.title: A directed trail: no repeated arc

n21683.title: A directed Euler tour: a closed directed trail using every arc

n21684.title: $D$ is unilateral: any two vertices are comparable by reachability

n21685.title: The 0/1 adjacency matrix of $D$
n21685.content:
\begin{definition}[The 0/1 adjacency matrix of $D$]
\lean{Digraph.adjMatrix}
\label{Digraph.adjMatrix}
\leanok
Record a $1$ where an arrow runs from $v_{i}$ to $v_{j}$ and $0$ otherwise.
Unlike the undirected case (\S{}1.3) this matrix is \emph{not} symmetric --- its asymmetry
encodes the orientations.  Exercise 10.1.8 shows $A^{k}$ counts directed walks of
length $k$, and \S{}10.7 uses the powers of $A$ to rank tournament players via the
level score vectors $s_{i} = A^{i}J$.

\textbf{!} Restated: \texttt{Digraph} has no arc multiplicities, so entries are
$0$ or $1$ rather than a count.  For strict digraphs --- which every \S{}10.7 statement
is about, tournaments being orientations --- the two agree, so nothing is lost where
it is used.  The value type $\alpha$ is left generic so the same matrix serves the
$\mathbb{N}$-valued counting of exercise 10.1.8 and any later numeric work.
\end{definition}

n21686.title: The condensation $\hat{D}$: dicomponents contracted
n21686.content:
\begin{definition}[The condensation $\hat{D}$: dicomponents contracted]
\lean{Digraph.condensation}
\label{Digraph.condensation}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.toQuiver}
Shrink each dicomponent to a single point and keep the arcs between
them.  Exercise 10.1.9 shows the condensation is \emph{acyclic} --- a directed cycle among
dicomponents would merge them into one --- so by exercise 10.1.3(b) the dicomponents
can be topologically ordered, which is what \S{}10.7 uses to rank the participants of a
non-diconnected tournament, and what exercise 10.2.1 uses on tournaments.

\textbf{!} The $a \ne b$ clause is a \textbf{recorded correction}, not a
transcription.  Taken literally the book's condition puts an arc from $w_{i}$ to $w_{i}$
whenever $D_{i}$ has any internal arc --- a loop at every non-trivial dicomponent --- which
would make \texttt{condensation\_acyclic} false, since a loop is a directed cycle of length
$1$.  B\&M plainly intend $i \ne j$.

The vertex type is \texttt{Quiver.StronglyConnectedComponent}, Mathlib's quotient by mutual
reachability, which is exactly the set of dicomponents.
\end{definition}

n21687.title: dirDist
n21687.content:
\begin{definition}[dirDist]
\lean{Digraph.dirDist}
\label{Digraph.dirDist}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.toQuiver}
$\vec{d}(u,v)$. \textbf{!} \texttt{Nat.sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} when $v$ is unreachable from $u$.

The fewest arrows you must follow to get from $u$ to $v$.  Unlike the
undirected distance of \S{}1.6 this is \emph{not symmetric} --- $\vec{d}(u,v)$ and $\vec{d}(v,u)$ may
differ, which is the whole reason \S{}10.7 needs $d + 3$ rather than something
symmetric.

\textbf{!} \texttt{Nat.sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}, so an unreachable $v$ gets distance $0$
rather than $\infty$.  The definition is therefore faithful only on diconnected
digraphs --- which is exactly where the book defines it, and both consumers
(\texttt{tournament\_adjMatrix\_pow\_pos}, \texttt{dirDiameter}) carry \texttt{hdicon}.  Minimising over
\texttt{Quiver.Path} lengths rather than over \texttt{Reachable} witnesses, since the \emph{length} is
what is wanted.
\end{definition}

n21688.title: dirDiameter
n21688.content:
\begin{definition}[dirDiameter]
\lean{Digraph.dirDiameter}
\label{Digraph.dirDiameter}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.dirDist}
The worst case of the directed distance --- how far apart two vertices
can be when you must respect the arrows.  Theorem 10.7 shows that for a diconnected
tournament on at least five vertices $A^{d+3}$ is entrywise positive, where $d$ is
this diameter, and corollary 10.7 turns that into the primitivity that makes the
\S{}10.7 ranking method converge.

A \texttt{Finset.sup} over all ordered pairs, so the diagonal $\vec{d}(v,v) = 0$
is included harmlessly.  Inherits \texttt{dirDist}'s \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} caveat: on a
non-diconnected digraph the diameter is silently too small.
\end{definition}

n21689.title: The associated digraph $D(G)$: each edge becomes two opposite arcs. \texttt{G.Adj} is already symmetric,\dots
n21689.content:
\begin{definition}[The associated digraph $D(G)$: each edge becomes two opposite arcs. \texttt{G.Adj} is already symmetric,\dots]
\lean{SimpleGraph.associatedDigraph}
\label{SimpleGraph.associatedDigraph}
\leanok
Make every street two-way.  This embeds undirected graph theory inside
directed graph theory: exercise 10.3.6 shows paths in $G$ correspond exactly to
directed paths in $D(G)$, and $D(G)$ is $k$-arc-connected exactly when $G$ is
$k$-edge-connected.  Exercise 10.3.1 uses the embedding to derive Dirac's theorem
4.3 from Ghouila-Houri's 10.4.

One line: \texttt{G.Adj} is already symmetric and irreflexive, so it
\emph{is} the arc relation of $D(G)$ --- the "two oppositely oriented arcs" are the two
directions of the symmetric relation.  Note $D(G)$ is emphatically \textbf{not} an
orientation of $G$ (\texttt{IsOrientationOf}'s second clause fails at every edge); the
contrast between doubling and orienting is exactly what \S{}10.6 is about.
\end{definition}

n21690.title: A primitive $\mathbb{N}$-matrix: some power is entrywise positive
n21690.content:
\begin{definition}[A primitive $\mathbb{N}$-matrix: some power is entrywise positive]
\lean{Matrix.IsPrimitive}
\label{Matrix.IsPrimitive}
\leanok
For the adjacency matrix this says: however you pick a starting and
finishing vertex, there is a directed walk of some \emph{common} length $k$ between them.
Corollary 10.7 characterises when a tournament's matrix is primitive --- exactly when
the tournament is diconnected with $\nu \ge 4$.  Primitivity is what licenses
Perron--Frobenius, which gives the convergence of the iterated score vectors
$s_{i} = A^{i}J$ used to rank the players.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib (0 hits).  Stated for \texttt{Matrix n n $\mathbb{N}$}
rather than the book's \emph{real} matrices, since the only instance needed is the
adjacency matrix; $0 < (R ^ k) i j$ is then the entrywise positivity $R^{k} > 0$.  Note
Mathlib's \texttt{Matrix} order is not entrywise by default, which is why the positivity is
spelled pointwise.
\end{definition}

n21691.title: The de Bruijn digraph $D_n$: vertices are $(n-1)$-bit strings, arcs are left-shifts
n21691.content:
\begin{definition}[The de Bruijn digraph $D_n$: vertices are $(n-1)$-bit strings, arcs are left-shifts]
\lean{deBruijnDigraph}
\label{deBruijnDigraph}
\leanok
A vertex is a window of $n-1$ bits; following an arc shifts the window
one place, dropping the leading bit and appending a new one.  Each arc therefore
corresponds to an $n$-bit string --- its label --- and a directed Euler tour reads off
every $n$-bit string exactly once, giving a cyclic binary sequence of length $2^{n}$ in
which all $2^{n}$ windows are distinct.

\emph{The application (\S{}10.5).}  A rotating drum's surface is divided into $2^{n}$
insulating or conducting sections, read by $k$ consecutive contacts.  *First note
that $k$ contacts yield a $k$-digit binary number, and there are $2^{k}$ such numbers.
Therefore, if all $2^{n}$ positions are to give different readings, we must have
$2^{k} \ge 2^{n}$, that is, $k \ge n$* --- and the de Bruijn sequence shows $n$ contacts
suffice.  For $n = 4$ the tour of figure 10.10 gives $0000111100101101$.  Due to
Good (1946).

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib and the Archive (0 hits).  A vertex is a
function \texttt{Fin (n-1) $\to$ Bool} rather than a list, so the shift condition is indexed:
\texttt{p ⟨i+1, \_⟩ = q i} for every $i$ with $i + 1 < n - 1$, which is the book's
$1 \le i \le n-2$ in 0-indexed form.  The last coordinate of $q$ is unconstrained, giving
the two out-arcs.  $D_n$ has \textbf{loops} (the all-zeros and all-ones vertices) but no
parallel arcs --- so it is not strict, which is fine, as no \S{}10.5 statement needs
strictness.  Arc labels are not modelled: the label is recoverable from the arc, and
\texttt{exists\_deBruijn\_sequence} states the conclusion about the sequence directly.
\end{definition}

n21695.title: exists\_topological\_ordering
n21695.content:
\begin{theorem}[exists\_topological\_ordering]
\lean{exists_topological_ordering}
\label{exists_topological_ordering}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedCycle, Digraph.toQuiver}
A \textbf{topological ordering}: line the vertices up so every arrow points
forwards.  Greedy construction via part (a) --- take a source, delete it, repeat.
These are the standard tool for scheduling tasks with prerequisites, and \S{}10.7 uses
the version for the \emph{condensation} of a tournament to order its dicomponents in a
way that preserves dominance.

The book's "every arc with head $v_{i}$ has its tail among the
earlier vertices" is contraposed into the equivalent and more usable
\texttt{D.Adj u v $\to$ f u < f v}.  Note no \texttt{[Nonempty V]} is needed here, unlike part (a) ---
the empty case is the induction's base.
\end{theorem}

n21698.title: converse\_reachable
n21698.content:
\begin{theorem}[converse\_reachable]
\lean{converse_reachable}
\label{converse_reachable}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.Reachable, Digraph.converse}
A directed path from $u$ to $v$ in the converse is exactly a directed
path from $v$ to $u$ in $D$, read backwards.  A useful consequence: diconnection is
\emph{self-dual} --- $D$ is diconnected exactly when $\breve{D}$ is --- since diconnection demands
reachability both ways.

This is the one place where defining \texttt{Reachable} as
\texttt{ReflTransGen} rather than via \texttt{Quiver.Path} pays off directly: no \texttt{Quiver} instance
is in play, so $D$ and \texttt{D.converse} appear in the same statement without
ambiguity.
\end{theorem}

n21699.title: exists\_outdegree\_zero\_of\_acyclic
n21699.content:
\begin{theorem}[exists\_outdegree\_zero\_of\_acyclic]
\lean{exists_outdegree_zero_of_acyclic}
\label{exists_outdegree_zero_of_acyclic}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedCycle, Digraph.outdegree, Digraph.toQuiver}
An acyclic digraph has both a "source" (nothing in) and a "sink"
(nothing out), which is what lets topological ordering be built from either end.
The point of the exercise is methodological: the converse converts one statement
into its dual with no new argument.

Step 1 needs a \texttt{Quiver.Path} reversal for \texttt{D.converse} versus
$D$; since \texttt{toQuiver} is not an instance, both quivers must be named explicitly.
Worth extracting as a standalone lemma, as \texttt{converse\_reachable} is the same fact one
level down.
\end{theorem}

n21702.title: adjMatrix\_pow\_apply\_eq\_card\_directedWalk
n21702.content:
\begin{theorem}[adjMatrix\_pow\_apply\_eq\_card\_directedWalk]
\lean{adjMatrix_pow_apply_eq_card_directedWalk}
\label{adjMatrix_pow_apply_eq_card_directedWalk}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.adjMatrix, Digraph.toQuiver}
The $(i,j)$ entry of $A$ counts arcs, i.e. walks of length one; matrix
multiplication sums over an intermediate vertex, and every walk of length $k$
decomposes uniquely as a shorter walk plus a final arc.  This is the directed
counterpart of exercise 1.6.2, and it is what makes \S{}10.7's ranking work: the
$i$-th level score vector is $A^{i}J$, counting directed walks of length $i$ out of
each player.  Theorem 10.7 consumes it directly.

\textbf{!} Restated for a $0/1$ matrix, \texttt{Digraph} having no arc
multiplicities; for the strict digraphs of \S{}10.7 this is no loss.  The right-hand
side is \texttt{Nat.card} of a subtype of \texttt{Quiver.Path}, which is finite because the length
is pinned --- but that finiteness may need to be supplied for \texttt{Nat.card} to behave.
\end{theorem}

n21703.title: condensation\_acyclic
n21703.content:
\begin{theorem}[condensation\_acyclic]
\lean{condensation_acyclic}
\label{condensation_acyclic}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedCycle, Digraph.condensation, Digraph.toQuiver}
A directed cycle among dicomponents would merge them into one, so
contracting always produces an acyclic digraph --- which by exercise 10.1.3(b) can be
topologically ordered.  \S{}10.7 uses exactly this to rank the dicomponents of a
non-diconnected tournament in a dominance-preserving order, and exercise 10.2.1 uses
it on tournaments.

Step 3 is where \texttt{Quiver.StronglyConnectedComponent}'s defining
property is consumed; the useful form is "same component $\leftrightarrow$ mutually reachable",
which should be extracted first.  Note the statement quantifies over all base points
$c$, since \texttt{IsDirectedCycle} is stated for closed paths at a given vertex.
\end{theorem}

n21704.title: exists\_balanced\_orientation
n21704.content:
\begin{theorem}[exists\_balanced\_orientation]
\lean{exists_balanced_orientation}
\label{exists_balanced_orientation}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsOrientationOf, Digraph.indegree, Digraph.outdegree}
Every graph can be made one-way in a \emph{balanced} way, with the traffic
into and out of each junction differing by at most one.  Contrast exercise 10.6.1,
which shows the stronger set-wise balance --- $||(S, \bar{S})| - |(\bar{S}, S)|| \le 1$ for every
vertex \emph{set} $S$ --- is \textbf{not} always achievable, the Petersen graph being a
counterexample.

The conclusion is stated as two $\mathbb{Z}$ inequalities rather than
$|\cdot| \le 1$, avoiding \texttt{Int.natAbs} juggling.  The \texttt{open scoped Classical in} supplies
decidability of the existentially-bound \texttt{D.Adj}; the outline's
\texttt{$\exists$ \_ : DecidableRel D.Adj} does not register as an instance inside the body, which
is why it was replaced.
\end{theorem}

n21705.title: roy\_gallai\_directed\_path
n21705.content:
\begin{theorem}[roy\_gallai\_directed\_path]
\lean{roy_gallai_directed_path}
\label{roy_gallai_directed_path}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedPath, Digraph.toQuiver}
(Roy, 1967; Gallai, 1968).  *A digraph $D$ contains a directed
path of length $\chi - 1$*, where $\chi$ is the chromatic number of the underlying
graph.

Striking because, as figure 10.3 shows, there is otherwise *no close
relationship between the lengths of paths and directed paths in a digraph* --- yet the
chromatic number of the underlying graph controls the latter exactly.  The remark
following shows the bound is best possible.

$k - 1$ is $\mathbb{N}$-subtraction, harmless as the goal is a lower bound.
$hk$ pins $\chi$ of \texttt{toSimpleGraphInclusive} --- the underlying graph --- to $k$ in $\mathbb{N}\infty$.
Step 4 is the mathematical core; steps 1 and 2 are both "choose a maximum/minimum in
a finite nonempty family" and should share a helper.
\end{theorem}

n21706.title: exists\_orientation\_longest\_directedPath\_le
n21706.content:
\begin{theorem}[exists\_orientation\_longest\_directedPath\_le]
\lean{exists_orientation_longest_directedPath_le}
\label{exists_orientation_longest_directedPath_le}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedPath, Digraph.IsOrientationOf, Digraph.toQuiver}
Orient every edge from the lower colour class to the higher.  Along a
directed path the colour index strictly increases, so the path has at most $\chi$
vertices.  Combined with theorem 10.1 this shows $\chi - 1$ is exactly the right
bound.  Note the orientation is automatically acyclic, the colour index being a
topological ordering --- so this also witnesses exercise 10.1.3(b) in reverse.

Stated with an arbitrary $k$-colouring rather than an optimal
one, which is the usable form: exercise 10.2.6(a) instantiates it at $k = \Delta + 1$
via corollary 8.1.2, not at $k = \chi$.  Step 4's injectivity is a cleaner invariant
to carry than the book's "no two vertices share a colour".
\end{theorem}

n21707.title: redei\_directed\_hamilton\_path
n21707.content:
\begin{theorem}[redei\_directed\_hamilton\_path]
\lean{redei_directed_hamilton_path}
\label{redei_directed_hamilton_path}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedPath, Digraph.IsTournament, Digraph.toQuiver}
(R\'edei, 1934).  *Every tournament has a directed Hamilton
path.*

B\&M define the term just above: *A directed Hamilton path of $D$ is a directed path
that includes every vertex of $D$.*

In any round-robin competition the players can be lined up so that
each beat the next.  The book cautions in \S{}10.7 that this does \emph{not} give a sensible
ranking, since a tournament generally has many directed Hamilton paths --- the
six-player example has $(3,1,2,4,5,6)$, $(1,2,4,5,6,3)$, $(1,4,6,3,2,5)$ and others,
declaring different winners.  That is what motivates the eigenvector method.

"Includes every vertex" is \texttt{$\forall$ w, w $\in$ p.vertices} rather than a
cardinality claim, which is what step 3 delivers most directly.  Exercise 10.2.3
gives an independent route not passing through theorem 10.1.
\end{theorem}

n21708.title: chvatal\_lovasz\_semikernel
n21708.content:
\begin{theorem}[chvatal\_lovasz\_semikernel]
\lean{chvatal_lovasz_semikernel}
\label{chvatal_lovasz_semikernel}
\leanok
(Chv\'atal and Lov\'asz, 1974).  *A loopless digraph $D$ has an
independent set $S$ such that each vertex of $D$ not in $S$ is reachable from a
vertex in $S$ by a directed path of length at most two.*

Such a set is called a \textbf{semi-kernel}.  The independence requirement
is what makes it non-trivial --- one wants mutually non-adjacent "dominators" from
which everything else is within two steps.  Corollary 10.2 is the tournament case,
where independence forces $|S| = 1$.

The $u = v$ disjunct in the goal covers the reflexive case and is
not in the book, which says "each vertex \emph{not in} $S$"; it is harmless and makes the
statement easier to instantiate.  \texttt{hloop : Irreflexive D.Adj} is B\&M's "loopless".
\texttt{IsIndepSet} is taken in \texttt{toSimpleGraphInclusive}, matching "independent set" for the
underlying graph.
\end{theorem}

n21709.title: tournament\_exists\_king
n21709.content:
\begin{theorem}[tournament\_exists\_king]
\lean{tournament_exists_king}
\label{tournament_exists_king}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsTournament}
*A tournament contains a vertex from which every other
vertex is reachable by a directed path of length at most two.*

Such a vertex is called a \textbf{king}: a player who, for every other
player $v$, either beat $v$ directly or beat someone who beat $v$.  Exercise 10.2.4
gives a direct proof --- take a vertex of maximum outdegree --- which is dropped from
this file as a second proof of the same statement.  Note a king need not have won
the most games, and a tournament may have several kings.

\texttt{[Nonempty V]} is load-bearing for step 3; without it $S = \emptyset$ is
a legitimate semi-kernel and no $u$ exists.
\end{theorem}
