n21712.title: tournament\_maximal\_directedPath\_insert
n21712.content:
\begin{theorem}[tournament\_maximal\_directedPath\_insert]
\lean{tournament_maximal_directedPath_insert}
\label{tournament_maximal_directedPath_insert}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsTournament}
*Let $P = (v_{1}, \dots, v_k)$ be a maximal directed path in a
tournament $D$.  Suppose $P$ is not a directed Hamilton path and let $v$ be any
vertex not on $P$.  Then for some $i$, both $(v_{i}, v)$ and $(v, v_{i+1})$ are arcs
of $D$.*

Because $D$ is a tournament, $v$ is joined to every vertex of $P$ in
one direction or the other; maximality forces $v_{1} \to v$ at the start and
$v \to v_k$ at the end, so travelling along $P$ the direction must switch somewhere.
Part (b) --- dropped here, being a re-derivation of corollary 10.1 --- inserts $v$ at
that point to get a longer directed path and repeats until it spans.

The path is presented as a \texttt{List V} with \texttt{IsChain D.Adj} rather
than as a \texttt{Quiver.Path}, since the statement indexes into it ($l[i]$, $l[i+1]$) and
lists index far more comfortably.  \texttt{[Inhabited V]} supports \texttt{head!}/\texttt{getLast!} in
\texttt{hmax}; \texttt{hne : l $\ne$ []} keeps those meaningful.
\end{theorem}

n21713.title: chvatal\_komlos\_monotone\_directedPath
n21713.content:
\begin{theorem}[chvatal\_komlos\_monotone\_directedPath]
\lean{chvatal_komlos_monotone_directedPath}
\label{chvatal_komlos_monotone_directedPath}
\leanok
\emph{ (Chv\'atal and Koml\'os).  }Let $D$ be a digraph with
$\chi > mn$, and let $f$ be a real-valued function on $V$.  Then $D$ has either a
directed path $(u_{0}, \dots, u_m)$ with $f(u_{0}) \le f(u_{1}) \le \dots \le f(u_m)$, or a directed path
$(v_{0}, \dots, v_n)$ with $f(v_{0}) > f(v_{1}) > \dots > f(v_n)$.*

Theorem 10.1 says a high chromatic number forces a long directed path;
this refines it by controlling how $f$ behaves along that path.  A large enough
chromatic number forces a \emph{monotone} directed path --- weakly increasing of length
$m$, or strictly decreasing of length $n$.  Part (b) reads off Erd\H{o}s--Szekeres.

Paths are \texttt{List V} with two \texttt{IsChain}s --- one for adjacency, one
for the $f$-comparison --- plus \texttt{Nodup}, rather than \texttt{Quiver.Path}s, so that the
monotonicity condition can be stated alongside.  Note the asymmetry $\le$ versus $>$
is the book's and is essential: with two weak orders step 3 would fail on an arc
where $f u = f w$.
\end{theorem}

n21714.title: erdos\_szekeres\_of\_chvatal\_komlos
n21714.content:
\begin{theorem}[erdos\_szekeres\_of\_chvatal\_komlos]
\lean{erdos_szekeres_of_chvatal_komlos}
\label{erdos_szekeres_of_chvatal_komlos}
\leanok
\emph{ (Erd\H{o}s and Szekeres).  }Deduce that any sequence of
$mn + 1$ distinct integers contains either an increasing subsequence of $m$ terms
or a decreasing subsequence of $n$ terms.*

The classical Erd\H{o}s--Szekeres theorem, obtained as a special case of a
statement about digraphs --- a good illustration of the chapter's theme that
chromatic number controls directed-path structure.

\textbf{!} Restated: Mathlib's \texttt{Archive} version is not importable, so
the statement is spelled out here and derived from (a) as the book intends.  $g$ is
$\mathbb{Z}$-valued (the book's "integers") while part (a) needs $\mathbb{R}$, hence the cast in step
2.  \texttt{hN : m * n < N} is the book's "$mn + 1$ terms", generalised to any longer
sequence.
\end{theorem}

n21715.title: exists\_orientation\_directedPath\_le\_maxDegree
n21715.content:
\begin{theorem}[exists\_orientation\_directedPath\_le\_maxDegree]
\lean{exists_orientation_directedPath_le_maxDegree}
\label{exists_orientation_directedPath_le_maxDegree}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedPath, Digraph.IsOrientationOf, Digraph.toQuiver}
*Using theorem 10.1 and corollary 8.1.2, show that $G$
has an orientation in which each directed path is of length at most $\Delta$.*

Chaining two results already available: $\chi \le \Delta + 1$ bounds the palette,
and the colour-increasing orientation turns a palette bound into a path bound.  Part
(b) of the exercise --- dropped here, being the same statement --- asks for a
constructive proof avoiding the chromatic detour.

\textbf{!} This rides chapter 8's corollary 8.1.2, which is out of
chapter; step 1 is therefore an import from
\texttt{TCSlib/GraphTheory/VertexColourings.lean} (\texttt{chromaticNumber\_le\_maxDegree\_add\_one})
rather than something proved here.  Note the shape of step 2: this is exactly why
the theorem-10.1 remark was stated for an arbitrary $k$-colouring rather than an
optimal one.
\end{theorem}

n21716.title: moon\_vertex\_pancyclic
n21716.content:
\begin{theorem}[moon\_vertex\_pancyclic]
\lean{moon_vertex_pancyclic}
\label{moon_vertex_pancyclic}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.Diconnected, Digraph.IsDirectedCycle, Digraph.IsTournament, Digraph.toQuiver}
(Moon, 1966).  *Each vertex of a diconnected tournament $D$
with $\nu \ge 3$ is contained in a directed $k$-cycle, $3 \le k \le \nu$.*

A digraph with this property is \textbf{vertex-pancyclic}: every vertex lies
on cycles of \emph{every} possible length.  Taking $k = \nu$, every diconnected tournament
has a directed Hamilton cycle --- first proved by Camion (1959).  Theorem 10.7
consumes the full strength, needing cycles of several specific lengths through a
given vertex.

The cycle is based at $u$ (\texttt{p : Path u u}), which is how "$u$ is
contained in" is expressed.  \textbf{!} The book's final splice $(v_{0}, v, w, v_{2}, \dots, v_n)$
silently assumes $v$ follows $v_{0}$ and $w$ precedes $v_{2}$; check the index bookkeeping
against $n \ge 3$ before trusting it.
\end{theorem}

n21717.title: ghouila\_houri\_directed\_hamilton\_cycle
n21717.content:
\begin{theorem}[ghouila\_houri\_directed\_hamilton\_cycle]
\lean{ghouila_houri_directed_hamilton_cycle}
\label{ghouila_houri_directed_hamilton_cycle}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedCycle, Digraph.IsStrict, Digraph.indegree, Digraph.outdegree, Digraph.toQuiver}
(a special case of Ghouila-Houri, 1960).  *If $D$ is strict and
\texttt{min\{$\delta^{-}$, $\delta^{+}$\} $\ge$ $\nu$/2 > 1}, then $D$ contains a directed Hamilton cycle.*

The directed extension of Dirac's theorem 4.3 --- a large minimum degree,
now in \emph{both} directions, forces a spanning cycle.  Exercise 10.3.1 recovers Dirac
from it by orienting a graph suitably.

\texttt{hdeg} states $\nu \le 2 d^{-}(v)$ and $\nu \le 2 d^{+}(v)$ rather than
\texttt{min\{$\delta^{-}$,$\delta^{+}$\} $\ge$ $\nu$/2}, avoiding division; $hv : 2 < \nu$ is the book's $\nu/2 > 1$.  The
result is only a \emph{special case} of Ghouila-Houri's theorem, as B\&M note.
\end{theorem}

n21718.title: exists\_directedEulerTour\_iff
n21718.content:
\begin{theorem}[exists\_directedEulerTour\_iff]
\lean{exists_directedEulerTour_iff}
\label{exists_directedEulerTour_iff}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedEulerTour, Digraph.indegree, Digraph.outdegree, Digraph.toQuiver}
*$D$ contains a directed Euler tour if and only if $D$ is
connected and $d^{+}(v) = d^{-}(v)$ for all $v \in V$.*

The directed analogue of Euler's theorem 4.1.  Every visit uses one
arrow in and one out, so the two counts must balance.  \emph{Why it is built early:}
\S{}10.5 depends on it --- the de Bruijn digraph $D_n$ is connected with every indegree
and outdegree $2$, so it has a directed Euler tour, and that tour is exactly the
binary sequence for the computer drum.

Connectivity is asked of \texttt{toSimpleGraphInclusive}, the underlying
graph, matching B\&M's "$D$ is connected" (a property of the underlying graph, per
\S{}10.1).

\textbf{+} \textbf{Statement repaired --- connectivity moved from the right-hand side into a
hypothesis.}  As previously written, \texttt{($\exists$ Euler tour) $\leftrightarrow$ (Connected $\land$ balanced)}, the
$\leftrightarrow$ was \textbf{false}, for two compounding reasons.

\emph{Counterexample 1.}  Let $D$ have no arcs and \texttt{card V $\ge$ 2}.  Then \texttt{Quiver.Path.nil} at
any $u$ satisfies \texttt{IsDirectedEulerTour} --- its arc list is $[]$ (so \texttt{Nodup}), and the
exhaustiveness clause \texttt{$\forall$ a b, D.Adj a b $\to$ \dots} is vacuous --- so the left side holds,
while the right side fails because $D$ is disconnected.

\emph{Counterexample 2.}  Adding arcs does not rescue it: take one directed cycle plus an
isolated vertex.  A tour of the cycle exhausts every arc, so the left side holds, but
the underlying graph is still disconnected.

So no strengthening of the left side repairs this; connectivity has to be assumed, not
concluded.  With \texttt{hconn} a hypothesis the equivalence is the honest directed Euler
theorem, and it now matches the shape of this library's undirected
\texttt{euler\_tour\_iff\_no\_odd\_degree} in \texttt{EulerHamilton.lean}.

\textbf{!} Note that unlike the undirected statement, \textbf{no arc-nonemptiness hypothesis is
needed}: \texttt{hconn} already forces the arc-free case to be the one-vertex graph, where
\texttt{nil} is an Euler tour and the balance condition holds vacuously, so the $\leftrightarrow$ is true
there.
\end{theorem}

n21719.title: exists\_arcDisjoint\_directedPaths
n21719.content:
\begin{theorem}[exists\_arcDisjoint\_directedPaths]
\lean{exists_arcDisjoint_directedPaths}
\label{exists_arcDisjoint_directedPaths}
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedPath, Digraph.arcsOf, Digraph.indegree, Digraph.outdegree, Digraph.toQuiver}
*Let $D$ be a digraph such that (i)
$d^{+}(x) - d^{-}(x) = l = d^{-}(y) - d^{+}(y)$ and (ii) $d^{+}(v) = d^{-}(v)$ for
$v \in V \ {x, y}$.  Show, using exercise 10.3.2, that there exist $l$ arc-disjoint
directed $(x, y)$-paths in $D$.*

The degree conditions say $x$ has an excess of $l$ outgoing arcs, $y$
an excess of $l$ incoming ones, and everything else is balanced --- so $l$ units of
"flow" must run from $x$ to $y$.  A small precursor of the max-flow min-cut
machinery of chapter 11.

\textbf{!} Two obstructions to the intended route, both recorded rather
than resolved.  (i) \texttt{Digraph} admits \textbf{no parallel arcs}, so step 1's "$l$ copies of
$(y,x)$" is not expressible on $D$; the construction has to move to
\texttt{Digraph (V $\oplus$ Fin l)}, routing each extra arc through its own new vertex.  The
\emph{statement} stays on $D$ and is well-typed.  (ii) The conclusion mentions \texttt{arcsOf},
which currently has a \texttt{sorry} body, so the arc-disjointness clause is presently
meaningless --- see that definition.  Degrees are compared in $\mathbb{Z}$ to let $hx$, $hy$
state genuine differences without $\mathbb{N}$-truncation.
\end{theorem}

n21720.title: exists\_directed\_odd\_cycle
n21720.content:
\begin{theorem}[exists\_directed\_odd\_cycle]
\lean{exists_directed_odd_cycle}
\label{exists_directed_odd_cycle}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.Diconnected, Digraph.IsDirectedCycle, Digraph.toQuiver}
\emph{.  }A diconnected digraph which contains an odd cycle also
contains a directed odd cycle.*

The hypothesis gives an odd cycle in the \emph{underlying} graph, whose arcs
may point every which way; the conclusion upgrades it to a genuinely directed odd
cycle.  Diconnection is essential --- without it the parity argument cannot be
propagated across the whole digraph, and the statement is false.

The undirected cycle enters as a \texttt{Walk} in
\texttt{toSimpleGraphInclusive} with \texttt{IsCycle} and \texttt{Odd length}; the directed conclusion is
a \texttt{Quiver.Path}.  Step 2's "decompose a closed walk into directed cycles" has no
Mathlib counterpart for \texttt{Quiver.Path} and will have to be built.
\end{theorem}

n21721.title: diconnected\_iff\_isKArcConnected\_one
n21721.content:
\begin{theorem}[diconnected\_iff\_isKArcConnected\_one]
\lean{diconnected_iff_isKArcConnected_one}
\label{diconnected_iff_isKArcConnected_one}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.Diconnected, Digraph.IsKArcConnected}
*A nontrivial digraph is diconnected if and only if it is
1-arc-connected.*

Diconnection is the $k = 1$ case of arc-connectivity, exactly as
connection is the $k = 1$ case of edge-connectivity in \S{}3.1.

\texttt{[Nontrivial V]} is the book's "nontrivial digraph" and is
load-bearing: on a one-vertex carrier there is no nonempty proper $S$, so
\texttt{IsKArcConnected 1} is vacuously true while \texttt{Diconnected} --- which is also true there
--- would make the $\leftrightarrow$ hold only by accident.  More importantly, its absence is what
breaks \texttt{associatedDigraph\_isKArcConnected\_iff} below.
\end{theorem}

n21722.title: associatedDigraph\_isKArcConnected\_iff
n21722.content:
\begin{theorem}[associatedDigraph\_isKArcConnected\_iff]
\lean{associatedDigraph_isKArcConnected_iff}
\label{associatedDigraph_isKArcConnected_iff}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsKArcConnected, SimpleGraph.associatedDigraph, edgeConnectivity}
*$D(G)$ is $k$-arc-connected if and only if $G$ is
$k$-edge-connected.*

The associated digraph faithfully preserves connectivity, so the
directed notion generalises the undirected one.  Contrast \S{}10.6, where the question
is which \emph{orientations} --- not the doubling --- preserve it; there the answer is much
more delicate (Robbins, Nash-Williams).

"$G$ is $k$-edge-connected" is spelled \texttt{k $\le$ edgeConnectivity G},
per \S{}3.1.  Step 2 needs that a minimal edge cut is $[S, S^{c}]$ for a component $S$,
which is the same fact the local \texttt{IsEdgeCut} docstring notes when reconciling the
book's shape-based definition with the deletion-based one used here.

\textbf{+} \textbf{Statement repaired --- \texttt{[Nontrivial V]} added.}  The $\leftrightarrow$ was \textbf{false on a
one-vertex carrier}.  Take \texttt{card V = 1}, so $G = \bot$, and $k = 1$.  \emph{Left side:} there
is no nonempty proper \texttt{S : Finset V}, so \texttt{IsKArcConnected 1} holds vacuously.  *Right
side:* $\bot$ on one vertex is \texttt{Connected}, so nothing disconnects it, $G$ has no edge cut
at all, and \texttt{edgeConnectivity G = 0}; the claim $1 \le 0$ fails.

\texttt{[Nontrivial V]} excludes exactly that carrier and is the hypothesis the book's
"nontrivial digraph" convention supplies implicitly (compare
\texttt{diconnected\_iff\_isKArcConnected\_one} above, which already carries it).  \textbf{!} Both Menger
statements in \texttt{Networks.lean} consume this lemma, so their hypotheses must be checked
against the added \texttt{Nontrivial} when they are proved.
\end{theorem}

n21725.title: deBruijnDigraph\_exists\_directedEulerTour
n21725.content:
\begin{theorem}[deBruijnDigraph\_exists\_directedEulerTour]
\lean{deBruijnDigraph_exists_directedEulerTour}
\label{deBruijnDigraph_exists_directedEulerTour}
\uses{Digraph.IsDirectedEulerTour, Digraph.toQuiver, deBruijnDigraph}
Each arc carries an $n$-bit label and the tour uses every arc exactly
once, so reading off the first digit of each label in order produces a cyclic binary
sequence of length $2^{n}$ in which all $2^{n}$ windows of length $n$ are distinct.

\emph{The application.}  Divide a rotating drum's surface into $2^{n}$ sections according to
that sequence; then $n$ consecutive contacts read a different $n$-bit number at each
of the $2^{n}$ positions, so all positions are distinguishable --- and $n$ is optimal,
since $k$ contacts give only $2^{k}$ readings.  For $n = 4$ the book's tour gives
$0000111100101101$.  Due to Good (1946).

\textbf{!} This is a three-line consequence of its two inputs, but it
inherits both defects of \texttt{exists\_directedEulerTour\_iff}: that theorem is currently
false as stated, and \texttt{IsDirectedEulerTour} is defined through the \texttt{sorry}-bodied
\texttt{arcsOf}.  Until those are repaired this statement is not the intended one.  Note
also that the \emph{labels} are not modelled --- the conclusion asserts a tour exists, and
turning it into the binary sequence is left to \texttt{exists\_deBruijn\_sequence}.
\end{theorem}

n21726.title: robbins\_orientation
n21726.content:
\begin{theorem}[robbins\_orientation]
\lean{robbins_orientation}
\label{robbins_orientation}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.Diconnected, Digraph.IsOrientationOf, edgeConnectivity}
(Robbins, 1939).  *If $G$ is 2-edge-connected, then $G$ has a
diconnected orientation.*

How to make a road system one-way so traffic can still flow
everywhere.  A graph with a cut edge clearly cannot manage it --- whichever way that
edge is directed, one side becomes unreachable --- and Robbins showed
2-edge-connectivity is not merely necessary but sufficient.  Intuitively, each new
vertex is given both a way in and a way out.

\textbf{!} Step 2 rides chapter 3's exercise 3.2.1, which this repo does
not have; budget for it before starting.  \texttt{h2ec : 2 $\le$ edgeConnectivity G} is
"$2$-edge-connected" per \S{}3.1.  Theorem 10.6 is the $k = 1$ case of a different
route to the same conclusion, so neither theorem subsumes the other.
\end{theorem}

n21727.title: exists\_kArcConnected\_orientation\_of\_eulerian
n21727.content:
\begin{theorem}[exists\_kArcConnected\_orientation\_of\_eulerian]
\lean{exists_kArcConnected_orientation_of_eulerian}
\label{exists_kArcConnected_orientation_of_eulerian}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.IsKArcConnected, Digraph.IsOrientationOf, edgeConnectivity}
*Let $G$ be a $2k$-edge-connected graph with an Euler trail.
Then $G$ has a $k$-arc-connected orientation.*

The easy special case of a theorem of Nash-Williams (1960), that
\emph{every} $2k$-edge-connected graph has a $k$-arc-connected orientation; the general
proof is difficult.  Robbins' theorem 10.5 is the case $k = 1$ --- proved there by a
quite different, ear-decomposition route.

\textbf{!} Step 4's $\lfloor m/2\rfloor$ is stated as \texttt{2 * count + 1 $\ge$ m} to keep $\mathbb{N}$
division out.  Step 2 is where an Euler \emph{trail} rather than a tour matters: an open
trail is what allows the discrepancy of one, and a closed tour would give equality.
Note \texttt{t : G.Walk u v} with $u$, $v$ unconstrained, so both cases are covered.
\end{theorem}

n21728.title: tournament\_adjMatrix\_pow\_pos
n21728.content:
\begin{theorem}[tournament\_adjMatrix\_pow\_pos]
\lean{tournament_adjMatrix_pow_pos}
\label{tournament_adjMatrix_pow_pos}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.Diconnected, Digraph.IsTournament, Digraph.adjMatrix, Digraph.dirDiameter}
*Let $D$ be a diconnected tournament with $\nu \ge 5$, and let $A$
be the adjacency matrix of $D$.  Then $A^{d+3} > 0$ (every entry positive), where
$d$ is the directed diameter of $D$.*

\emph{Why it matters (\S{}10.7).}  The $i$-th level score vector of a
tournament is $s_{i} = A^{i}J$, each player's score being the sum of the scores of those
they beat.  Primitivity of $A$ is what lets Perron--Frobenius guarantee these vectors
converge to a positive eigenvector, giving a well-defined ranking.

\textbf{!} The arithmetic $d - d_{ij} + 3$ is $\mathbb{N}$-subtraction but never
truncates, since $d_{ij} \le d$; still, establish that inequality before the case split
rather than relying on it implicitly.  $\nu \ge 5$ is load-bearing in step 4 only.
\end{theorem}

n21729.title: tournament\_adjMatrix\_isPrimitive\_iff
n21729.content:
\begin{theorem}[tournament\_adjMatrix\_isPrimitive\_iff]
\lean{tournament_adjMatrix_isPrimitive_iff}
\label{tournament_adjMatrix_isPrimitive_iff}
\leanok
\uses{Digraph.Diconnected, Digraph.IsTournament, Digraph.adjMatrix, Matrix.IsPrimitive}
*The adjacency matrix $A$ of a tournament $D$ is primitive
if and only if $D$ is diconnected and $\nu \ge 4$.*

\emph{The ranking method (\S{}10.7).}  When $A$ is primitive, Perron--Frobenius
gives a largest real eigenvalue $r$ with \texttt{lim\_i (A/r)$^{i}$ J = s}, a positive
eigenvector; the normalised $\bar{s}$ measures relative strengths.  For the book's
six-player example $r \approx 2.232$ and $\bar{s} \approx (.238, .164, .231, .113, .150, .104)$,
ranking the players $1, 3, 2, 5, 4, 6$.  Non-diconnected tournaments are handled by
ranking within dicomponents and then ordering the dicomponents by dominance
(exercises 10.1.9 and 10.1.3(b)).  Due to Wei (1952) and Kendall (1955).

\textbf{!} Steps 2 and 4 are the awkward ones: B\&M discharge them by
pointing at a figure the source omits, so the two small tournaments have to be
identified and checked from scratch.  Everything else follows from theorem 10.7 and
exercise 10.1.8.
\end{theorem}

n21730.title: Colour $i$ is \emph{represented} at $v$: some edge incident with $v$ has colour $i$
n21730.content:
\begin{definition}[Colour $i$ is \emph{represented} at $v$: some edge incident with $v$ has colour $i$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsRepresentedAt}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsRepresentedAt}
\leanok
A $k$-edge colouring is a plain function \texttt{C : G.edgeSet $\to$ Fin k}, deliberately
\textbf{not} assumed proper --- that is the whole point, since Lemma 6.1.2, Theorem 6.1
and Vizing's Theorem 6.2 all operate on improper colourings and repair them.

"Represented at $v$" is \texttt{$\exists$ e, ↑e $\in$ G.incidenceSet v $\land$ C e = i}.

\textbf{!} Note this file uses \textbf{two different} colouring encodings.  Here a colouring is
a raw function \texttt{G.edgeSet $\to$ Fin k}; but \texttt{IsUniquelyEdgeColourable} below and the
\texttt{edgeChromaticNumber} results use Mathlib's \texttt{G.lineGraph.Coloring (Fin k)}, which
is proper by construction.  The two are not interchangeable, and any proof
crossing between \S{}6.1's machinery and a $\chi'$ statement must convert explicitly.
\end{definition}

n21731.title: $c(v)$: the number of distinct colours represented at $v$

n21732.title: An optimal $k$-edge colouring: one that cannot be improved, where an improvement strictly increases $\sum\dots$
n21732.content:
\begin{definition}[An optimal $k$-edge colouring: one that cannot be improved, where an improvement strictly increases $\sum\dots$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsOptimalEdgeColouring}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsOptimalEdgeColouring}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.numColoursAt}
Among all $k$-edge colourings --- proper or not --- prefer those spreading colours
most widely, measured by $\sum_v c(v)$.  Rendered directly as
\texttt{$\forall$ C', $\sum$ v, numColoursAt C' v $\le$ $\sum$ v, numColoursAt C v}, i.e. $C$ attains the
maximum.

Since $c(v) \le d(v)$ with equality everywhere iff proper, a proper colouring is
automatically optimal.  The chapter's strategy is the converse direction: start
from an optimal colouring and show that if it were \emph{not} proper it could be
improved after all.

\textbf{!} Note this is a static extremal condition, not a procedure --- no improvement
algorithm is defined here.  Existence of an optimal colouring (needed by
Theorem 6.1 and Vizing) follows from finiteness of the colouring space but is
\textbf{not stated as a lemma anywhere in this file}, and both proofs will need it.
\end{definition}

n21733.title: $G(E_i \cup E_j)$, the subgraph on the edges coloured $i$ or $j$
n21733.content:
\begin{definition}[$G(E_i \cup E_j)$, the subgraph on the edges coloured $i$ or $j$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.twoColourSubgraph}
\label{SimpleGraph.twoColourSubgraph}
\leanok
Erase every edge except those coloured $i$ or $j$:
\texttt{fromEdgeSet \{e | $\exists$ h : e $\in$ G.edgeSet, C ⟨e,h⟩ = i $\lor$ C ⟨e,h⟩ = j\}}.

If the colouring is proper this leaves maximum degree $2$ --- a disjoint union of
paths and cycles alternating between the two colours.  Recolouring inside such a
component is the fundamental move of the chapter; Lemma 6.1.2 says the only
components resisting improvement in an \emph{optimal} colouring are odd cycles.

\textbf{!} The book's $G[\cdot]$ is edge-induced, so isolated vertices are irrelevant to it.
Mathlib's \texttt{fromEdgeSet} keeps the full vertex type $V$, so the resulting graph
has isolated vertices wherever neither colour appears.  This matters when
speaking of "the component containing $u$": in the Lean rendering that component
is a single vertex when $u$ meets neither colour, whereas the book's $G[E_{i} \cup E_{j}]$
would not contain $u$ at all.
\end{definition}

n21734.title: $G$ is uniquely $k$-edge-colourable: any two proper $k$-edge colourings agree up to a permutation of the\dots
n21734.content:
\begin{definition}[$G$ is uniquely $k$-edge-colourable: any two proper $k$-edge colourings agree up to a permutation of the\dots]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsUniquelyEdgeColourable}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsUniquelyEdgeColourable}
\leanok
Colours are arbitrary labels, so what a colouring really determines is the
partition into colour classes.  Unique colourability means that partition is
forced, and any two proper colourings differ only by renaming --- which is what the
permutation $\sigma$ expresses.

Proper $k$-edge colourings are rendered as \texttt{G.lineGraph.Coloring (Fin k)}, using
Mathlib's line graph: adjacent \emph{edges} of $G$ become adjacent \emph{vertices} of
\texttt{G.lineGraph}, so a proper vertex colouring there is a proper edge colouring
here.

\textbf{!} "Induce the same partition" and "differ by a permutation of colours" are
equivalent only when every colour is actually \emph{used}.  If $k$ exceeds the number
of classes, two colourings can induce the same partition while no single $\sigma$
relates them pointwise --- and conversely $\sigma$ may permute unused colours freely.
For the intended application ($k = 3$, 3-regular, so all three classes nonempty)
this is harmless, but the definition is not faithful in general.
\end{definition}

n21741.title: Theorem 6.1 (K\"onig) \textbf{!} BLOCKED: if $G$ is bipartite then $\chi' = \Delta$
n21741.content:
\begin{theorem}[Theorem 6.1 (K\"onig) \textbf{!} BLOCKED: if $G$ is bipartite then $\chi' = \Delta$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.edgeChromaticNumber_eq_maxDegree_of_isBipartite}
\label{SimpleGraph.edgeChromaticNumber_eq_maxDegree_of_isBipartite}
Contrapositive: if $\chi' > \Delta$, an optimal $\Delta$-colouring cannot be proper, so by
(6.3) some $u$ has $c(u) < d(u)$ --- a colour missing while another repeats.  That
is Lemma 6.1.2's hypothesis, which forces an odd cycle, so $G$ is not bipartite.

\textbf{!} The book's "Clearly, $u$ satisfies the hypothesis of lemma 6.1.2" compresses a
real step.  From $c(u) < d(u)$ one gets \emph{some} colour repeated at $u$; getting a
colour \emph{not represented} at $u$ needs the pigeonhole $c(u) < d(u) \le \Delta$ --- i.e.
that only $\Delta$ colours are available and fewer than $d(u)$ are used.  With
$d(u) \le \Delta$ this is tight and worth isolating.

\textbf{!} The odd cycle produced by Lemma 6.1.2 lives in \texttt{twoColourSubgraph C i j}, a
\emph{subgraph} of $G$.  Transporting it to an odd cycle of $G$ (to contradict
bipartiteness) requires a walk-level map along \texttt{twoColourSubgraph $\le$ G}, which is
not stated in this file.
\end{theorem}

n21744.title: exists\_rebalanced\_matchings
n21744.content:
\begin{theorem}[exists\_rebalanced\_matchings]
\lean{SimpleGraph.exists_rebalanced_matchings}
\label{SimpleGraph.exists_rebalanced_matchings}
Swapping roles along $P$ moves exactly one edge from the larger matching to the
smaller, leaving the union unchanged.  Repeated application \emph{balances} a family
of matchings --- in \S{}6.3's timetabling reading, spreading lessons evenly across
periods so fewer classrooms are needed at once.

$|M'| = |M| - 1$ is stated additively as \texttt{M'.ncard + 1 = M.ncard} to avoid $\mathbb{N}$
subtraction.

Matchings are carried as \texttt{Set (Sym2 V)} together with an existential witness
\texttt{$\exists$ S : G.Subgraph, S.IsMatching $\land$ S.edgeSet = M}, rather than as subgraphs
directly --- which makes the set operations $\setminus$, $\cup$ in the book's formulas
literal, at the cost of re-deriving the subgraph witness for $M'$ and $N'$.
\end{theorem}

n21745.title: exists\_balanced\_matching\_decomposition
n21745.content:
\begin{theorem}[exists\_balanced\_matching\_decomposition]
\lean{SimpleGraph.exists_balanced_matching_decomposition}
\label{SimpleGraph.exists_balanced_matching_decomposition}
\textbf{!} In the book's notation $[x]$ is the \textbf{floor} and ${x}$ the \textbf{ceiling} --- the
opposite of the modern convention for ${}$.  So (6.5) reads
$\lfloor\varepsilon/p\rfloor \le |M_{i}| \le \lceil\varepsilon/p\rceil$, rendered here as
\texttt{G.edgeFinset.card / p $\le$ \dots $\le$ (G.edgeFinset.card + p - 1) / p} in $\mathbb{N}$ division.

\textbf{!} The book's "repeatedly applying lemma 6.3 ... we eventually obtain" is an
induction whose \textbf{termination is not argued}.  In Lean it needs an explicit
measure --- e.g. $\sum_{i} |M_{i}|^{2}$, which strictly decreases on each rebalancing since
moving an edge from a larger to a smaller class reduces the sum of squares.
Supplying that measure is a real part of the formalisation the book skips.
\end{theorem}

n21746.title: Ex 6.1.3(a): every bipartite $G$ has a $\Delta$-regular bipartite supergraph \textbf{!} carrier change
n21746.content:
\begin{theorem}[Ex 6.1.3(a): every bipartite $G$ has a $\Delta$-regular bipartite supergraph \textbf{!} carrier change]
\lean{SimpleGraph.exists_regular_bipartite_supergraph}
\label{SimpleGraph.exists_regular_bipartite_supergraph}
Pad until every vertex has degree exactly $\Delta$.  Enlarge the smaller side with
isolated vertices so the sides match; then repeatedly join a deficient vertex on
each side --- both sides have equal total deficiency, so such a pair always exists.

\textbf{!} Carrier changes, so the statement produces a new type $W$ together with an
embedding $G \hookrightarrow g H$.

\textbf{!} \textbf{The $\hookrightarrow g$ here is a \texttt{RelEmbedding}, i.e. an \emph{induced} embedding} --- the same
trap that sank the original statement of exercise 1.4.1 in
\texttt{GraphsAndSubgraphs.lean} (recorded in
\texttt{GraphTheory/ExtractionArchive/MathlibDuplicates.md}, entry 5).
It demands \texttt{H.Adj (f a) (f b) $\leftrightarrow$ G.Adj a b}, so the padding edges must never join
two images of $G$-vertices.  The two-disjoint-copies construction respects this;
the naive "add edges between deficient vertices of $G$ itself" does \textbf{not}, and
would make the statement false.  Worth checking carefully before proving.

Part (b) is the alternative proof of Theorem 6.1: a $\Delta$-regular bipartite graph
is 1-factorable (exercise 5.2.3(a)), hence properly $\Delta$-edge colourable, and
restricting to $G$ gives $\chi'(G) \le \Delta$.

\textbf{+} \textbf{This route avoids Lemma 6.1.1 and the Euler theorem entirely}, so it is the
recommended path to Theorem 6.1 in Lean --- see the note there.
\end{theorem}

n21747.title: Ex 6.1.6 (Gupta) \textbf{!} BLOCKED: bipartite with $\delta > 0$ $\Rightarrow$ a $\delta$-edge colouring\dots
n21747.content:
\begin{theorem}[Ex 6.1.6 (Gupta) \textbf{!} BLOCKED: bipartite with $\delta > 0$ $\Rightarrow$ a $\delta$-edge colouring\dots]
\lean{SimpleGraph.exists_edge_colouring_all_represented_of_isBipartite}
\label{SimpleGraph.exists_edge_colouring_all_represented_of_isBipartite}
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsRepresentedAt}
The \textbf{dual} of proper colouring.  Proper asks that no colour appear \emph{twice} at a
vertex, using $\Delta$ colours; this asks that every colour appear \emph{at least once} at
every vertex, using $\delta$ colours.  Since the least degree is $\delta$, that is the most
one could force everywhere.

The colouring is explicitly \textbf{not} required to be proper, so the statement is
about \texttt{IsRepresentedAt} rather than about \texttt{lineGraph.chromaticNumber} --- one of
the few places the raw-function encoding is the right one.

Exercise 6.2.8 is the simple-graph analogue with $\delta - 1$ colours; it is not
stated in this file.
\end{theorem}

n21748.title: Ex 6.2.1*: $\chi'(K_{2n- 1}) = 2n- 1$ (explicit colouring --- bypasses Vizing)
n21748.content:
\begin{theorem}[Ex 6.2.1*: $\chi'(K_{2n- 1}) = 2n- 1$ (explicit colouring --- bypasses Vizing)]
\lean{SimpleGraph.edgeChromaticNumber_completeGraph_odd}
\label{SimpleGraph.edgeChromaticNumber_completeGraph_odd}
$K_{2n-1}$ has odd order, so no colour class is a perfect matching and each
misses a vertex.  With $\varepsilon = (2n-1)(n-1)$ and classes of size $\le n - 1$, at least
$2n - 1$ colours are needed --- one more than $\Delta = 2n - 2$.  So odd complete graphs
sit on the \textbf{upper} side of Vizing's dichotomy.

The explicit colouring: place the vertices at the corners of a regular
$(2n-1)$-gon and colour each edge by the axis of symmetry it is perpendicular to.
Each class is a matching of $n - 1$ edges missing one vertex, and there are
$2n - 1$ axes.

Concretely in \texttt{ZMod (2n-1)}: colour $s(a, b)$ by $a + b$.  Two edges at a shared
vertex get different sums because $2$ is invertible mod an odd number --- which is
exactly where oddness enters.
\end{theorem}

n21752.content:
\begin{theorem}[Ex 6.2.3(b)(i) \textbf{!} BLOCKED: subdividing one edge of an even-order $k$-regular graph ($k \ge 2$)\dots]
\lean{SimpleGraph.edgeChromaticNumber_subdivide_eq_maxDegree_add_one}
\label{SimpleGraph.edgeChromaticNumber_subdivide_eq_maxDegree_add_one}
\uses{SimpleGraph.subdivide}
Start from $k$-regular on $2n$ vertices, $\varepsilon = kn$.  Subdividing inserts a
degree-$2$ vertex: $2n + 1$ vertices --- now odd --- and $kn + 1$ edges, with $\Delta$
still $k$ provided $k \ge 2$.  Part (a) then applies since
$kn + 1 > kn = n\Delta$.

A single subdivision flips the parity of the vertex count and pushes the graph
from the lower to the upper side of Vizing's dichotomy.

\textbf{!} $hk : 2 \le k$ is load-bearing: at $k = 1$ the new degree-$2$ vertex would
\emph{raise} $\Delta$ to $2$, and the count $n\Delta$ would change with it, breaking the
application of part (a).
\end{theorem}

n21754.title: Ex 6.2.5: every uniquely 3-edge-colourable 3-regular graph is hamiltonian
n21754.content:
\begin{theorem}[Ex 6.2.5: every uniquely 3-edge-colourable 3-regular graph is hamiltonian]
\lean{SimpleGraph.isHamiltonian_of_uniquely_three_edge_colourable}
\label{SimpleGraph.isHamiltonian_of_uniquely_three_edge_colourable}
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsUniquelyEdgeColourable}
In a cubic graph a proper 3-edge colouring splits the edges into three perfect
matchings.  Any \emph{two} of them form a spanning 2-regular subgraph --- a disjoint
union of even cycles.  If that union had more than one cycle, swapping the two
colours around a single cycle would give a genuinely different partition,
contradicting uniqueness.  So each pair of classes is a \emph{single} spanning cycle,
i.e. a Hamilton cycle.

\textbf{!} \textbf{\texttt{hcol} is mandatory.}  \texttt{IsUniquelyEdgeColourable} quantifies over proper
3-colourings; if none exists the condition holds \textbf{vacuously}, and the statement
would then assert that every cubic graph with no 3-edge-colouring is
hamiltonian --- false, the Petersen graph being a counterexample ($\chi' = 4$,
nonhamiltonian).  Requiring \texttt{G.lineGraph.Colorable 3} rules that out.
\end{theorem}

n21755.title: Ex 6.2.6(a) \textbf{!} BLOCKED (Vizing): $\chi'(G \square K_{2}) = \Delta(G \square K_{2})$
n21755.content:
\begin{theorem}[Ex 6.2.6(a) \textbf{!} BLOCKED (Vizing): $\chi'(G \square K_{2}) = \Delta(G \square K_{2})$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.edgeChromaticNumber_boxProd_completeGraph_two}
\label{SimpleGraph.edgeChromaticNumber_boxProd_completeGraph_two}
The book's "product" is exactly Mathlib's \texttt{boxProd}, written $\square$.

$G \square K_{2}$ is two disjoint copies of $G$ plus a perfect matching joining
corresponding vertices, so every degree rises by one and
$\Delta(G \square K_{2}) = \Delta(G) + 1$.

Vizing gives $G$ a proper $(\Delta(G)+1)$-colouring.  Use it on both copies, then
colour the connecting matching edges by recycling --- each vertex of a copy already
omits at least one of the $\Delta(G)+1$ colours, and the two copies can be arranged to
omit \emph{different} ones, so each matching edge finds a free colour.
\end{theorem}

n21756.title: Ex 6.2.6(b) \textbf{!} BLOCKED (via (a)): if $H$ is nontrivial ($0 < \Delta(H)$) with $\chi'(H) =\dots$
n21756.content:
\begin{theorem}[Ex 6.2.6(b) \textbf{!} BLOCKED (via (a)): if $H$ is nontrivial ($0 < \Delta(H)$) with $\chi'(H) =\dots$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.edgeChromaticNumber_boxProd}
\label{SimpleGraph.edgeChromaticNumber_boxProd}
$G \square H$ has degree $d(u) + d(v)$ at $(u, v)$, so $\Delta(G \square H) = \Delta(G) + \Delta(H)$.
Decompose $H$ into $\Delta(H)$ matchings via its optimal colouring; each matching
crossed with $G$ reproduces part (a)'s situation, and assembling gives
$\Delta(G) + \Delta(H)$ colours.

So the class attaining $\chi' = \Delta$ is closed under products with any nontrivial
member --- one of the few general constructions guaranteeing the lower Vizing
class.

$H$ nontrivial is \texttt{0 < H.maxDegree}; without it $H$ is edgeless, $G \square H$ is a
disjoint union of copies of $G$, and the claim reduces to $\chi'(G) = \Delta(G)$ which
need not hold.
\end{theorem}

n21757.title: $G$ is eulerian: it has a closed Euler trail (an Euler tour)
n21757.content:
\begin{definition}[$G$ is eulerian: it has a closed Euler trail (an Euler tour)]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsEulerianGraph}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsEulerianGraph}
\leanok
\texttt{$\exists$ u, $\exists$ p : G.Walk u u, p.IsEulerian} --- a closed walk using every edge exactly
once.  Mathlib's \texttt{Walk.IsEulerian} is defined via \texttt{List.count} on \texttt{p.edges},
which is why \texttt{[DecidableEq V]} is genuinely required here and not merely
convenient.

Note the book's three-way vocabulary collapses in Lean: \texttt{IsEulerian} already
implies \texttt{IsTrail}, so "closed Euler trail" and "Euler tour" are the same
predicate on a \texttt{Walk u u}.
\end{definition}

n21759.title: join
n21759.content:
\begin{definition}[join]
\lean{SimpleGraph.join}
\label{SimpleGraph.join}
\leanok
$G \lor H$, rebuilt on Mathlib: within-side edges from $\oplus g$, all cross
edges from \texttt{completeBipartiteGraph}. \texttt{symm}/\texttt{loopless} are inherited from $\sqcup$.

Lay the two graphs side by side keeping all their own edges, then add every
edge running between them.  The book's $G + H$ (disjoint union) is Mathlib's
$\oplus g$, and "joining each vertex of $G$ to each vertex of $H$" is exactly
\texttt{completeBipartiteGraph V W}, so

    join G H = (G $\oplus$g H) $\sqcup$ completeBipartiteGraph V W

on carrier $V \oplus W$.  Building it as a $\sqcup$ of two existing graphs means \texttt{symm}
and \texttt{loopless} are inherited and need no proof.

The building block of the graphs \texttt{Cmn} below.
\end{definition}

n21760.title: $C_{m,n} = K_m \lor (K_m^c + K_{n-2m})$, with $+$ the Mathlib disjoint sum $\oplus g$
n21760.content:
\begin{definition}[$C_{m,n} = K_m \lor (K_m^c + K_{n-2m})$, with $+$ the Mathlib disjoint sum $\oplus g$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Cmn}
\label{SimpleGraph.Cmn}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.join}
Take $m$ "hub" vertices forming a complete graph, $m$ isolated vertices, and a
complete graph on the remaining $n - 2m$; then join every hub to everything
else.  Carrier \texttt{Fin m $\oplus$ (Fin m $\oplus$ Fin (n - 2 * m))}, with $K_m^{c} = \bot$ on \texttt{Fin m}.

Degrees: the $m$ hubs have degree $n - 1$, the $m$ isolated vertices have degree
$m$, and the remaining $n - 2m$ have degree $n - m - 1$.  That is the degree
sequence Theorem 4.6 majorises against.

\textbf{!} The side condition $1 \le m < n/2$ is \textbf{not} carried in the type.  For $m = 0$
or $2m > n$ the definition still elaborates (with $n - 2 * m$ truncating to $0$)
but no longer matches the book's figure.  Callers must supply the bound.
\end{definition}

n21761.title: The sorted (ascending) degree sequence of $G$
n21761.content:
\begin{definition}[The sorted (ascending) degree sequence of $G$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.degreeSequence}
\label{SimpleGraph.degreeSequence}
\leanok
Simply list how many neighbours each vertex has, smallest first.

Degree is written \texttt{Nat.card (G.neighborSet v)} rather than \texttt{G.degree v}, so the
definition works for any graph on a \texttt{Fintype} without threading a
\texttt{DecidableRel G.Adj} instance; the two agree when $V$ is finite.

The book indexes from $1$ ($d_{1} \le \dots \le d_\nu$); the Lean list is $0$-indexed, so the
book's $d_m$ is \texttt{degreeSequence.getD (m - 1) 0}.  Statements below that quote
Theorem 4.5 must account for that shift.

Chv\'atal's Theorem 4.5 reads hamiltonicity off this list alone; Theorem 4.6 and
Corollary 4.6 compare two such lists via \texttt{DegreeMajorised}.
\end{definition}

n21763.title: One Bondy--Chv\'atal closure step: add a nonadjacent pair whose degree sum is $\ge$ $\nu$
n21763.content:
\begin{definition}[One Bondy--Chv\'atal closure step: add a nonadjacent pair whose degree sum is $\ge$ $\nu$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ClosureStep}
\label{SimpleGraph.ClosureStep}
\leanok
Look for two vertices not yet joined but which between them already have at
least $\nu$ neighbours; Lemma 4.4.1 says adding the edge changes nothing about
hamiltonicity, so add it.  Repeat until no such pair is left.

\texttt{ClosureStep G H} captures a \emph{single} such addition, \texttt{H = G $\sqcup$ edge u v}.  The
closure is then reached by \texttt{Relation.ReflTransGen ClosureStep}, and "no such pair
remains" is expressed at the use site as $H = \top$ or as the absence of a further
step, rather than by a fixpoint operator.

Defining $c(G)$ as a function presupposes Lemma 4.4.2 --- that the result is
independent of the order in which edges are added --- and that lemma is itself one
of the chapter's results.  Positing the fixpoint would therefore assume what the
chapter sets out to prove.  Using the step relation keeps the development honest;
the price is that statements below quantify over \texttt{ReflTransGen ClosureStep}
chains instead of mentioning $c(G)$ directly.

Degree is \texttt{Nat.card (G.neighborSet $\cdot$)} so the relation is well-typed for
arbitrary graphs on $V$ without a \texttt{DecidableRel} instance.
\end{definition}

n21764.title: $G$ is Hamilton-connected: every ordered pair is joined by a Hamilton path (Ex 4.2.11)
n21764.content:
\begin{definition}[$G$ is Hamilton-connected: every ordered pair is joined by a Hamilton path (Ex 4.2.11)]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsHamiltonConnected}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsHamiltonConnected}
\leanok
Not merely that \emph{some} spanning path exists, but that both endpoints may be
prescribed arbitrarily: \texttt{$\forall$ u v, u $\ne$ v $\to$ $\exists$ p : G.Walk u v, p.IsHamiltonian}.

Substantially stronger than being hamiltonian, and correspondingly forces many
edges --- part (a) is \texttt{hamiltonConnected\_edge\_bound} below, part (b) is
\texttt{exists\_extremal\_hamiltonConnected}.

The book's $[x]$ here denotes the ceiling, so $[\tfrac{1}{2}(3\nu+1)]$ is $(3 * \nu + 1 + 1) / 2$
in natural-number division.
\end{definition}

n21765.title: $G$ is hypohamiltonian: not Hamiltonian, but every vertex-deleted subgraph is (Ex 4.2.12)
n21765.content:
\begin{definition}[$G$ is hypohamiltonian: not Hamiltonian, but every vertex-deleted subgraph is (Ex 4.2.12)]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsHypohamiltonian}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsHypohamiltonian}
\leanok
The graph just barely fails to be hamiltonian: no spanning cycle itself, yet
deleting any single vertex repairs the defect.

$G - v$ is \texttt{G.induce (\{v\}$^{c}$ : Set V)}, whose carrier is a \emph{subtype}, so each
\texttt{IsHamiltonian} obligation is about a different vertex type.  The \texttt{open scoped
Classical in} above the definition is what discharges the resulting
\texttt{Fintype}/\texttt{DecidableEq} instances on those carriers.

\texttt{petersen\_isHypohamiltonian} below --- the exercise itself.
\end{definition}

n21770.title: Lem 4.4.1: for nonadjacent $u,v$ with $d(u)+d(v) \ge \nu$, $G$ is hamiltonian iff $G+uv$ is
n21770.content:
\begin{theorem}[Lem 4.4.1: for nonadjacent $u,v$ with $d(u)+d(v) \ge \nu$, $G$ is hamiltonian iff $G+uv$ is]
\lean{SimpleGraph.bondy_chvatal}
\label{SimpleGraph.bondy_chvatal}
The book's proof is two sentences only because it \emph{reuses} the $S$/$T$ counting
argument (4.4) from Theorem 4.3.  In Lean that argument has to exist somewhere
concrete --- so this lemma, not Dirac, is the right place to write it out, and
Dirac then follows from the closure machinery.

Expanded, (4.4) is: from a Hamilton cycle of $G + uv$ that must use $uv$, extract
a Hamilton path $v_{1} \dots v_\nu$ in $G$ with $v_{1} = u$, $v_\nu = v$.  Put
$S = {v_{i} | u ~ v_{i+1}}$ and $T = {v_{i} | v_{i} ~ v}$.  Then $v_\nu \notin S \cup T$ gives
$|S \cup T| < \nu$, and $S \cap T = \emptyset$ because a common $v_{i}$ would close the Hamilton
cycle $v_{1} \dots v_{i} v_\nu v_{\nu-1} \dots v_{i+1} v_{1}$ in $G$.  Hence
$d(u) + d(v) = |S| + |T| < \nu$.
\end{theorem}

n21774.title: Thm 4.5 (counting form): the Chv\'atal degree condition implies hamiltonicity
n21774.content:
\begin{theorem}[Thm 4.5 (counting form): the Chv\'atal degree condition implies hamiltonicity]
\lean{SimpleGraph.chvatal_hamiltonian}
\label{SimpleGraph.chvatal_hamiltonian}
\textbf{!} The hypothesis is formalised in \textbf{counting form}, not by indexing the sorted
degree sequence.  The book's $d_m \le m$ says "at least $m$ vertices have degree
$\le m$", and $d_{\nu-m} < \nu - m$ says "at least $\nu - m$ vertices have degree
$< \nu - m$" --- precisely the two \texttt{Finset.filter} cardinalities in \texttt{hcond}.  This
avoids all $1$- versus $0$-indexing hazards around \texttt{degreeSequence}, at the cost
of no longer looking like the book's inequality.

The book's $m < \nu/2$ is written $2 * m < \nu$, and $m \ge 1$ is made explicit
(the book's $m$ is a degree $d'(u)$, and $m = 0$ is excluded by connectivity
considerations implicit in "as large as possible").
\end{theorem}

n21776.title: Cor 4.6a: $\varepsilon > C(\nu- 1,2) + 1$ implies hamiltonicity
n21776.content:
\begin{theorem}[Cor 4.6a: $\varepsilon > C(\nu- 1,2) + 1$ implies hamiltonicity]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ore_bondy_edge_bound}
\label{SimpleGraph.ore_bondy_edge_bound}
Enough edges guarantee a spanning cycle, and this pins down exactly how many
"enough" is: a nonhamiltonian graph has at most $C(\nu-1, 2) + 1$ edges.

"By theorem 1.1" is the handshaking lemma --- degree majorisation transfers to an
edge-count inequality because $2\varepsilon = \sum d(v)$.

\textbf{!} The book's algebra is over $\mathbb{Q}$ (note the $\tfrac{1}{2}$); in $\mathbb{N}$ the identity
$\tfrac{1}{2}(m^{2} + (\nu-2m)(\nu-m-1) + m(\nu-1)) = C(\nu-1,2) + 1 - \tfrac{1}{2}(m-1)(m-2) - (m-1)(\nu-2m-1)$
involves subtraction that truncates.  Either clear denominators and work with
$2\varepsilon$ throughout, or cast to $\mathbb{Z}$/$\mathbb{Q}$ for the identity and cast back.  The latter
is likely cleaner.
\end{theorem}

n21777.title: Cor 4.6b: the extremal nonhamiltonian graphs at $C(\nu- 1,2)+1$ edges are $C_{1,\nu}$ (and $C_{2,5}$)
n21777.content:
\begin{theorem}[Cor 4.6b: the extremal nonhamiltonian graphs at $C(\nu- 1,2)+1$ edges are $C_{1,\nu}$ (and $C_{2,5}$)]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ore_bondy_extremal}
\label{SimpleGraph.ore_bondy_extremal}
\uses{SimpleGraph.Cmn}
The equality analysis of the first half.  The final inequality is tight only when
both subtracted terms $\tfrac{1}{2}(m-1)(m-2)$ and $(m-1)(\nu-2m-1)$ vanish, which happens
only for $m = 1$, or $m = 2$ together with $\nu = 5$.

So the bound is attained by exactly one graph for each $\nu$, plus one sporadic
extra at $\nu = 5$: the densest nonhamiltonian simple graphs there are.

\textbf{!} The book's closing "which is easily seen to imply that $G \cong C_{1,\nu}$" is
the hardest step to formalise, and it is \textbf{not} easy in Lean.  Degree sequence
does not in general determine a graph up to isomorphism; the implication holds
here only because of the specific structure of $C_{1,\nu}$ and $C_{2,5}$, and
recovering an explicit \texttt{$\simeq$g} requires constructing the vertex bijection by hand.
\end{theorem}

n21778.title: Ex 4.1.4: no odd degree $\Rightarrow$ an edge-disjoint decomposition into cycles
n21778.content:
\begin{theorem}[Ex 4.1.4: no odd degree $\Rightarrow$ an edge-disjoint decomposition into cycles]
\lean{SimpleGraph.even_degree_cycle_decomposition}
\label{SimpleGraph.even_degree_cycle_decomposition}
Even degrees everywhere means no "loose ends".  Peel cycles off one at a time:
removing a cycle subtracts $2$ from the degree of each vertex it visits, so all
degrees stay even and the argument repeats until no edges are left.

"$E(G) = \bigcup E(C_{i})$ with the $C_{i}$ edge-disjoint" is rendered as the single
$\exists!$ statement --- every edge lies in exactly one of the cycles --- which packages
covering and disjointness together.

Note this needs \textbf{no connectivity hypothesis}: it is the local content of
Euler's theorem.  Connectivity is what additionally lets the cycles be spliced
into one tour (Theorem 4.1).
\end{theorem}

n21779.title: Ex 4.1.5: exactly $2k$ odd-degree vertices $\Rightarrow$ $k$ edge-disjoint covering trails
n21779.content:
\begin{theorem}[Ex 4.1.5: exactly $2k$ odd-degree vertices $\Rightarrow$ $k$ edge-disjoint covering trails]
\lean{SimpleGraph.odd_vertices_trail_cover}
\label{SimpleGraph.odd_vertices_trail_cover}
By Corollary 1.1 the odd-degree vertices come in pairs, so there are $k$ pairs.
Pair them up and add $k$ new edges joining the members of each pair; every vertex
of the enlarged graph then has even degree, so Theorem 4.1 gives an Euler tour.
Deleting the $k$ added edges cuts that tour into exactly $k$ trails, which are
edge-disjoint and between them cover every edge of $G$.

The practical reading: a road network with $2k$ awkward junctions needs $k$
separate pen-strokes; one Euler trail is the case $k = 1$.
\end{theorem}

n21780.title: Ex 4.2.1(a): not 2-connected (with $\nu \ge 3$) $\Rightarrow$ nonhamiltonian (restated on the repo\dots
n21780.content:
\begin{theorem}[Ex 4.2.1(a): not 2-connected (with $\nu \ge 3$) $\Rightarrow$ nonhamiltonian (restated on the repo\dots]
\lean{SimpleGraph.nonhamiltonian_of_not_two_connected}
\label{SimpleGraph.nonhamiltonian_of_not_two_connected}
\uses{SimpleGraph.vertexConnectivity}
A graph that is not 2-connected is either disconnected or has a cut vertex $v$.
Disconnected: no cycle reaches every vertex.  Cut vertex: take $S = {v}$ in
Theorem 4.2 --- deleting $v$ leaves at least two components, so
$\omega(G - S) \ge 2 > 1 = |S|$, violating the necessary condition.

A Hamilton cycle visits every vertex and returns, which needs two independent
routes out of every vertex --- exactly 2-connectivity.  Necessary but far from
sufficient (the Petersen graph is 3-connected and nonhamiltonian).

Stated against this file's local \texttt{vertexConnectivity}, not the one in
\texttt{Connectivity.lean} --- see the warning on that definition above.
\end{theorem}

n21786.title: Ex 4.2.8: Erd\H{o}s' edge bound $\nu \ge 6\delta$, $\varepsilon > C(\nu-\delta,2) + \delta^{2}$\dots
n21786.content:
\begin{theorem}[Ex 4.2.8: Erd\H{o}s' edge bound $\nu \ge 6\delta$, $\varepsilon > C(\nu-\delta,2) + \delta^{2}$\dots]
\lean{SimpleGraph.erdos_hamiltonian}
\label{SimpleGraph.erdos_hamiltonian}
Corollary 4.6 gives a sufficient edge count taking no account of the minimum
degree.  Erd\H{o}s' refinement: when $\delta$ is known and small relative to $\nu$, a weaker
count suffices --- $C(\nu-\delta, 2) + \delta^{2}$ rather than $C(\nu-1, 2) + 1$.

The shape of the bound reflects the extremal configuration: a clique on $\nu - \delta$
vertices with $\delta$ low-degree vertices attached, the densest way to be
nonhamiltonian while holding the minimum degree at $\delta$.  $\nu \ge 6\delta$ keeps $\delta$
genuinely small.
\end{theorem}

n21788.title: Ex 4.2.10: a $2k$-regular graph on $4k+1$ vertices is hamiltonian (Nash-Williams)
n21788.content:
\begin{theorem}[Ex 4.2.10: a $2k$-regular graph on $4k+1$ vertices is hamiltonian (Nash-Williams)]
\lean{SimpleGraph.nash_williams_regular_hamiltonian}
\label{SimpleGraph.nash_williams_regular_hamiltonian}
Such a graph has $\delta = \Delta = 2k$ and $\nu = 4k + 1 = 2\delta + 1$, one vertex above the
threshold $\nu \ge 2\delta$ of Dirac's cycle remark.  That remark yields a cycle of length
at least $2\delta = 4k$ --- missing at most one vertex --- and regularity plus parity then
force the cycle to pick up the last vertex too.

\textbf{!} The Lean signature omits the book's $k \ge 1$.  At $k = 0$ the statement reads
"every $0$-regular graph on $1$ vertex is hamiltonian", which is false in
Mathlib: a Hamilton cycle needs length $\ge 3$, so the one-vertex graph is not
\texttt{IsHamiltonian}.  The hypothesis $1 \le k$ must be added.
\end{theorem}

n21789.title: Ex 4.2.11(a): a Hamilton-connected graph satisfies $3\nu + 1 \le 2\varepsilon$ (Moon)
n21789.content:
\begin{theorem}[Ex 4.2.11(a): a Hamilton-connected graph satisfies $3\nu + 1 \le 2\varepsilon$ (Moon)]
\lean{SimpleGraph.hamiltonConnected_edge_bound}
\label{SimpleGraph.hamiltonConnected_edge_bound}
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsHamiltonConnected}
Hamilton-connectedness demands a spanning path between \emph{every} pair, forcing many
edges.  Every vertex must have degree at least $3$: a degree-$2$ vertex has both
its edges forced into any spanning path through it as an interior vertex, leaving
no way to make it an endpoint of a spanning path to a third vertex.  Summing
$d(v) \ge 3$ and applying handshaking gives $2\varepsilon \ge 3\nu$, and a parity refinement
pushes this to $2\varepsilon \ge 3\nu + 1$.

Formalised as $3\nu + 1 \le 2\varepsilon$ to stay in the natural numbers and avoid the ceiling.

\textbf{!} The Lean signature omits the book's $\nu \ge 4$.  It is needed: for $\nu = 3$,
$\top$ on three vertices is Hamilton-connected with $\varepsilon = 3$, but $3\nu + 1 = 10 > 6 = 2\varepsilon$.
So the statement as written is \textbf{false at $\nu = 3$} and \texttt{4 $\le$ Fintype.card V} must
be added.
\end{theorem}

n21790.title: nonempty\_iso\_iff
n21790.content:
\begin{theorem}[nonempty\_iso\_iff]
\lean{SimpleGraph.nonempty_iso_iff}
\label{SimpleGraph.nonempty_iso_iff}
\leanok
B\&M's general isomorphism needs two bijections, one on vertices and one
on edges, respecting incidence.  For \emph{simple} graphs the edge bijection carries no
information --- at most one edge joins any pair --- so an adjacency-preserving vertex
bijection already induces it.  This is precisely why Mathlib can define $G $\simeq$g H$ as
an equivalence of vertex types with \texttt{G.Adj u v $\leftrightarrow$ H.Adj ($\theta$ u) ($\theta$ v)}, and this
exercise is the justification for using it throughout the file.
\end{theorem}

n21794.title: Ex 1.2.10: the $k$-cube --- vertices are $k$-bit strings, adjacent iff they differ in exactly one coordinate
n21794.content:
\begin{definition}[Ex 1.2.10: the $k$-cube --- vertices are $k$-bit strings, adjacent iff they differ in exactly one coordinate]
\lean{SimpleGraph.hypercube}
\label{SimpleGraph.hypercube}
\leanok
Each vertex is a binary string of length $k$, equivalently a corner of a
$k$-dimensional cube; two corners are joined when their descriptions agree everywhere
but one position.  For $k = 3$ this is literally the corners and edges of an ordinary
cube --- the book's figure 1.4b.

Mathlib has no named hypercube graph, so this is built here.
Tuples are \texttt{Fin k $\to$ Bool}; "differ in exactly one coordinate" is $\exists! i, x i \ne y i$.
\texttt{SimpleGraph.fromRel} symmetrises the relation and removes the diagonal, which is
what makes the result a \texttt{SimpleGraph} without a separate looplessness proof --- at the
cost that \texttt{Adj} unfolds to $x \ne y \land (R x y \lor R y x)$, as the \texttt{hypercube\_bipartite}
proof has to unpack.
\end{definition}

n21832.title: isBipartite\_iff\_forall\_subgraph\_two\_mul\_indepNum\_le
n21832.content:
\begin{theorem}[isBipartite\_iff\_forall\_subgraph\_two\_mul\_indepNum\_le]
\lean{SimpleGraph.isBipartite_iff_forall_subgraph_two_mul_indepNum_le}
\label{SimpleGraph.isBipartite_iff_forall_subgraph_two_mul_indepNum_le}
($\Rightarrow$) Every subgraph of a bipartite graph is bipartite, and the larger side of a
bipartition is an independent set with at least half the vertices.

($\Leftarrow$) If $G$ were not bipartite it would contain an odd cycle (Thm 1.2).  That
cycle on $2k+1$ vertices has $\alpha = k$, and $2k < 2k+1$, so the condition fails at
that subgraph.

Stated as $\nu(H) \le 2\cdot\alpha(H)$ to avoid division.

"Subgraph $H$ of $G$" is \texttt{H : G.Subgraph}, which carries its own \texttt{verts} --- so
$\nu(H)$ genuinely shrinks and the odd-cycle witness is expressible.  \texttt{H.coe} is
the subgraph viewed as a \texttt{SimpleGraph ↥H.verts}, and \texttt{H.verts.ncard} is used in
place of \texttt{Fintype.card ↥H.verts} to avoid an instance that \texttt{[Fintype V]} alone
does not supply.
\end{theorem}

n21833.title: isBipartite\_iff\_forall\_subgraph\_indepNum\_eq\_edgeCoveringNumber
n21833.content:
\begin{theorem}[isBipartite\_iff\_forall\_subgraph\_indepNum\_eq\_edgeCoveringNumber]
\lean{SimpleGraph.isBipartite_iff_forall_subgraph_indepNum_eq_edgeCoveringNumber}
\label{SimpleGraph.isBipartite_iff_forall_subgraph_indepNum_eq_edgeCoveringNumber}
\uses{SimpleGraph.edgeCoveringNumber}
($\Rightarrow$) Theorem 7.3 applied subgraph-wise, every subgraph of a bipartite graph being
bipartite.

($\Leftarrow$) Contrapositive: an odd cycle $H$ on $2k+1$ vertices has $\delta(H) = 2 > 0$,
$\alpha(H) = k$ and $\beta'(H) = k + 1$, so the equality fails there.

So the identity $\alpha = \beta'$ --- which Theorem 7.3 gives for bipartite graphs ---
actually \emph{characterises} them.

\textbf{!} The instance binders \texttt{[Fintype H.verts] $\to$ [DecidableRel H.coe.Adj] $\to$} sit
\textbf{inside} the $\forall H$, as hypotheses rather than instance arguments.  That is
unusual and means a user must supply them explicitly at each application; it also
means the ($\Leftarrow$) direction gets to \emph{assume} them for its witness, which is harmless
here but worth noticing.
\end{theorem}

n21838.title: two\_mul\_coveringNumber\_le
n21838.content:
\begin{theorem}[two\_mul\_coveringNumber\_le]
\lean{SimpleGraph.two_mul_coveringNumber_le}
\label{SimpleGraph.two_mul_coveringNumber_le}
\uses{SimpleGraph.coveringNumber}
Stated as $2\beta \le \varepsilon + 1$ to avoid division.

A minimum covering touches every edge, and in a connected graph the edges are
linked tightly enough that each covering vertex can be charged at least two
edges, with one left over for a spanning tree's root.

\textbf{!} Note the book states this under 7.1.3, whose preamble defines $\beta$-critical ---
but part (b) does \textbf{not} assume $\beta$-criticality, only connectivity, and the Lean
signature correctly reflects that.  (The docstring previously implied the
$\beta$-critical hypothesis carried over; it does not.)

Connectivity is essential: a disjoint union of $k$ edges has $\beta = k = \varepsilon$, which
violates the bound for $k \ge 2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[ramseyMulti\_recursion]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ramseyMulti_recursion}
\label{SimpleGraph.ramseyMulti_recursion}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumberMulti}
Generalises Theorem 7.4's recursion.  Fix $v$ in a large $K_{n}$ and classify the
other vertices by the colour of their edge to $v$.  If every colour class were
smaller than $r(\dots, k_{i}-1, \dots)$, the classes could not cover all vertices --- which is
exactly what the bound arranges.  Some class is then big enough for a
monochromatic complete subgraph, and $v$ extends it in colour $i$.

subtraction $- m + 2$.

keeps it from truncating.

n21875.title: The composition (lexicographic product) $G(H)$
n21875.content:
\begin{definition}[The composition (lexicographic product) $G(H)$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.composition}
\label{SimpleGraph.composition}
Replace each vertex of $G$ by a copy of $H$.  Vertices in \emph{different} copies are
joined iff the corresponding $G$-vertices are adjacent; within one copy, iff
adjacent in $H$.  The $G$-structure dominates --- hence the alternative name
\emph{lexicographic product}.

\textbf{+} Fully defined, \texttt{symm} and \texttt{loopless} both discharged --- no \texttt{sorry}.

\textbf{!} Distinct from chapter 6's \texttt{boxProd} ($G \square H$), where within-copy and
across-copy edges are treated symmetrically.  Composition is not commutative.

Parts (b) and (c) of the exercise, to multiply Ramsey lower bounds.
\end{definition}

n21877.title: ramsey\_product\_lower
n21877.content:
\begin{theorem}[ramsey\_product\_lower]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ramsey_product_lower}
\label{SimpleGraph.ramsey_product_lower}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ramseyNumber}
Take $(k+1,k+1)$- and $(l+1,l+1)$-Ramsey graphs $G$, $H$ --- so $\omega, \alpha \le k$ and
$\le l$ respectively --- and form $G[H]$, which has the product vertex count.  Part
(a) gives $\alpha(G[H]) \le kl$; complementing gives $\omega(G[H]) \le kl$.  So $G[H]$ avoids
both a $(kl+1)$-clique and a $(kl+1)$-independent set.

Stated additively ($\dots + 1 \le r(\dots)$) to avoid $\mathbb{N}$ subtraction on the outside --- though
the two inner $- 1$s remain.

\textbf{!} The complement step needs $(G[H])^{c} \cong G^{c}[H^{c}]$, which is \textbf{true but not
obvious} and is not stated in this file.  Without it, part (a) bounds only $\alpha$
and the clique side has to be argued separately.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[The generalised Ramsey number $r(G_{1},\dots,G_m)$ over Mathlib's containment $\sqsubseteq$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.generalisedRamseyNumber}
\label{SimpleGraph.generalisedRamseyNumber}
\leanok
Instead of a monochromatic \emph{complete} subgraph, a monochromatic copy of a
prescribed graph.  All $G_{i}$ complete recovers \texttt{ramseyNumberMulti}.

"Subgraph isomorphic to $G_{i}$" is Mathlib's containment $\sqsubseteq$, and the colour-$i$
graph is \texttt{fromEdgeSet \{e | $\chi$ e = i $\land$ $\lnot$ e.IsDiag\}} --- the \texttt{$\lnot$ IsDiag} guard being
what stops the diagonal from creating spurious loops.

\textbf{!} Same \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} trap again, with \textbf{no} existence lemma for this notion
either.  So all four generalised-Ramsey results below are vacuous as stated.

\textbf{!} The graphs are indexed by \texttt{W : Fin m $\to$ Type*}, so each $G_{i}$ may live on a
different carrier --- flexible, but it means \texttt{![pathGraph 4, pathGraph 4]} below
must elaborate its motive carefully.
\end{definition}

n21881.title: tree\_isContained\_of\_minDegree\_le
n21881.content:
\begin{theorem}[tree\_isContained\_of\_minDegree\_le]
\lean{SimpleGraph.tree_isContained_of_minDegree_le}
\label{SimpleGraph.tree_isContained_of_minDegree_le}
\emph{ (absent from Mathlib).  }If $\delta(G) \ge m - 1$
then every tree $T$ on $m$ vertices embeds in $G$.*

Build the embedding greedily.  A tree on $m$ vertices can be listed so each new
vertex attaches to exactly one already-placed vertex (peel leaves).  Placing the
$j$-th, its unique placed neighbour has $\ge m - 1$ neighbours in $G$, of which at
most $j - 1 \le m - 2$ are used --- a fresh image always exists.

The standard "minimum degree forces every small tree" lemma; it is what makes
tree-target Ramsey numbers exactly computable.

\textbf{!} $m$ is a free variable in the signature, tied to $W$ only through
\texttt{hm : Fintype.card W = m} --- so $m$ is determined but Lean will not infer it;
callers must supply it.
\end{theorem}

n21882.title: generalisedRamsey\_tree\_star
n21882.content:
\begin{theorem}[generalisedRamsey\_tree\_star]
\lean{SimpleGraph.generalisedRamsey_tree_star}
\label{SimpleGraph.generalisedRamsey_tree_star}
\uses{SimpleGraph.generalisedRamseyNumber}
$K_{1,n}$ is the \textbf{star} with $n$ leaves, so a blue copy is a vertex with $n$
blue edges.  On $m + n - 1$ points, if no vertex has $n$ blue edges then every
vertex has $\ge (m+n-2) - (n-1) = m - 1$ red edges, and
\texttt{tree\_isContained\_of\_minDegree\_le} embeds $T$ in red.

Lower bound: a colouring of $K_{m+n-2}$ with no red $T$ and no blue star.  The
divisibility $(m-1) \mid (n-1)$ is exactly what lets the red graph be
$(m-2)$-regular --- too sparse for $T$, while leaving every vertex under $n$ blue
edges.

\textbf{!} The two targets live on \textbf{different carriers} ($W$ and \texttt{Fin 1 $\oplus$ Fin n}), so
$![T, K_{1,n}]$ cannot elaborate --- \texttt{Matrix.vecCons} is homogeneous.  Hence the
dependent spelling \texttt{Fin.cons T (Fin.cons \_ finZeroElim)} with an explicit type
family \texttt{W := ![W, Fin 1 $\oplus$ Fin n]}, and \texttt{W : Type} rather than \texttt{Type*}.
\end{theorem}

n21883.title: chvatal\_tree\_complete
n21883.content:
\begin{theorem}[chvatal\_tree\_complete]
\lean{SimpleGraph.chvatal_tree_complete}
\label{SimpleGraph.chvatal_tree_complete}
\uses{SimpleGraph.generalisedRamseyNumber}
One of the cleanest results in generalised Ramsey theory: the answer depends on
the tree only through its \textbf{number of vertices}, not its shape.

\emph{Lower bound.}  Partition $(m-1)(n-1)$ points into $n-1$ groups of $m-1$; red
inside groups, blue between.  Red is a disjoint union of $K_{m-1}$s, too small
for a tree on $m$ vertices; blue is complete $(n-1)$-partite, so its largest
clique has $n-1$ vertices --- no $K_{n}$.

\emph{Upper bound.}  On $(m-1)(n-1) + 1$ points, if blue has no $K_{n}$ then Tur\'an-type
reasoning gives red minimum degree $\ge m-1$ somewhere, and the sub-lemma embeds
$T$.

\textbf{!} Same heterogeneous-carrier spelling as part (b).

\textbf{!} The upper bound's "Tur\'an-type reasoning" is genuinely \S{}7.3's Theorem 7.9 ---
so this exercise depends on the \emph{next} section, not just on \S{}7.2.
\end{theorem}

n21885.title: degreeMajorised\_of\_forall\_degree\_le
n21885.content:
\begin{theorem}[degreeMajorised\_of\_forall\_degree\_le]
\lean{SimpleGraph.degreeMajorised_of_forall_degree_le}
\label{SimpleGraph.degreeMajorised_of_forall_degree_le}
\uses{SimpleGraph.DegreeMajorised}
(absent from Mathlib).  *If $d_G(v) \le d_H(v)$ for
every vertex $v$, then $G$ is degree-majorised by $H$.*

Degree-majorisation compares \emph{sorted} sequences entrywise.  Pointwise domination
survives sorting: the $i$-th smallest degree of $G$ cannot exceed the $i$-th
smallest of $H$.

\textbf{!} \textbf{Two problems with this as stated.}

1. \texttt{degreeSequence} in this file is \textbf{unsorted}, so "sorting preserves
   domination" is not what the predicate says --- the entrywise comparison is
   against \texttt{Finset.univ.toList}'s arbitrary order.  With both graphs on the same
   $V$ that order is at least \emph{the same} on both sides, so pointwise domination
   does happen to give the conclusion --- but only by accident of the shared
   carrier, not because the lemma is right.
2. It is stated for \texttt{G H : SimpleGraph V} on the \textbf{same} carrier, whereas
   Theorem 7.8 needs it across different carriers ($G$ on $V$, $H$ on $W$).  So
   it does not actually discharge the step it was extracted for.
\end{theorem}

n21888.title: triangle\_of\_not\_bipartite\_of\_card\_edgeFinset\_gt
n21888.content:
\begin{theorem}[triangle\_of\_not\_bipartite\_of\_card\_edgeFinset\_gt]
\lean{SimpleGraph.triangle_of_not_bipartite_of_card_edgeFinset_gt}
\label{SimpleGraph.triangle_of_not_bipartite_of_card_edgeFinset_gt}
Forbidding bipartiteness on top of triangle-freeness drops the cap from $\nu^{2}/4$ to
$(\nu-1)^{2}/4 + 1$.  A triangle-free non-bipartite graph contains an odd cycle of
length $\ge 5$, which is an inefficient use of vertices; the densest such graph is
essentially $C_{5}$ blown up.

The \textbf{stability} phenomenon of extremal graph theory: near-extremal graphs all
resemble the extremal one, so departing from it costs edges.

Cleared to $(\nu-1)^{2} + 4 < 4\varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}

n21893.content:
\begin{theorem}[isContained\_completeBipartite\_of\_card\_edgeFinset\_gt]
\lean{SimpleGraph.isContained_completeBipartite_of_card_edgeFinset_gt}
\label{SimpleGraph.isContained_completeBipartite_of_card_edgeFinset_gt}
Generalises 7.3.4 from $K_{2,m}$ to $K_{m,m}$.  Count \emph{stars} --- a vertex with $m$
of its neighbours --- two ways: each $v$ contributes $C(d(v), m)$, and each
$m$-set can be the leaf-set of $\le m-1$ stars unless a $K_{m,m}$ appears.
Convexity converts the degree sum into an edge count.

The exponent $2 - 1/m$ is the point: forbidding a complete \emph{bipartite} subgraph
caps $\varepsilon$ at strictly sub-quadratic order, unlike Tur\'an's constant fraction of
$\nu^{2}$.  Whether the exponent is tight for every $m$ is the \textbf{Zarankiewicz
problem}, still open.

\textbf{!} The \texttt{rpow} exponent varies with $m$, so this is irreducibly real-valued; and
$(m - 1 : \mathbb{R})$ with $hm : 1 \le m$ means the base can be $0$ at $m = 1$, where
$0 ^ (1/1) = 0$ --- check that boundary case does not make the hypothesis vacuous.
\end{theorem}

n21904.title: A maximum matching: a matching no larger than which exists
n21904.content:
\begin{definition}[A maximum matching: a matching no larger than which exists]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Subgraph.IsMaximumMatching}
\label{SimpleGraph.Subgraph.IsMaximumMatching}
\leanok
Mathlib supplies "matching" (\texttt{Subgraph.IsMatching}), "saturates"
(\texttt{v $\in$ M.verts}) and "perfect" (\texttt{Subgraph.IsPerfectMatching}), but has \textbf{no
matching-number notion}, so maximality has to be said by hand:

    M.IsMatching $\land$ $\forall$ M', M'.IsMatching $\to$ M'.edgeSet.ncard $\le$ M.edgeSet.ncard

This is a \emph{global} maximum, not a maximal matching (one admitting no extension).
The two genuinely differ, and Berge's Theorem 5.1 is exactly the tool that
certifies the global property from a local check.
\end{definition}

n21905.title: $M$-alternating walk: consecutive edges alternate in/out of $M$
n21905.content:
\begin{definition}[$M$-alternating walk: consecutive edges alternate in/out of $M$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Walk.IsAlternatingWalk}
\label{SimpleGraph.Walk.IsAlternatingWalk}
\leanok
Walk along the graph using a matching edge, then a non-matching edge, then a
matching edge, and so on.  Rendered as a chain condition on consecutive edges:

    List.IsChain (fun e f => e $\in$ M.edgeSet $\leftrightarrow$ f $\notin$ M.edgeSet) p.edges

\textbf{!} Mathlib's \texttt{SimpleGraph.IsAlternating} (\texttt{Matching.lean}) is a \emph{graph-level}
relation between two graphs and is \textbf{not} this notion; do not reach for it.

Note the definition is on a \texttt{Walk}, not a \texttt{Path} --- the book's "path" is imposed
separately in \texttt{IsAugmenting} below via \texttt{p.IsPath}.

Alternating paths are the mechanism by which a matching improves: swapping which
edges along such a path belong to $M$ keeps $M$ a matching.
\end{definition}

n21906.title: $M$-augmenting path: alternating, both ends $M$-unsaturated
n21906.content:
\begin{definition}[$M$-augmenting path: alternating, both ends $M$-unsaturated]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Walk.IsAugmenting}
\label{SimpleGraph.Walk.IsAugmenting}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.Walk.IsAlternatingWalk}
An alternating path both of whose endpoints are still unmatched.  Such a path has
odd length and begins and ends with non-matching edges, so it holds one more
non-$M$ edge than $M$ edge.  Flipping the roles along it --- discarding its
$M$-edges, adopting its non-$M$-edges --- yields a matching one edge \emph{larger},
which is why it is called augmenting.

\textbf{!} The conjunct $u \ne v$ is \textbf{load-bearing} and has no counterpart in the book's
wording.  Without it \texttt{Walk.nil} at an $M$-unsaturated vertex would satisfy every
other clause vacuously, so \emph{every} non-perfect matching would admit an
"augmenting path" and Berge's theorem would be false in the ($\Leftarrow$) direction.  The
book gets this for free because a path in its sense has at least one edge.
\end{definition}

n21907.title: A minimum covering

n21908.title: A $k$-factor: a $k$-regular spanning subgraph
n21908.content:
\begin{definition}[A $k$-factor: a $k$-regular spanning subgraph]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Subgraph.IsKFactor}
\label{SimpleGraph.Subgraph.IsKFactor}
\leanok
Keep every vertex, and select edges so each vertex retains exactly $k$.  A
$1$-factor is precisely a perfect matching; a $2$-factor is a spanning union of
disjoint cycles.

Degree is written \texttt{(H.neighborSet v).ncard} rather than \texttt{H.degree v} --- equal in
value, but avoiding the \texttt{Fintype}/\texttt{DecidableRel} instance juggling that
\texttt{Subgraph.degree} would drag in on every use.
\end{definition}

n21909.title: $G$ is $k$-factorable: it decomposes into edge-disjoint $k$-factors
n21909.content:
\begin{definition}[$G$ is $k$-factorable: it decomposes into edge-disjoint $k$-factors]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsKFactorable}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsKFactorable}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.Subgraph.IsKFactor}
The edges of $G$ partition into groups, each a $k$-regular spanning subgraph.
The book's $G = H_{1} \cup \dots \cup H_n$ becomes $(\bigsqcup i, H i) = \top$ in the \texttt{Subgraph} lattice,
where $\top$ is $G$ viewed as a subgraph of itself.

Being $1$-factorable means the edges split into perfect matchings: $K_{n,n}$ and
$K_{2n}$ are (exercise 5.1.5(a)(i)), the Petersen graph is not
(exercise 5.1.5(a)(ii)).

$1$-factorability is exactly proper edge colouring with $\Delta$ colours: each factor
is a colour class.  So exercise 5.1.5(a)(ii) is the statement that the Petersen
graph has chromatic index $4$, which reappears in \texttt{EdgeColourings.lean}.
\end{definition}

n21910.title: The $k$-cube $Q_k$
n21910.content:
\begin{definition}[The $k$-cube $Q_k$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.cube}
\label{SimpleGraph.cube}
The corners and edges of a $k$-dimensional cube: $k$-regular, bipartite (split by
the parity of the number of $1$s), $2^k$ vertices, $k\cdot 2^{k-1}$ edges.

Adjacency is the book's condition literally: $\exists! i, x i \ne y i$.

\textbf{!} Note this file defines \texttt{cube} directly as a structure, whereas
\texttt{GraphsAndSubgraphs.lean} defines the same graph as
\texttt{SimpleGraph.fromRel (fun x y => $\exists$! i, x i $\ne$ y i)}.  The two are equal but not
definitionally so, and neither imports the other.
\end{definition}

n21911.title: The $m \times n$ grid graph
n21911.content:
\begin{definition}[The $m \times n$ grid graph]
\lean{SimpleGraph.gridGraph}
\label{SimpleGraph.gridGraph}
Vertices are the squares of an $m \times n$ board, adjacent when they share a side.
A perfect matching is exactly a tiling by $1 \times 2$ dominoes, since each domino
covers precisely one side-adjacent pair.

Adjacency is spelled out coordinatewise: same row and columns differing by one,
or same column and rows differing by one.  Written on $\mathbb{N}$ values (\texttt{p.2.val + 1 =
q.2.val}) rather than on \texttt{Fin} arithmetic, which would wrap around and wrongly
join the last column to the first.
\end{definition}

n21926.title: Ex 5.1.1(b): number of perfect matchings of $K_{2n}$ is $(2n)! / (2^n n!)$
n21926.content:
\begin{theorem}[Ex 5.1.1(b): number of perfect matchings of $K_{2n}$ is $(2n)! / (2^n n!)$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.card_perfectMatching_completeGraph}
\label{SimpleGraph.card_perfectMatching_completeGraph}
A perfect matching of $K_{2n}$ partitions $2n$ labelled objects into $n$
unordered pairs.  Lining them up gives $(2n)!$ arrangements; each matching arises
from $2^n \cdot n!$ of them (swap within each pair, permute the pairs).  So the count
is $(2n)! / (2^n \cdot n!)$, the double factorial $(2n-1)!! = 1 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdots (2n-1)$.

\textbf{!} The Lean statement uses \textbf{natural-number division}.  It happens to be exact
here, but the proof cannot manipulate it as division --- it must establish
\texttt{Nat.card \dots \emph{ (2 \^{} n } n !) = (2 * n)!} and then divide, or the \texttt{Nat.div} will
obstruct every rewrite.
\end{theorem}

n21933.title: Ex 5.2.2(a): bipartite perfect-matching criterion
n21933.content:
\begin{theorem}[Ex 5.2.2(a): bipartite perfect-matching criterion]
\lean{SimpleGraph.bipartite_perfectMatching_iff}
\label{SimpleGraph.bipartite_perfectMatching_iff}
Hall's Theorem 5.2 gives a matching saturating $X$ from the condition on subsets
of $X$ alone.  Demanding it for \emph{all} subsets of $V$ is symmetric in $X$ and $Y$,
so it yields matchings saturating each side; together these force $|X| = |Y|$ and
a perfect matching.

\textbf{!} \texttt{hcov : X $\cup$ Y = Set.univ} is \textbf{required} and has no counterpart in the book's
wording, which takes "bipartition" to cover all vertices by definition.
Mathlib's \texttt{IsBipartiteWith} does not, so without \texttt{hcov} the bipartition could
miss vertices that no matching could ever saturate.
\end{theorem}

n21937.title: Ex 5.2.6(a): the K\"onig--Ore defect formula (stated additively to avoid $\mathbb{N}$ subtraction)
n21937.content:
\begin{theorem}[Ex 5.2.6(a): the K\"onig--Ore defect formula (stated additively to avoid $\mathbb{N}$ subtraction)]
\lean{SimpleGraph.konig_ore_defect}
\label{SimpleGraph.konig_ore_defect}
\uses{SimpleGraph.Subgraph.IsMaximumMatching}
Hall's theorem says a matching saturating $X$ exists exactly when
$|S| - |N(S)| \le 0$ for all $S \subseteq X$.  The defect formula quantifies failure: the
largest $|S| - |N(S)|$, the \textbf{deficiency}, is exactly how many vertices of $X$
a maximum matching must leave unsaturated.  Hall is the zero-deficiency case.

Formalised additively as \texttt{|M| + deficiency = |X|} to avoid $\mathbb{N}$ subtraction on the
outside.

\textbf{!} But the \emph{inner} \texttt{S.ncard - ($\bigcup$ \dots).ncard} is still natural subtraction, so it
truncates to $0$ exactly when Hall's condition holds at $S$ --- which is what makes
the $\bigsqcup$ compute the book's \texttt{max\{\dots\}} correctly only because the book's max is
also effectively taken against $0$ (via $S = \emptyset$).  This is a happy accident
rather than a faithful rendering, and is worth re-checking when the proof is
attempted.
\end{theorem}

\label{SimpleGraph.doublyStochastic_card_eq}
Sum every entry two ways.  By rows: $1$ each, so $m$ in total.  By columns: $1$
each, so $n$.  Hence $m = n$.

\textbf{!} \textbf{Restated, not transcribed.}  Mathlib's \texttt{doublyStochastic} is square *by
type*, so the literal statement would be vacuous.  This version takes a genuinely
rectangular \texttt{Matrix m n $\mathbb{R}$} with the two summation hypotheses given explicitly,
which is what the exercise actually asks.

Note the non-negativity hypothesis is not needed for this part and is omitted.
\end{theorem}
