n21942.title: Ex 5.3.3: a tree has a perfect matching iff $o(G - v) = 1$ for every vertex $v$
n21942.content:
\begin{theorem}[Ex 5.3.3: a tree has a perfect matching iff $o(G - v) = 1$ for every vertex $v$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.isTree_perfectMatching_iff}
\label{SimpleGraph.isTree_perfectMatching_iff}
Tutte's condition quantifies over all $S$, but for trees the singletons already
decide it.

($\Rightarrow$) The partner of $v$ lies in one component of $G - v$, and a parity count shows
exactly one component is odd.

($\Leftarrow$) $o(G - v) = 1$ for every $v$ is Tutte's condition at singletons, and
acyclicity makes that enough: build greedily from the leaves, each leaf forced to
match its unique neighbour.

Combined with exercise 5.1.2, a tree's perfect matching --- when it exists --- is
unique and locally detectable.
\end{theorem}

n21943.title: Ex 5.3.4*: the Berge--Tutte defect formula (stated additively to avoid $\mathbb{N}$ subtraction)
n21943.content:
\begin{theorem}[Ex 5.3.4*: the Berge--Tutte defect formula (stated additively to avoid $\mathbb{N}$ subtraction)]
\lean{SimpleGraph.berge_tutte_defect}
\label{SimpleGraph.berge_tutte_defect}
\uses{SimpleGraph.Subgraph.IsMaximumMatching}
Tutte says a perfect matching exists exactly when $o(G - S) - |S| \le 0$ for all
$S$.  Berge's formula quantifies failure: the maximum, the \textbf{deficiency} $d$, is
exactly how many vertices a maximum matching leaves unsaturated; the remaining
$\nu - d$ pair up.

$d = 0$ recovers Theorem 5.4.  The general-graph analogue of the K\"onig--Ore defect
formula (5.2.6(a)).

Formalised additively as $2|M| + d = \nu$ to avoid $\mathbb{N}$ subtraction on the outside.

\textbf{!} Same caveat as \texttt{konig\_ore\_defect}: the \emph{inner} \texttt{oddComponents.ncard - S.ncard}
is still natural subtraction and truncates at $0$.  Here that is actually
\emph{correct}, since $S = \emptyset$ always contributes $o(G) - 0 \ge 0$ and the book's max is
over a set containing a non-negative value --- but it should be re-verified rather
than assumed.
\end{theorem}

n21944.title: Ex 5.3.5(b): $\nu$ even, $\delta < \nu/2$, and a large edge count $\Rightarrow$ a perfect matching
n21944.content:
\begin{theorem}[Ex 5.3.5(b): $\nu$ even, $\delta < \nu/2$, and a large edge count $\Rightarrow$ a perfect matching]
\lean{SimpleGraph.perfectMatching_of_card_edges_gt}
\label{SimpleGraph.perfectMatching_of_card_edges_gt}
An edge-count sufficient condition, in the spirit of Corollary 4.6 for
hamiltonicity.  The threshold is the edge count of the densest simple graph on
$\nu$ vertices with minimum degree $\delta$ that still violates Tutte's condition: a
$\delta$-set $S$ whose removal leaves too many odd components, plus as many edges as
can be packed around it.  Exceeding it leaves no room to violate Tutte.

Part (a) --- "characterise the maximal simple graphs which have no perfect
matching" --- has no propositional content and is dropped; the book's answer is
recorded in the dropped-items section at the end of this file.
\end{theorem}

n21945.title: A network $N = (D, X, Y, c)$
n21945.content:
\begin{definition}[A network $N = (D, X, Y, c)$]
\lean{Networks.Network}
\label{Networks.Network}
\leanok
A transportation network: goods are produced at the sources, consumed
at the sinks, and shipped along the arcs, each with a maximum throughput.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib (0 hits for flow/network/capacity).
Capacity is carried as a \emph{function} \texttt{cap : V $\to$ V $\to$ $\mathbb{N}$}, with \texttt{cap u v = 0} encoding
"no arc $u \to v$"; this makes $f^{+}$/$f^{-}$ plain \texttt{Finset.sum}s.  \textbf{!} It cannot represent
\textbf{parallel arcs}, which is a real restriction --- lemma 11.4 is about a network in
which every arc has unit capacity, and B\&M's digraphs may have several arcs between
the same pair.

The structure carries \textbf{both} $X$, $Y$ (the source/sink \emph{sets} of \S{}11.1) and the
distinguished $x$, $y$ used from \S{}11.2 onward.  That is because the book reduces
the first to the second: *adjoin two new vertices $x$ and $y$; join $x$ to each
vertex in $X$ by an arc of capacity $\infty$; join each vertex in $Y$ to $y$ by an arc
of capacity $\infty$; designate $x$ as the source and $y$ as the sink of $N'$* --- after
which *throughout the next three sections, we shall confine our attention to
networks that have a single source $x$ and a single sink $y$*.  That reduction is
exercise 11.1.4, which is deferred here (it needs an $\mathbb{N}\infty$-capacity parallel
carrier), so the two are simply both recorded in the structure.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Structural defect: $x$, $y$ are unrelated to $X$, $Y$.}  Nothing in the
structure requires \texttt{N.x $\in$ N.X}, let alone \texttt{N.X = \{N.x\}}.  But \texttt{val} is defined over
the \emph{set} $X$ while every \S{}11.2--\S{}11.3 result is about cuts separating the single
$x$ from the single $y$.  The two therefore measure different things, and \textbf{lemma
11.1, theorem 11.1 in both forms, corollary 11.1 and theorem 11.3 are all false as
stated}.

\emph{Counterexample} (one network refutes all of them).  $V = {x_{1}, x_{2}, y_{1}}$,
$X = {x_{1}, x_{2}}$, $Y = {y_{1}}$, \texttt{N.x = x$_{1}$}, \texttt{N.y = y$_{1}$}; capacities $c(x_{1},y_{1}) = c(x_{2},y_{1}) = 1$
and $0$ elsewhere.  Then $I = \emptyset$, so any $f$ within capacity is a flow; take
$f(x_{1},y_{1}) = f(x_{2},y_{1}) = 1$.
\item \texttt{val f = f$^{+}$(X) - f$^{-}$(X) = 2}.
\item $S = {x_{1}}$ is a cut ($x_{1} \in S$, $y_{1} \notin S$), with $f^{+}(S) - f^{-}(S) = 1$ and
  \texttt{cap S = 1}.
\item So lemma 11.1 asserts $2 = 1$; theorem 11.1 asserts $2 \le 1$.
\item Max flow value is $2$, minimum cut capacity is $1$, so theorem 11.3 asserts
  $2 = 1$.
\item Corollary 11.1 fails too: $f'(x_{1},y_{1}) = 1$, $f'(x_{2},y_{1}) = 0$ has
  \texttt{val f' = 1 = cap\{x$_{1}$\}}, yet $f'$ is not a maximum flow.

\emph{The repair} is to add the fields \texttt{hx : N.X = \{N.x\}} and \texttt{hy : N.Y = \{N.y\}} to the
structure (the book's standing convention for \S{}\S{}11.2--11.4), or equivalently to add
them as hypotheses on the affected theorems.  The \S{}11.1 results --- exercises 11.1.2
and 11.1.3 --- are unaffected and should keep the general $X$, $Y$.
\end{definition}

A way of severing the network so the source is on one side and the
sink on the other.  Every unit of flow must cross every cut, which is why cuts
bound flows from above (theorem 11.1) --- and, more surprisingly, why the best cut
exactly matches the best flow (theorem 11.3).

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  Identified with the \emph{vertex set} $S$
rather than the arc set $(S, \bar{S})$, since $S$ determines the arcs and is far easier
to quantify over.  \texttt{capOf} then computes the arc set's capacity.  Note $y \notin S$ is
the book's $y \in \bar{S}$.
\end{definition}

n21955.title: An $f$-incrementing path from the source
n21955.content:
\begin{definition}[An $f$-incrementing path from the source]
\lean{Networks.Network.IncPath}
\label{Networks.Network.IncPath}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network}
A route from source to sink along which the flow can still be pushed
up.  Crucially it may travel \emph{against} an arc --- a \textbf{reverse arc} --- provided that
arc currently carries positive flow, which can then be cancelled.  This is what
lets the algorithm undo earlier bad choices, exactly as an augmenting path in
matching theory rearranges an existing matching; B\&M make the analogy explicit:
*the r\^ole played by incrementing paths in flow theory is analogous to that of
augmenting paths in matching theory* (compare theorem 5.1).  The book's example is
figure 11.5(a), where $P = xv_{1}v_{2}v_{3}y$ is $f$-incrementing with $\iota(P) = 2$.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib; an honest, complete inductive family ---
\emph{static}, not procedural.  \texttt{nil} starts at \texttt{N.x}; \texttt{fwd} extends along an
$f$-unsaturated arc (\texttt{f u v < cap u v}); \texttt{back} extends \emph{against} an $f$-positive
arc ($0 < f v u$).  The index is the current endpoint, so \texttt{N.IncPath f N.y} is
exactly an $f$-incrementing path.

\textbf{!} This is a directed \textbf{walk} --- repeated vertices are allowed --- not a path.  That
is deliberate and is what theorem 11.2's proof actually uses: the set $S$ of
vertices reachable by $f$-unsaturated \emph{walks} is what the cut is built from, and
restricting to paths would complicate the reachability closure for no gain.
\end{definition}

n21956.title: The residual capacity $\iota(P) > 0$ of an incrementing path --- a recursion over \texttt{IncPath}
n21956.content:
\begin{definition}[The residual capacity $\iota(P) > 0$ of an incrementing path --- a recursion over \texttt{IncPath}]
\lean{Networks.Network.IncPath.iota}
\label{Networks.Network.IncPath.iota}
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IncPath}
The bottleneck along the path.  A forward arc has room $c(a) - f(a)$
left; a reverse arc can give back at most the $f(a)$ it currently carries.  The
smallest of these slacks is how much extra can be pushed through in one go.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: this definition has a \texttt{sorry} body.}  $\iota(P)$ is therefore an opaque
natural number, not the bottleneck of anything.  Consequences: exercise 11.3.1
(\texttt{revisedFlow\_isFlow\_and\_val}) asserts \texttt{val $\hat{f}$ = val f + $\iota$(P)} about two opaque
constants and so says nothing, and the forward direction of theorem 11.2 --- which
needs $\iota(P) > 0$ to get a strictly better flow --- has no content to appeal to.
This also violates the project convention (\texttt{.claude/CLAUDE.md}): *never \texttt{sorry} in
a \texttt{def}*.

\emph{The repair} is a structural recursion over the \texttt{IncPath} family, carrying the
running minimum:

    iota nil          = $\top$ (or: recurse with an accumulator seeded at the first arc)
    iota (fwd P h)    = min (iota P) (cap u v - f u v)
    iota (back P h)   = min (iota P) (f v u)

The only wrinkle is \texttt{nil}, which has no arcs and so no minimum; either return a
sentinel and prove \texttt{0 < iota P} for non-\texttt{nil} paths, or index the recursion by a
running minimum passed in.  The second is cleaner and avoids $\mathbb{N}\infty$.
\end{definition}

n21957.title: The revised flow $\hat{f}$ (11.9) obtained by pushing $\iota(P)$ along $P$
n21957.content:
\begin{definition}[The revised flow $\hat{f}$ (11.9) obtained by pushing $\iota(P)$ along $P$]
\lean{Networks.Network.revisedFlow}
\label{Networks.Network.revisedFlow}
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IncPath}
Push $\iota(P)$ more along every forward arc of the path and take $\iota(P)$
back off every reverse arc.  Conservation survives because at each interior vertex
the increase in and the increase out match; and the value rises by exactly $\iota(P)$
(exercise 11.3.1).  This is the engine of the labelling method: repeatedly find an
incrementing path and revise, until none exists --- at which point theorem 11.2
certifies maximality.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: this definition has a \texttt{sorry} body.}  $\hat{f}$ is an opaque function, so
exercise 11.3.1 --- the only statement about it --- is vacuous, and theorem 11.2's
forward direction has nothing to revise with.  Same convention violation as
\texttt{iota}.

\emph{The repair} is a structural recursion over \texttt{IncPath} mirroring \texttt{iota}'s, adjusting
one arc per constructor:

    revisedFlow nil       = f
    revisedFlow (fwd P \_) = Function.update$_{2}$ (revisedFlow P) u v (f u v + iota P)
    revisedFlow (back P \_)= Function.update$_{2}$ (revisedFlow P) v u (f v u - iota P)

\textbf{!} Note \texttt{iota P} must be the bottleneck of the \textbf{whole} path, not of the prefix, or
the capacity constraint fails on early arcs --- so \texttt{iota} should be computed once and
threaded, rather than recomputed at each step.  That coupling is the reason both
definitions were deferred together, and it is why repairing \texttt{iota} first is the
right order.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The associated digraph $D(G)$: each edge becomes two opposite arcs (cited as ex 10.3.6)]
\lean{Networks.associatedDigraph}
\label{Networks.associatedDigraph}
Make every street two-way.  B\&M call it \emph{a simple trick}: it is how
theorems 11.5 and 11.7 are deduced from their directed counterparts 11.4 and 11.6,
since paths in $G$ correspond exactly to directed paths in $D(G)$.

One line --- \texttt{G.Adj} is already symmetric, so it \emph{is} the arc
relation.  A local copy of chapter 10's \texttt{SimpleGraph.associatedDigraph}; the
path correspondence that makes the trick work is that file's
\texttt{associatedDigraph\_pathEquiv}, which is itself \texttt{sorry}-bodied there.

n21974.title: The vertex-splitting digraph $D'$ of Theorem 11.6, on $V \oplus V$: \texttt{inl v = v'}, \texttt{inr v =\dots}
n21974.content:
\begin{definition}[The vertex-splitting digraph $D'$ of Theorem 11.6, on $V \oplus V$: \texttt{inl v = v'}, \texttt{inr v =\dots}]
\lean{Networks.splitDigraph}
\label{Networks.splitDigraph}
\leanok
Each vertex becomes a tiny one-way corridor $v' \to v''$, so *passing
through* $v$ now costs an arc.  This converts vertex-destruction into
arc-destruction, letting the vertex form of Menger's theorem be read off from the
arc form: *two directed $(x,y)$-paths in $D'$ are arc-disjoint if and only if the
corresponding paths in $D$ are internally-disjoint.*

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  Carrier $V \oplus V$, with \texttt{inl v = v'} and
\texttt{inr v = v''}; internal arcs are \texttt{inl u $\to$ inr v} when $u = v$, and original arcs
become \texttt{inr u $\to$ inl v}.

\textbf{!} \textbf{Simplified: it does not special-case $x$ and $y$.}  The book splits only
$V \ {x, y}$, leaving the endpoints intact; this splits \emph{every} vertex.  The
consequence is that $x$ and $y$ also acquire internal arcs, so a destroying set in
$D'$ could cut $x$'s or $y$'s own corridor --- which corresponds to deleting $x$ or
$y$ themselves, something the book's vertex-destruction forbids.  Statements about
\texttt{splitDigraph} therefore address \texttt{Sum.inr x} and \texttt{Sum.inl y} (the far ends of those
corridors), which sidesteps the issue for exercise 11.4.1; but the simplification
should be checked before it is relied on elsewhere.
\end{definition}

Nobody ships more than they can produce, and everybody receives at

n21976.title: $(p,q)$ is realisable by a simple bipartite graph: there is a $(0,1)$-matrix $B$ with row sums $p$ and\dots
n21976.content:
\begin{definition}[$(p,q)$ is realisable by a simple bipartite graph: there is a $(0,1)$-matrix $B$ with row sums $p$ and\dots]
\lean{Networks.RealisableBipartite}
\label{Networks.RealisableBipartite}
\leanok
Can two prescribed lists of degrees occur as the two sides of a
bipartite graph?  The book's $p = (3,2,2,2,1)$, $q = (3,3,2,1,1)$ is realisable
(figure 11.12), whereas $p = q = (5,4,4,2,1)$ is not (exercise 11.5.2) even though
the sums agree.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib (0 hits for Gale--Ryser).  Carried as a
$(0,1)$-\textbf{matrix} \texttt{B : Fin m $\to$ Fin n $\to$ Bool} rather than a bipartite \texttt{SimpleGraph},
following the book's own closing remark: *With each simple bipartite graph $G$ \dots
we can associate an $m \times n$ matrix $B$ in which $b_ij = 1$ or $0$, depending on
whether $x_{i}y_{j}$ is an edge of $G$ or not.  Conversely, every $m \times n$ $(0,1)$-matrix
corresponds in this way to a simple bipartite graph.*  The two are equivalent and
the matrix avoids constructing a graph on \texttt{Fin m $\oplus$ Fin n} with a bipartition proof.
Due to Ryser (1957).
\end{definition}

n21977.title: $G$ is $(m,n)$-orientable: it admits an orientation in which every indegree is $m$ or $n$
n21977.content:
\begin{definition}[$G$ is $(m,n)$-orientable: it admits an orientation in which every indegree is $m$ or $n$]
\lean{Networks.IsOrientable}
\label{Networks.IsOrientable}
\leanok
Make every edge one-way so each vertex ends up receiving exactly $m$
arrows, or exactly $n$.  Since $G$ is $(m+n)$-regular, indegree $m$ forces outdegree
$n$ and conversely, so an orientation splits the vertices into two classes.
Exercise 11.5.5(a) characterises orientability by a cut condition, and (b) shows the
classes can always be rebalanced one step towards each other.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib (0 hits for "orientable").  The
orientation is spelled out inline as a \texttt{Digraph D} with three clauses --- $D \subseteq G$, $D$
never two-way, $D$ covers every edge --- rather than reusing chapter 10's
\texttt{IsOrientationOf}, which this file does not import.  The fourth clause is the
indegree condition.  Note the $(m+n)$-regularity is \emph{not} part of this definition;
it appears as a hypothesis on the theorems that use it.
\end{definition}

n21978.title: $|(S, \bar{S})|$: the number of edges of $G$ crossing the cut $(S, \bar{S})$ (Ex 11.5.5)

\begin{definition}[$|(S, \bar{S})|$: the number of edges of $G$ crossing the cut $(S, \bar{S})$ (Ex 11.5.5)]
\lean{Networks.edgeBoundaryCard}
\label{Networks.edgeBoundaryCard}
\leanok
The size of the undirected edge cut at $S$ --- how many edges would have
to be severed to separate $S$ from the rest.  In exercise 11.5.5(a) it is the
capacity available to carry the imbalance the prescribed indegrees force across

A double sum of indicators rather than a \texttt{Finset.card}, matching

n21979.title: sum\_resultant\_eq\_fOut\_sub\_fIn
n21979.content:
\begin{theorem}[sum\_resultant\_eq\_fOut\_sub\_fIn]
\lean{Networks.sum_resultant_eq_fOut_sub_fIn}
\label{Networks.sum_resultant_eq_fOut_sub_fIn}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.fIn, Networks.Network.fOut}
Summing the \emph{net} outflow over the vertices of $S$ gives the net
outflow of $S$ as a whole.  The book flags the trap: *in general,
$\sum_{v \in S} f^{+}(v) \ne f^{+}(S)$ and $\sum_{v \in S} f^{-}(v) \ne f^{-}(S)$* --- only the difference
behaves, and only because the internal arcs cancel.

\textbf{*} \textbf{Build this first} --- lemma 11.1 and theorem 11.1 both rest on
it, and it is where the $\mathbb{Z}$-valuedness of \texttt{val} earns its keep: in $\mathbb{N}$ step 3's
cancellation is false, since $f^{+}{v} - f^{-}{v}$ truncates at each vertex individually.
Note it needs \textbf{no} \texttt{IsFlow} hypothesis: it is pure bookkeeping about an arbitrary
$f$.
\end{theorem}

n21981.title: val\_eq\_fOut\_sub\_fIn
n21981.content:
\begin{theorem}[val\_eq\_fOut\_sub\_fIn]
\lean{Networks.val_eq_fOut_sub_fIn}
\label{Networks.val_eq_fOut_sub_fIn}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IsCut, Networks.Network.IsFlow, Networks.Network.fIn, Networks.Network.fOut, Networks.Network.val}
The value of a flow can be measured across \emph{any} cut, not just at the
source: all the material has to cross somewhere, and nothing is lost in between.
This is the observation from which theorem 11.1 immediately follows.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Statement defect.}  This is \textbf{false as stated} --- the seam between \S{}11.1's
multi-source setting and \S{}11.2's single-source one.  B\&M close it by fiat
(*throughout the next three sections, we shall confine our attention to networks
that have a single source $x$ and a single sink $y$*), but the \texttt{Network} structure
here relates $x$, $y$ to $X$, $Y$ in no way at all, so \texttt{val} (defined over $X$) and
the cut (separating $x$ from $y$) measure different things.  The three-vertex
counterexample is worked out in full in the \texttt{Network} docstring above.  \emph{The repair}
is the hypothesis \texttt{N.X = \{N.x\}} (with \texttt{N.Y = \{N.y\}}), either as a structure field or
on this statement.  \textbf{The skeleton assumes it} --- step 1 is not derivable without
it.
\end{theorem}

n21991.title: maxFlow\_min\_cut
n21991.content:
\begin{theorem}[maxFlow\_min\_cut]
\lean{Networks.maxFlow_min_cut}
\label{Networks.maxFlow_min_cut}
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IsMaxFlow, Networks.Network.IsMinCut, Networks.Network.capOf, Networks.Network.val}
Theorem 11.1 gave the easy half --- \texttt{val f $\le$ cap K} for every flow and
cut; this says the bound is always achieved, so the bottleneck is not merely an
upper limit but the exact answer.  B\&M call it *of central importance in graph
theory\emph{: }many results on graphs turn out to be easy consequences of this theorem as
applied to suitably chosen networks*, as \S{}\S{}11.4 and 11.5 demonstrate with Menger's
theorems and the Gale--Ryser criterion.

\emph{The labelling method} (Ford and Fulkerson, 1957), which the constructive proof
yields: start from the zero flow and repeatedly grow an $f$-unsaturated tree from
$x$, until either it reaches $y$ (\textbf{breakthrough}, giving an incrementing path to
revise along) or it stops growing (certifying maximality by theorem 11.2).  B\&M note
it is \emph{not} a good algorithm --- figure 11.9 gives a network needing $2m + 1$
iterations for arbitrary $m$ --- but Edmonds and Karp (1970) showed that scanning
"first-labelled first-scanned", i.e. always taking a \emph{shortest} incrementing path,
makes it good.

Steps 1--4 are all already-stated results, so this theorem is
five lines once its inputs are filled --- but it sits at the top of the dependency
chain and inherits every defect below it, including the \texttt{sorry}-bodied $\iota$ and
\texttt{revisedFlow} via step 2.
\end{theorem}

n22000.content:
\begin{theorem}[dirac\_k\_vertices\_on\_cycle]
\lean{Networks.dirac_k_vertices_on_cycle}
\label{Networks.dirac_k_vertices_on_cycle}
\uses{Networks.vertexConnectivity}
High connectivity forces any prescribed set of $k$ vertices onto a
single cycle.  For $k = 2$ this is corollary 3.2.1 --- in a 2-connected graph any two
vertices lie on a common cycle.  One of the classic applications of Menger's
theorem, illustrating B\&M's remark that *many results on graphs turn out to be easy
consequences* of max-flow min-cut.

Depends on exercise 11.4.3, hence on two \texttt{sorry}-bodied
definitions; but note the \emph{statement} here mentions none of them --- it is about
\texttt{Walk}/\texttt{IsCycle} only, so it is well-formed and would be meaningful once its
dependency is repaired.  Among the \S{}11.4 items, this is the one whose statement is
already honest.
\end{theorem}

n22001.title: gale\_feasible\_flow
n22001.content:
\begin{theorem}[gale\_feasible\_flow]
\lean{Networks.gale_feasible_flow}
\label{Networks.gale_feasible_flow}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IsFeasible, Networks.Network.capOf}
A feasible flow exists exactly when, for every way of splitting the
vertices, the capacity available for shipping into $\bar{S}$ covers the \emph{net} demand there
--- the demand of the sinks in $\bar{S}$ less whatever supply already sits inside $\bar{S}$.
Necessity is obvious (that much material must cross the boundary); the content is
sufficiency.

\textbf{!} Steps 3--4 use corollary 11.1 and theorem 11.3, both currently
false for want of the \texttt{N.X = \{N.x\}} link --- though note $N'$ is built with a genuine
single source and sink, so the repair is satisfied \emph{there}; the defect bites only if
one tries to apply those results to $N$ itself.  Step 1's construction is the
largest single piece of work in \S{}11.5.
\end{theorem}

n22002.title: galeRyser\_realisable
n22002.content:
\begin{theorem}[galeRyser\_realisable]
\lean{Networks.galeRyser_realisable}
\label{Networks.galeRyser_realisable}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.RealisableBipartite}
Equal sums (11.16) are necessary --- both count the edges --- but not
sufficient, as $p = q = (5,4,4,2,1)$ shows.  Condition (11.18) adds that the $k$
largest demands can actually be met: each $x_{i}$ can supply at most \texttt{min\{p$_{i}$, k\}} of
them, having only $p_{i}$ edges and only $k$ targets.

\emph{Matrix form.}  Let $B*$ have its first $p_{i}$ entries of row $i$ equal to $1$, and let
$p*$ be its column sums --- the \textbf{conjugate} of $p$ (that of $(5,4,4,2,1)$ is
$(5,4,3,3,1)$).  Row $i$ contributes \texttt{min\{p$_{i}$, k\}} to $\sum_{j\le k} p*_{j}$, so (11.18) says
exactly $\sum_{j\le k} p*_{j} \ge \sum_{j\le k} q_{j}$ --- the conjugate of $p$ dominates $q$.  Due to
Ryser (1957).

The chapter's hardest item.  $k$ is a \texttt{Fin n} and the book's
$1 \le k \le n$ becomes \texttt{k.val + 1} in the \texttt{min}, so check the off-by-one against the
book when filling.  The $(0,1)$-matrix carrier is used rather than a bipartite-graph
predicate; see \texttt{RealisableBipartite}.
\end{theorem}

n22003.title: realisable\_iff\_reduced
n22003.content:
\begin{theorem}[realisable\_iff\_reduced]
\lean{Networks.realisable_iff_reduced}
\label{Networks.realisable_iff_reduced}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.RealisableBipartite}
The bipartite analogue of the Havel--Hakimi reduction for degree
sequences (exercise 1.5.7): the vertex $x_{1}$ may as well spend its $p_{1}$ edges on the
$p_{1}$ highest-demand vertices of $Y$.  Part (b) --- dropped here as procedural --- turns
this into a construction algorithm.

\textbf{!} Two departures, both flagged in the source comment.  (i) $q'$
uses \textbf{truncated} natural subtraction ($q j - 1$ is $0$ when $q j = 0$), which is
harmless only because a realisable $q$ has $q j \ge 1$ wherever row $0$ puts an edge ---
worth checking rather than assuming.  (ii) B\&M's $q'$ is \textbf{re-sorted} into
nonincreasing order, which this statement elides; without re-sorting, $q'$ need not
satisfy (11.17), so this reduction cannot be chained with theorem 11.9 as the book
intends.  If the intent is to iterate the reduction, the re-sorting must be
restored.
\end{theorem}

n22004.title: isOrientable\_iff\_exists\_partition
n22004.content:
\begin{theorem}[isOrientable\_iff\_exists\_partition]
\lean{Networks.isOrientable_iff_exists_partition}
\label{Networks.isOrientable_iff_exists_partition}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.IsOrientable, Networks.edgeBoundaryCard}
An $(m+n)$-regular graph is to be oriented so every indegree is $m$ or
$n$.  The partition names in advance which vertices get which, and the inequality is
a feasibility condition in Gale's sense.

\textbf{!} Step 2 needs an \textbf{eulerian orientation}, which comes from
chapters 4 and 10 (every graph with all degrees even has an Euler tour; orient along
it) --- a genuine import, absent from this file.  Note $(m+n)$-regular forces every
degree even only when $m + n$ is even, so the eulerian step may itself need the
odd-degree patch of chapter 10's exercise 10.1.10.  The absolute value is written as
a \textbf{two-sided bound} to avoid \texttt{abs} and keep the arithmetic in $\mathbb{Z}$.
\end{theorem}

n22005.title: isOrientable\_pred\_succ
n22005.content:
\begin{theorem}[isOrientable\_pred\_succ]
\lean{Networks.isOrientable_pred_succ}
\label{Networks.isOrientable_pred_succ}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.IsOrientable}
The two permitted indegrees can always be moved one step closer
together.  Iterating, an $(m,n)$-orientable graph is $(m',n')$-orientable for every
admissible pair with $m' + n' = m + n$ and $|m' - n'| \le |m - n|$ --- in particular the
most balanced orientation is always available.

A short deduction \emph{given} part (a), which is the starred and
substantial half.  Step 2's "scales down" should be checked at the sign: the bound
is two-sided, so both directions shrink only because $|m - n - 2| \le |m - n|$ when
$m - n \ge 1$.
\end{theorem}

n22006.title: A walk is internally disjoint from a subgraph $H$: no \emph{internal} vertex lies in $H$
n22006.content:
\begin{definition}[A walk is internally disjoint from a subgraph $H$: no \emph{internal} vertex lies in $H$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Walk.InternallyDisjointFrom}
\label{SimpleGraph.Walk.InternallyDisjointFrom}
\leanok
The walk may start and end on $H$, but between those endpoints it
must stay entirely outside $H$.  This is what makes the bridge relation an
equivalence, and it is why a bridge is a maximal chunk of the graph hanging off
$H$ and touching it only at its attachment points.

\texttt{p.support.tail.dropLast} is the walk's interior --- drop the
first vertex (\texttt{tail}) and the last (\texttt{dropLast}).  \textbf{!} This is \textbf{not} the repo's
\texttt{InternallyDisjoint} (\texttt{TwoConnected.lean:58}), which relates a walk to another
\emph{walk}; here the second argument is a \texttt{Subgraph}.  A walk of length $\le 1$ has empty
interior and so is vacuously internally disjoint from everything --- which is
intended, and is what makes \texttt{bridgeRel} reflexive on single edges.
\end{definition}

n22007.title: B\&M's relation $~$ on $E(G) \ E(H)$: $e_{1} ~ e_{2}$ iff joined by a walk internally disjoint from $H$\dots
n22007.content:
\begin{definition}[B\&M's relation $~$ on $E(G) \ E(H)$: $e_{1} ~ e_{2}$ iff joined by a walk internally disjoint from $H$\dots]
\lean{SimpleGraph.bridgeRel}
\label{SimpleGraph.bridgeRel}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.Walk.InternallyDisjointFrom}
Two edges outside $H$ are related when you can travel from one to the
other without passing through $H$.  Grouping edges into classes carves
$G - E(H)$ into the pieces that hang off $H$ --- those pieces are the bridges.

\texttt{Relation.EqvGen} wraps the book's raw condition in its
reflexive--symmetric--transitive closure, which \emph{discharges} the book's "it is easy
to verify" rather than proving it: whatever the raw relation does, the closure is
an equivalence by construction.  This is a deliberate trade --- the file gains an
equivalence for free, at the cost that \texttt{bridgeRel} is a priori coarser than $\sim$.
It is not actually coarser (the book's $\sim$ really is an equivalence), but nothing
here proves that, so do not appeal to "\texttt{bridgeRel e f} gives a single connecting
walk" --- it gives a \emph{chain} of them.  Several skeletons below rely on this
distinction.
\end{definition}

n22008.title: The bridge of $H$ in $G$ containing the edge $e$: the subgraph induced by $e$'s $~$-class
n22008.content:
\begin{definition}[The bridge of $H$ in $G$ containing the edge $e$: the subgraph induced by $e$'s $~$-class]
\lean{SimpleGraph.bridgeOf}
\label{SimpleGraph.bridgeOf}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.bridgeRel}
A bridge is one of the connected pieces remaining when $H$ is
removed, together with the attachment points where it touches $H$.  The three
"immediate" facts quoted above are \texttt{bridgeOf\_connected},
\texttt{exists\_path\_internallyDisjoint} and \texttt{bridge\_inter\_subset\_cycle} below --- none of
them is actually immediate once $\sim$ is a closure.  In planar graph theory bridges
carry the argument: theorem 9.8 says inner bridges of a cycle avoid one another,
theorem 9.9 that a bridge avoiding every outer bridge is transferable, and together
these drive Kuratowski's theorem 9.10.

Indexed by a \emph{representative edge} $e$ rather than by a class,
so "the bridge containing $e$"; two edges give the same bridge exactly when
\texttt{bridgeRel H e f}.  Built with \texttt{Subgraph.mk} directly --- \textbf{not} with
\texttt{SimpleGraph.toSubgraph} (\texttt{Subgraph.lean:559}), which is \emph{spanning} and would put
every vertex of $G$ into every bridge.  Note \texttt{verts} is the union of the class's
edges, so it automatically includes the attachment points.

\textbf{!} Because \texttt{bridgeRel} is reflexive for \emph{any} $e$ (it is an \texttt{EqvGen}), \texttt{bridgeOf H e}
is nonempty even for an $e$ that is not an edge of $G$ at all --- it then has two
vertices and no edges.  Statements about bridges must therefore carry
\texttt{e $\in$ G.edgeSet \textbackslash\{\} H.edgeSet} explicitly.  Two of them below originally omitted it and
were false as a result; both now carry it (see the module header).
\end{definition}

n22009.title: Vertices of attachment of the bridge of $e$ to the cycle traced by $c$: $V(B) \cap V(C)$
n22009.content:
\begin{definition}[Vertices of attachment of the bridge of $e$ to the cycle traced by $c$: $V(B) \cap V(C)$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.attach}
\label{SimpleGraph.attach}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.bridgeOf}
The points at which the bridge touches down onto the cycle.  Almost
everything in \S{}9.4 is a statement about how two bridges' attachment sets interleave
around $C$ --- \texttt{Overlaps}, \texttt{Skew} and the segments below are all built on this one
set.

Specialised to \texttt{H = c.toSubgraph} for a closed walk $c$, since
\S{}9.4 only ever needs bridges of a \emph{cycle}.  A \texttt{Set V}, not a \texttt{Finset}, so that
\texttt{.ncard} is used for $k$ (see theorem 9.6's conclusion).  "$B$ is a $k$-bridge"
is spelled \texttt{(G.attach c e).ncard = k}, and "$B$ and $B'$ are equivalent" is
\texttt{G.attach c e = G.attach c e'}.
\end{definition}

n22010.title: Position of a vertex along a cycle (index into its support)
n22010.content:
\begin{definition}[Position of a vertex along a cycle (index into its support)]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Walk.cycleIdx}
\label{SimpleGraph.Walk.cycleIdx}
\leanok
Walking around the cycle from its base point, this records how many
steps it takes to reach $x$.  Comparing indices is how "cyclic order" is expressed
here.

\textbf{!} Mathlib's \texttt{CircularOrder}/\texttt{Btw}/\texttt{SBtw} are order classes on a
\emph{type} and do not apply to the support list of a particular cycle, so they are no
help.  \textbf{!} \texttt{List.idxOf} silently returns the list's \texttt{length} for an absent element,
so every use must be guarded by \texttt{x $\in$ c.support} --- unguarded, all missing vertices
quietly share one position past the end.  Note also that this is genuinely
\emph{linear}, not cyclic: it is measured from $c$'s base point, so \texttt{InCyclicOrder}
below expresses a cyclic condition only up to the choice of that base point.
\end{definition}

n22011.title: Four vertices in cyclic order on $c$
n22011.content:
\begin{definition}[Four vertices in cyclic order on $c$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Walk.InCyclicOrder}
\label{SimpleGraph.Walk.InCyclicOrder}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.Walk.cycleIdx}
Travelling once round the cycle, the four vertices are met in that
order.  This is the configuration making two bridges \emph{skew}: each bridge's two
attachments separate the other's, so drawn inside the same region their connecting
paths would have to cross --- which is precisely the Jordan-curve contradiction in
theorem 9.8.

Rendered as a chain of strict \texttt{cycleIdx} inequalities, i.e. as
a \emph{linear} order from $c$'s base point rather than a genuinely cyclic one.  This is
weaker than the book's phrase: the book's "cyclic order $u, u', v, v'$" is invariant
under rotation, whereas this version distinguishes rotations.  It suffices for
\texttt{Skew}, which existentially quantifies over which attachment plays which role and so
recovers rotation-invariance, but do not reuse \texttt{InCyclicOrder} where genuine
rotation-invariance is needed.
\end{definition}

n22012.title: Forward distance along $c$ from $a$ to $x$, in steps, wrapping at the base point
n22012.content:
\begin{definition}[Forward distance along $c$ from $a$ to $x$, in steps, wrapping at the base point]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Walk.cycleDist}
\label{SimpleGraph.Walk.cycleDist}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.Walk.cycleIdx}
Stand at $a$ and walk forwards around the cycle; this counts the steps
until $x$ is reached.  Unlike \texttt{cycleIdx} --- which is measured from $c$'s own base
point and so is merely linear --- this is genuinely cyclic: it is what lets an arc
"wrap round" past the base point.

\textbf{!} Guard uses by \texttt{a, x $\in$ c.support}.  \texttt{cycleIdx} returns
\texttt{c.support.length} for an absent vertex, which here yields a meaningless distance.
For $a$ on the cycle the $\mathbb{N}$-subtraction never truncates: \texttt{cycleIdx a $\le$ c.length}
(the base point occurs first at index $0$), so \texttt{cycleIdx x + c.length $\ge$ cycleIdx a}.
The \texttt{\% c.length} is what performs the wraparound; for a degenerate $c$ of length $0$
it is the identity ($n \% 0 = n$ in Lean), which is harmless since every use site
carries \texttt{hc : c.IsCycle}.
\end{definition}

n22013.title: $x$ lies on the closed arc of $c$ running forwards from $a$ to $b$
n22013.content:
\begin{definition}[$x$ lies on the closed arc of $c$ running forwards from $a$ to $b$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Walk.OnArc}
\label{SimpleGraph.Walk.OnArc}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.Walk.cycleDist}
Walking forwards from $a$, you meet $x$ no later than $b$.  Both
endpoints count as being on the arc, matching the book's segments, which share their
endpoints with the neighbouring segments and so are edge-disjoint but not
vertex-disjoint.

Stated via \texttt{cycleDist}, so the wraparound is handled: the arc
from $a$ to $b$ may pass through $c$'s base point.  The \texttt{x $\in$ c.support} conjunct is
the guard that keeps vertices off the cycle out, since \texttt{cycleDist} would otherwise
give them a spurious finite distance.
\end{definition}

n22014.title: $a$ and $b$ are consecutive vertices of attachment of the bridge of $e$: both are attachments, and no\dots

n22015.title: Two bridges of a cycle avoid one another: all the attachments of one lie in a single segment of the other

n22016.title: Two bridges of a cycle overlap: they do not avoid one another
n22016.content:
\begin{definition}[Two bridges of a cycle overlap: they do not avoid one another]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Overlaps}
\label{SimpleGraph.Overlaps}
\uses{SimpleGraph.Avoids}
Neither bridge's attachments fit inside a single segment of the other,
so drawn on the same side of $C$ they would be forced to cross.  Theorem 9.8 says
this cannot happen for two inner (or two outer) bridges of a plane graph, and
theorem 9.6 says overlapping comes in only two shapes.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Repaired --- previously \texttt{sorry}.}  This definition formerly had the body
\texttt{Prop := sorry}, making it an \emph{opaque, unspecified} proposition and rendering
\texttt{overlap\_imp\_skew\_or\_equivalent\_three\_bridge} (theorem 9.6) vacuous: with \texttt{Overlaps}
opaque, that theorem said nothing about bridges and "proving" it would have
established nothing.  It also violated the project convention
(\texttt{.claude/CLAUDE.md}): \emph{never \texttt{sorry} in a \texttt{def}} --- a \texttt{sorry}-ed proof is an honest
debt, a \texttt{sorry}-ed definition is a silent change of meaning.

It is now the honest negation of \texttt{Avoids}, built on the segment machinery above
(\texttt{cycleDist} $\to$ \texttt{OnArc} $\to$ \texttt{ConsecutiveAttach} $\to$ \texttt{Avoids}), which is the layer B\&M
assume when they speak of segments.  \textbf{!} \texttt{[DecidableEq V]} had to be added to the
signature, since \texttt{cycleIdx} needs it; every use site already had the instance.
\end{definition}

n22017.title: Two bridges of a cycle are skew: they have attachments $a, a', b, b'$ occurring in that cyclic order on\dots
n22017.content:
\begin{definition}[Two bridges of a cycle are skew: they have attachments $a, a', b, b'$ occurring in that cyclic order on\dots]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Skew}
\label{SimpleGraph.Skew}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.Walk.InCyclicOrder, SimpleGraph.attach}
The two bridges interleave around the cycle.  In a plane graph this is
fatal for two bridges on the same side: their connecting paths would have to cross,
contradicting the Jordan curve theorem --- which is exactly the (dropped) proof of
theorem 9.8.

The book asks for \emph{four distinct} vertices; the Lean version
requires only $a \ne b$ and $a' \ne b'$.  The remaining distinctness is implied by the
strict \texttt{cycleIdx} chain in \texttt{InCyclicOrder}, since distinct indices force distinct
vertices --- provided all four lie on \texttt{c.support}, which the \texttt{attach} memberships
supply.  Rotation-invariance is recovered by the existential over which attachment
plays which role, compensating for \texttt{InCyclicOrder} being measured from $c$'s base
point.
\end{definition}

n22018.title: A longest cycle
n22018.content:
\begin{definition}[A longest cycle]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Walk.IsLongestCycle}
\label{SimpleGraph.Walk.IsLongestCycle}
\leanok
A cycle no shorter than any other cycle of $G$.  This is the standard
extremal device: assume the longest cycle is not a Hamilton cycle, then derive a
contradiction from the structure of the bridges hanging off it.  That is exactly how
Chv\'atal--Erd\H{o}s is proved below.

\textbf{!} Not \texttt{girth}/\texttt{egirth}, which are the \emph{shortest} cycle --- the
opposite extremum.  The maximality clause quantifies over cycles at \emph{every} base
point $w$, not just at $u$, which is what makes it a genuine global maximum.  Note
the definition does not assert existence: \texttt{IsLongestCycle} is a hypothesis to be
supplied, and producing one requires knowing $G$ has a cycle at all.
\end{definition}

n22019.title: minDegree\_le\_five\_of\_card\_edge\_le
n22019.content:
\begin{theorem}[minDegree\_le\_five\_of\_card\_edge\_le]
\lean{SimpleGraph.minDegree_le_five_of_card_edge_le}
\label{SimpleGraph.minDegree_le_five_of_card_edge_le}
\leanok
A planar graph cannot be everywhere dense: Euler's formula caps its
edge count at $3\nu - 6$, so the average degree is below $6$ and some vertex has
degree at most $5$.  This is the fact driving the five-colour theorem 9.11 --- every
planar graph has a vertex of degree at most five to induct on --- and it is why the
arithmetic core was worth salvaging even though the planarity around it was not.

\textbf{!} This is \textbf{not} corollary 9.5.3 as the book states it.
Planarity is replaced by the hypothesis $h\varepsilon$, which corollary 9.5.2 (dropped, being
unstatable without faces) would have supplied.  Ship it under the name
\texttt{minDegree\_le\_five\_of\_card\_edge\_le}, never as \texttt{planar\_minDegree\_le\_five}: the
theorem proved is the arithmetic half only.  Stated additively ($\varepsilon + 6 \le 3\nu$) to
dodge truncated $\mathbb{N}$-subtraction.

Worth knowing while filling: \textbf{\texttt{h$\nu$ : 3 $\le$ Fintype.card V} is unused.}  Steps 1--4
never mention $\nu$ except through the two inequalities $2\varepsilon + 12 \le 6\nu$ and
$6\nu \le 2\varepsilon$, whose contradiction is independent of the size of $\nu$.  The book needs
its $\nu = 1, 2$ caveat because it invokes corollary 9.5.2, which carries $\nu \ge 3$;
once that corollary is replaced by the raw hypothesis $h\varepsilon$, the caveat evaporates.
$h\nu$ is kept only so the statement still reads as the book's; do not go looking for
a place to use it.
\end{theorem}

n22020.title: card\_edgeFinset\_add\_card\_edgeFinset\_compl
n22020.content:
\begin{theorem}[card\_edgeFinset\_add\_card\_edgeFinset\_compl]
\lean{SimpleGraph.card_edgeFinset_add_card_edgeFinset_compl}
\label{SimpleGraph.card_edgeFinset_add_card_edgeFinset_compl}
\leanok
$\varepsilon(G) + \varepsilon(G^{c}) = C(\nu, 2)$.

Every unordered pair of distinct vertices carries an edge in exactly
one of $G$ and $G^{c}$ --- that is precisely what complementation means --- so the two
edge counts partition the $C(\nu, 2)$ available pairs.  Together with the planar edge
bound applied to \emph{both} graphs, this is the whole of exercise 9.3.3(a).

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib (0 hits at the time of writing; step 3 is
the part most likely to exist already, so search before building).  Needs both
\texttt{DecidableRel G.Adj} and \texttt{DecidableRel G$^{c}$.Adj} as instances, since \texttt{edgeFinset} is
only available with decidable adjacency.
\end{theorem}

n22021.title: not\_both\_card\_edge\_le\_of\_eleven\_le
n22021.content:
\begin{theorem}[not\_both\_card\_edge\_le\_of\_eleven\_le]
\lean{SimpleGraph.not_both_card_edge_le_of_eleven_le}
\label{SimpleGraph.not_both_card_edge_le_of_eleven_le}
\leanok
Planarity forces sparsity, and a graph and its complement cannot both
be sparse: between them they must carry \emph{every} possible edge, and $C(\nu,2)$ outgrows
$2(3\nu-6)$ at exactly $\nu = 11$.  Part (b) of the exercise confirms the bound is
sharp in spirit --- there is a simple planar graph on $\nu = 8$ vertices whose
complement is also planar.

\textbf{!} This is \textbf{not} exercise 9.3.3(a) as stated.  "Planar" is
replaced by the corollary-9.5.2 edge bound on \emph{both} sides, so what is proved is
that the two bounds are jointly unsatisfiable --- the arithmetic obstruction, with
the topology stripped out.  The conclusion is therefore a negated conjunction
rather than "$G^{c}$ is nonplanar".
\end{theorem}

n22022.title: bridge\_inter\_subset\_cycle
n22022.content:
\begin{theorem}[bridge\_inter\_subset\_cycle]
\lean{SimpleGraph.bridge_inter_subset_cycle}
\label{SimpleGraph.bridge_inter_subset_cycle}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.bridgeOf, SimpleGraph.bridgeRel}
Bridges can only meet on $H$ itself.  If a vertex outside $H$ lay in
two bridges, edges of both would meet there, and a walk through it from one to the
other stays outside $H$ --- so those edges are related and the two bridges were the
same class all along.  This is what makes the bridge decomposition genuinely a
decomposition: the bridges partition $E(G) \ E(H)$ and meet only at attachment
points.

"Distinct bridges" is \texttt{hne : $\lnot$ G.bridgeRel H e e'} --- two
representative edges in different classes --- rather than a disequality of subgraphs,
which would be weaker and harder to use.  The hypotheses $he$, $he'$ placing both
edges in \texttt{G.edgeSet \textbackslash\{\} H.edgeSet} are present and are needed: without them
\texttt{bridgeOf} degenerates (see its docstring).
\end{theorem}

n22023.title: bridgeOf\_connected

n22024.title: exists\_path\_internallyDisjoint
n22024.content:
\begin{theorem}[exists\_path\_internallyDisjoint]
\lean{SimpleGraph.exists_path_internallyDisjoint}
\label{SimpleGraph.exists_path_internallyDisjoint}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.Walk.InternallyDisjointFrom, SimpleGraph.bridgeOf}
Not only is a bridge connected, but the connection can be made without
re-entering $H$.  This is the form actually used downstream: theorem 9.7 needs
$(v_{1},v_{2})$-paths inside a bridge avoiding the cycle internally, and the dropped
theorem 9.8 needs the same to reach its Jordan-curve contradiction.

The path is asked for as a \texttt{G.Walk}, not a walk in the bridge.
That is equivalent and more convenient: a walk in $G$ between two bridge vertices
that is internally disjoint from $H$ automatically has all its edges in the bridge's
class.  Note the trans case in step 1 is the reason this is genuinely harder than
\texttt{bridgeOf\_connected} and not a corollary of it.
\end{theorem}

n22025.title: bridge\_tripod\_of\_three\_attachments
n22025.content:
\begin{theorem}[bridge\_tripod\_of\_three\_attachments]
\lean{SimpleGraph.bridge_tripod_of_three_attachments}
\label{SimpleGraph.bridge_tripod_of_three_attachments}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.bridgeOf}
The picture is a \textbf{tripod}: a hub $v_{0}$ strictly off the cycle, with
three legs reaching down to the three attachment points.  This is what the dropped
theorem 9.8 uses to dispose of equivalent 3-bridges, and what Kuratowski's theorem
9.10 uses to locate $K_{3,3}$ subdivisions.

The "only the vertex $v_{0}$ in common" conditions are spelled as
three \texttt{$\forall$ x, x $\in$ \_.support $\to$ x $\in$ \_.support $\to$ x = v$_{0}$} clauses rather than as set
equalities, which is what the \texttt{takeUntil}/\texttt{dropUntil} lemmas deliver directly.
Note step 5 is genuinely extra work: the book states $v_{0} \in V(B) \ V(C)$ in the
theorem but never justifies it in the proof.
\end{theorem}

n22026.title: overlap\_imp\_skew\_or\_equivalent\_three\_bridge
n22026.content:
\begin{theorem}[overlap\_imp\_skew\_or\_equivalent\_three\_bridge]
\lean{SimpleGraph.overlap_imp_skew_or_equivalent_three_bridge}
\label{SimpleGraph.overlap_imp_skew_or_equivalent_three_bridge}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.Overlaps, SimpleGraph.Skew, SimpleGraph.attach}
Overlapping comes in exactly two flavours.  This dichotomy is what the
dropped theorem 9.8 disposes of --- the skew case by the Jordan curve theorem, the
equivalent-3-bridge case by the tripod of theorem 9.7.  It is the reason theorem 9.7
exists at all.

"Equivalent 3-bridges" is rendered as the conjunction
\texttt{attach c e = attach c e' $\land$ (attach c e).ncard = 3}, matching the book's definition
of equivalent $k$-bridges.  Steps 2--4 all reduce to arc arithmetic on \texttt{cycleIdx},
so the segment machinery built for \texttt{Overlaps} will carry most of them.
\end{theorem}

n22029.title: chvatal\_erdos\_hamiltonian
n22029.content:
\begin{theorem}[chvatal\_erdos\_hamiltonian]
\lean{SimpleGraph.chvatal_erdos_hamiltonian}
\label{SimpleGraph.chvatal_erdos_hamiltonian}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.vertexConnectivity}
$\alpha$ is the independence number and $\kappa$ the connectivity, so the
hypothesis says the graph is at least as well connected as it is "spread out".  This
is one of the most elegant sufficient conditions for hamiltonicity known, and the
whole bridge apparatus of \S{}9.4 that survives in this file exists to reach it --- it is
the prize of the surviving combinatorial core.

\textbf{!} \texttt{h$\nu$ : 3 $\le$ Fintype.card V} is \textbf{load-bearing} and is \emph{not} in
B\&M --- the statement is false without it.  $K_{2}$ has $\alpha = 1$ and $\kappa = 1$, so $\alpha \le \kappa$
holds, yet $K_{2}$ has no Hamilton cycle, there being no cycle of length two.  ($K_{1}$ is
similar.)  Step 5 is where most of the work sits; step 4's cut argument is the part
most likely to need its own supporting lemma.
\end{theorem}

n22030.title: lineGraph\_colorable\_three\_of\_isHamiltonian\_of\_three\_regular
n22030.content:
\begin{theorem}[lineGraph\_colorable\_three\_of\_isHamiltonian\_of\_three\_regular]
\lean{SimpleGraph.lineGraph_colorable_three_of_isHamiltonian_of_three_regular}
\label{SimpleGraph.lineGraph_colorable_three_of_isHamiltonian_of_three_regular}
\leanok
A cubic hamiltonian graph splits into an even cycle plus a perfect
matching; two colours alternate around the cycle and the third takes the matching.

\emph{Why this matters (\S{}9.7).}  Tait (1880) showed the four-colour conjecture equivalent
to "every simple 3-regular 3-connected planar graph has a Tait colouring" (theorem
9.12(iii)), and then \emph{by mistakenly assuming that every such graph is hamiltonian},
gave a "proof" of the conjecture using exactly this exercise.  Over half a century
later Tutte (1946) exhibited a nonhamiltonian 3-regular 3-connected planar graph,
invalidating the argument.  So this exercise is sound; only Tait's extra assumption
was not.

A Tait colouring is spelled \texttt{G.lineGraph.Colorable 3}, needing
no new definitions --- \texttt{lineGraph} has the edges of $G$ as vertices, adjacent when
they share an end, so a proper colouring of it \emph{is} a proper edge colouring of $G$.
Step 3's parity assignment is the fiddly part: it needs a function from an edge of
$c$ to its index along $c$, which \texttt{c.edges} provides as a list position.
\end{theorem}

n22031.title: An edge cut set: a set of edges whose deletion disconnects $G$
n22031.content:
\begin{definition}[An edge cut set: a set of edges whose deletion disconnects $G$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsEdgeCutSet}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsEdgeCutSet}
\leanok
Split the vertices into two nonempty groups and collect the edges
running between them; deleting them severs every route from one group to the other.

B\&M define an edge cut \emph{by its shape} $[S, \bar{S}]$; this takes the
operational characterisation --- a subset of \texttt{edgeSet} whose removal leaves $G$
disconnected --- which for \textbf{connected} $G$ describes the same collections.  \textbf{!} For
disconnected $G$ they diverge, and $\emptyset$ satisfies this predicate; that is the source of
the \texttt{IsBond} defect below.
\end{definition}

n22032.title: A bond (\S{}2.2): a minimal (nonempty) edge cut, i.e
n22032.content:
\begin{definition}[A bond (\S{}2.2): a minimal (nonempty) edge cut, i.e]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsBond}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsBond}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsEdgeCutSet}
An edge cut with nothing to spare --- remove all of it and the graph falls
apart, but put any single edge back and it is connected again.  Exercise 2.2.8
characterises when $[S, \bar{S}]$ is a bond: exactly when both $G[S]$ and $G[\bar{S}]$ are
connected.  Bonds are the notion \textbf{dual} to cycles, a duality chapter 12 develops in
full --- theorem 2.6 here is the mirror of theorem 2.5.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defect: $\emptyset$ is a bond when $G$ is disconnected.}  The docstring above claims
nonemptiness is automatic because "deleting $\emptyset$ leaves $G$ connected" --- but that holds
only for connected $G$.  For disconnected $G$, \texttt{IsEdgeCutSet $\emptyset$} unfolds to
\texttt{$\lnot$ G.Connected}, which is true, and there is no $B' \subset \emptyset$ to test, so the minimality
clause is vacuous.  Hence \texttt{IsBond G $\emptyset$}, contradicting \emph{minimal \textbf{nonempty} edge cut}.

\emph{The repair:} add \texttt{B.Nonempty} as a conjunct, or carry \texttt{G.Connected} as a hypothesis
wherever \texttt{IsBond} is used (theorem 2.6 already does --- its \texttt{hG} is available).
\end{definition}

n22033.title: The number of spanning trees $\tau(G)$: the number of tree subgraphs $T \le G$ on the full vertex set
n22033.content:
\begin{definition}[The number of spanning trees $\tau(G)$: the number of tree subgraphs $T \le G$ on the full vertex set]
\lean{SimpleGraph.numSpanningTrees}
\label{SimpleGraph.numSpanningTrees}
\leanok
\textbf{!} $\tau(G)$ counts the \emph{distinct} spanning trees, \textbf{not} the
non-isomorphic ones.  B\&M stress the difference: $K_{6}$ has six non-isomorphic spanning
trees (figure 2.1) but $6^{4} = 1296$ distinct ones.  $\tau$ satisfies deletion--contraction
(theorem 2.8) and, for complete graphs, Cayley's formula (theorem 2.9); the general
determinant formula is chapter 12's matrix-tree theorem.

"Spanning" is automatic: a \texttt{T : SimpleGraph W} lives on the whole
vertex type, so \texttt{T $\le$ H $\land$ T.IsTree} already means a spanning tree.  \textbf{!} \texttt{IsTree} bundles
\texttt{Connected}, which requires \texttt{Nonempty W} --- so on an empty carrier $\tau = 0$.  That is
where \texttt{cayley} fails at $n = 0$.
\end{definition}

n22034.title: contract
n22034.content:
\begin{definition}[contract]
\lean{SimpleGraph.contract}
\label{SimpleGraph.contract}
$G \cdot e$ (\S{}2.4).  Mathlib has no edge contraction for \texttt{SimpleGraph}.
NOTE: a genuine contraction identifies the ends of $e$ and therefore changes the carrier
type (to $|V| - 1$ vertices).  Here it is \emph{stubbed on the same carrier} $V$ as a placeholder,
purely so that the deletion--contraction recurrence (Theorem 2.8) can be typed.

Think of $e = uv$ as a string pulled tight until $u$ and $v$ merge;
everything attached to either is now attached to the merged vertex, and $e$
disappears.  For a link, $\nu(G\cdot e) = \nu - 1$, $\varepsilon(G\cdot e) = \varepsilon - 1$, $\omega(G\cdot e) = \omega$ --- so
contracting an edge of a tree again yields a tree, which is what makes
deletion--contraction work.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective on two counts.}
1. \emph{\texttt{sorry} body.}  $G \cdot e$ is an opaque graph, so theorem 2.8 relates opaque
   quantities and asserts nothing.
2. \emph{Wrong carrier.}  A genuine contraction has $\nu - 1$ vertices; this is stubbed on
   the \textbf{same} carrier $V$ purely so theorem 2.8 can be typed.  Even given an honest
   body on $V$, the identity $\nu(G\cdot e) = \nu - 1$ could not hold.

\emph{The repair} is to move to the quotient carrier ${x : V // x \ne v}$ with $v$'s
incidences re-pointed at $u$, exactly as chapter 10's \texttt{Digraph.contractEdge} does ---
that definition is honest and complete, and can be transcribed.
\end{definition}

n22038.content:
\begin{theorem}[cutEdge\_iff\_no\_cycle]
\lean{SimpleGraph.cutEdge_iff_no_cycle}
\label{SimpleGraph.cutEdge_iff_no_cycle}
\leanok
Cut edges are exactly the edges lying on no cycle: an edge on a cycle has
a detour around it, while an edge on no cycle is the sole link between the two sides it
joins.

Mathlib's \texttt{IsBridge} is B\&M's \emph{cut edge}.  Note the conclusion
carries \texttt{G.Adj v w} as a conjunct, which \texttt{IsBridge} includes --- a non-edge is not a
bridge.
\end{theorem}

n22042.title: spanningTree\_add\_edge\_exists\_cycle
n22042.content:
\begin{theorem}[spanningTree\_add\_edge\_exists\_cycle]
\lean{SimpleGraph.spanningTree_add_edge_exists_cycle}
\label{SimpleGraph.spanningTree_add_edge_exists_cycle}
\leanok
A spanning tree already offers a unique route between the ends of $e$;
adding $e$ supplies a second, and the two close off precisely one cycle --- the
\textbf{fundamental cycle} of $e$ with respect to $T$.  \textbf{*} The engine of the exchange
argument for Kruskal's optimality (theorem 2.10), and of chapter 12's tree-basis of the
cycle space.

\textbf{!} Only the \textbf{existence} half is stated: uniqueness of a cycle in
Lean holds only up to rotation and reflection of the walk, which is awkward to phrase
directly.  Chapter 12's \texttt{fundamentalCycle} needs the uniqueness half, so this gap
propagates there.
\end{theorem}
