n22048.title: exists\_min\_weight\_spanningTree
n22048.content:
\begin{theorem}[exists\_min\_weight\_spanningTree]
\lean{SimpleGraph.exists_min_weight_spanningTree}
\label{SimpleGraph.exists_min_weight_spanningTree}
\leanok
Assign each edge a weight and each spanning tree the total; the connector
problem asks for the least, and theorem 2.10 guarantees Kruskal's greedy procedure ---
repeatedly take the cheapest edge not closing a cycle --- always finds one.

\textbf{!} The algorithm is a \emph{procedure}, not a proposition, so what is
stated is the mathematical target it attains: \textbf{existence} of a minimum-weight
spanning tree.  That is strictly weaker than theorem 2.10, which asserts the *greedy
output* is optimal --- the exchange argument quoted above is not exercised by the
skeleton, which is a three-line finiteness argument instead.  Formalising the real
theorem would need Kruskal's algorithm defined first.  Weights are $\mathbb{R}$-valued, matching
B\&M's remark that the algorithm is valid for arbitrary real weights.
\end{theorem}

n22049.title: $G$ is critical: $\chi(H) < \chi(G)$ for every proper subgraph $H \subset G$
n22049.content:
\begin{definition}[$G$ is critical: $\chi(H) < \chi(G)$ for every proper subgraph $H \subset G$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsCritical}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsCritical}
\leanok
A critical graph is "minimally" $k$-chromatic: remove any vertex or
any edge and the chromatic number drops.  Critical graphs are useful precisely
because they carry the whole difficulty of a colouring problem --- every
$k$-chromatic graph contains a $k$-critical subgraph, so statements about
$k$-chromatic graphs reduce to the critical case, which is how corollary 8.1.1,
Brooks' theorem 8.4 and theorem 8.5 all begin.

The quantifier ranges over \texttt{G.Subgraph}, not over the order
on \texttt{SimpleGraph V}.  This is load-bearing (Scaffolding judgement 1): the
\texttt{SimpleGraph V} order can only \emph{remove edges}, never vertices, whereas the book's
"proper subgraph" includes $G - v$.  Under the weaker order $\bot$ on two vertices
would be vacuously 1-critical --- it has no proper edge-subgraph --- contradicting
exercise 8.1.7, which says the only 1-critical graph is $K_{1}$.
\end{definition}

n22050.title: $G$ is $k$-critical: $k$-chromatic and critical

n22051.title: $G \cdot uv$: contract the edge $uv$ by identifying $v$ into $u$
n22051.content:
\begin{definition}[$G \cdot uv$: contract the edge $uv$ by identifying $v$ into $u$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.contractEdge}
\label{SimpleGraph.contractEdge}
\leanok
Pull the edge $uv$ tight until $u$ and $v$ merge into a single
vertex, which inherits the neighbours of both.  Contraction appears twice in this
chapter: in theorem 8.3, where $G_{2} \cdot uv$ is shown to be $k$-critical, and in
theorem 8.6, the deletion--contraction recursion for the chromatic polynomial ---
which the book notes *bears a close resemblance to the recursion formula for
$\tau(G)$* in theorem 2.8.

Identification is realised by \emph{dropping} $v$ from the carrier
and re-pointing its edges at $u$, so the carrier is ${x : V // x \ne v}$ and the
merged vertex is $u$.  The $a \ne b$ conjunct in \texttt{Adj} restores looplessness: the
book's contraction of a multigraph may create loops and parallel edges, and
taking the underlying simple graph is exactly what discarding them means.  This
is harmless for both uses --- theorem 8.6 is stated for simple $G$, and colourings
never see loops or multiplicities.
\end{definition}

n22052.title: $\pi_k(G)$, the number of distinct proper $k$-colourings
n22052.content:
\begin{definition}[$\pi_k(G)$, the number of distinct proper $k$-colourings]
\lean{SimpleGraph.numColorings}
\label{SimpleGraph.numColorings}
\leanok
Count the proper colourings as \emph{labelled} objects, not up to
permutation of the colours --- the triangle example is exactly the warning against
quotienting.  Birkhoff (1912) introduced this counting approach as a possible
route to the four-colour conjecture.

\texttt{Nat.card (G.Coloring (Fin k))} rather than \texttt{Fintype.card}:
the two agree over a \texttt{Fintype}, but \texttt{Nat.card} needs no instance, which lets the
\S{}8.4 statements elaborate over \texttt{Subgraph} and component carriers without bespoke
\texttt{Fintype} derivations.  A \texttt{G.Coloring (Fin k)} is a function on vertices, so
distinctness is pointwise --- precisely the book's criterion.
\end{definition}

n22053.title: A ${u,v}$-component: $G(C \cup {u,v})$ for $C$ a component of $G - {u,v}$
n22053.content:
\begin{definition}[A ${u,v}$-component: $G(C \cup {u,v})$ for $C$ a component of $G - {u,v}$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.uvComponent}
\label{SimpleGraph.uvComponent}
\leanok
Cut the graph at $S$ and put $S$ back onto each resulting piece, so
the pieces overlap in exactly $S$.  A colouring of $G$ is then the same thing as a
family of colourings of the $S$-components that \emph{agree on $S$} --- that equivalence
is the entire mechanism behind theorems 8.2 and 8.3, both of which proceed by
colouring the pieces separately and then trying to reconcile them on $S$.

Only the case $S = {u, v}$ is needed (theorem 8.3), so the
definition is specialised to it and indexed by a connected component $c$ of
$G - {u,v}$ rather than by a numeral $i$.  The result is a \texttt{G.Subgraph}, which is
what lets theorem 8.3(i) state $G = G_{1} \cup G_{2}$ as a $\sqcup$ in the subgraph lattice.
\end{definition}

n22054.title: Type 1: every $(k-1)$-colouring assigns $u$ and $v$ the same colour
n22054.content:
\begin{definition}[Type 1: every $(k-1)$-colouring assigns $u$ and $v$ the same colour]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Subgraph.IsType1}
\label{SimpleGraph.Subgraph.IsType1}
\leanok
The component forces $u$ and $v$ to agree.  The quantifier is
universal --- not that \emph{some} colouring identifies them, but that \emph{no} colouring can
separate them.  This is only interesting because $u$ and $v$ are nonadjacent in a
critical graph (the consequence of theorem 8.2 recorded below), so a priori a
colouring is free to do either.

Stated for a \texttt{G.Subgraph} $H$ with explicit membership proofs
$hu$, $hv$, since \texttt{H.coe} lives on \texttt{H.verts} and $u$, $v$ must be named as
elements of it.  \texttt{Fin (k - 1)} uses $\mathbb{N}$-subtraction; every use site has $k \ge 2$, so
no truncation occurs.
\end{definition}

n22055.title: Type 2: every $(k-1)$-colouring assigns $u$ and $v$ different colours
n22055.content:
\begin{definition}[Type 2: every $(k-1)$-colouring assigns $u$ and $v$ different colours]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Subgraph.IsType2}
\label{SimpleGraph.Subgraph.IsType2}
\leanok
The component forces $u$ and $v$ to disagree.  A type-1 component
and a type-2 component make irreconcilable demands, so their union admits no
$(k-1)$-colouring at all --- which is exactly the contradiction driving theorem 8.3,
and the reason a critical graph with a 2-vertex cut has precisely two pieces, one
of each type.

As for \texttt{IsType1}.  Note that "type 1" and "type 2" are not
exhaustive: a component may admit both kinds of $(k-1)$-colouring and be of
neither type.  Theorem 8.3 has to \emph{prove} that the two pieces it produces are of
opposite types; it is not true by definition.
\end{definition}

n22056.title: $G$ contains a subdivision of $K_{4}$: four distinct branch vertices joined pairwise by six paths,\dots
n22056.content:
\begin{definition}[$G$ contains a subdivision of $K_{4}$: four distinct branch vertices joined pairwise by six paths,\dots]
\lean{SimpleGraph.HasK4Subdivision}
\label{SimpleGraph.HasK4Subdivision}
\leanok
A "topological $K_{4}$": four \textbf{branch vertices}, each of the six pairs
joined by a path, the six paths sharing no interior vertices with one another or
with the branch vertices.  Drawn on paper it is $K_{4}$ with beads threaded onto its
edges.

The book says "obtainable from $K_{4}$ by subdividing edges",
which is a statement about an abstract graph; what a \emph{containment} claim needs is
the witness form above --- six \texttt{Walk}s in $G$ with disjointness conditions.  The two
are equivalent, and only this direction is ever used.  The three side conditions
say, in order: the branch vertices are distinct; each of the six walks is a path;
no path's interior meets a branch vertex; and no two paths' interiors meet.
\texttt{support.tail.dropLast} is the interior of a walk (drop both endpoints).
\end{definition}

n22057.title: mycielskian
n22057.content:
\begin{definition}[mycielskian]
\lean{SimpleGraph.mycielskian}
\label{SimpleGraph.mycielskian}
\leanok
on \texttt{V $\oplus$ V $\oplus$ Unit}: \texttt{inl} = the old graph, \texttt{inr $\circ$ inl} = the
shadows $u_{i}$ (joined to $v_{i}$'s neighbours), \texttt{inr $\circ$ inr} = the apex (joined to every shadow).
\textbf{!} MISSING from Mathlib.

Each original vertex $v_{i}$ gets a \textbf{shadow} $u_{i}$ attached to $v_{i}$'s
neighbourhood but \emph{not} to $v_{i}$ itself, and a single \textbf{apex} $v$ is joined to all
the shadows.  The construction preserves triangle-freeness while raising the
chromatic number by exactly one; starting from $K_{2}$ it yields the 5-cycle, then
the Gr\"otzsch graph, and in general a triangle-free $k$-chromatic graph on
$3\cdot 2^{k-2} - 1$ vertices.  Theorem 8.7 is the proof that it does this.

Carrier \texttt{V $\oplus$ V $\oplus$ Unit}: \texttt{inl a} is the original $v_a$,
\texttt{inr (inl a)} its shadow $u_a$, \texttt{inr (inr ())} the apex.  Reading the \texttt{Adj} match
against the book: \texttt{inl}--\texttt{inl} copies $G$; \texttt{inl}--\texttt{inr $\circ$ inl} joins $u_a$ to the
neighbours of $v_a$ (note \texttt{G.Adj a b}, not $a = b$, so $u_a$ is \emph{not} joined to
$v_a$); \texttt{inr $\circ$ inl}--\texttt{inr $\circ$ inr} joins every shadow to the apex.  Everything else
is \texttt{False}, which in particular leaves the shadows independent and the apex
nonadjacent to the original vertices.
\end{definition}

n22058.title: The wheel with $n$ spokes: $C_n \lor K_{1}$
n22058.content:
\begin{definition}[The wheel with $n$ spokes: $C_n \lor K_{1}$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.wheel}
\label{SimpleGraph.wheel}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.join}
A hub joined to every vertex of a rim cycle.  As a join $C_n \lor K_{1}$
it inherits $\chi = \chi(C_n) + 1$ from exercise 8.1.10(a), so a wheel with an odd rim
is 4-chromatic and one with an even rim is 3-chromatic.  Exercise 8.4.5(b)
computes its chromatic polynomial.

"$n$ spokes" means $n$ rim vertices, so the rim is
\texttt{cycleGraph n} and the hub is the unique vertex of \texttt{$\top$ : SimpleGraph Unit}.  Since
\texttt{join} adds \emph{all} cross edges and the hub side is a single vertex, the added edges
are exactly the $n$ spokes.
\end{definition}

n22059.title: $G$ is uniquely $k$-colourable: any two $k$-colourings induce the same partition
n22059.content:
\begin{definition}[$G$ is uniquely $k$-colourable: any two $k$-colourings induce the same partition]
\lean{SimpleGraph.UniquelyColorable}
\label{SimpleGraph.UniquelyColorable}
\leanok
Colours are arbitrary labels, so what a colouring really determines
is the partition into colour classes.  $G$ is uniquely $k$-colourable when that
partition is forced --- two $k$-colourings can then differ only by renaming the
colours.  Complete graphs are the obvious examples, which is why exercise 8.1.8
(no vertex cut of a $k$-critical graph induces a uniquely $(k-1)$-colourable
subgraph) generalises theorem 8.2 (no vertex cut is a clique).

\texttt{Coloring.colorClasses} is the induced partition, so the book's
"induce the same partition" is a literal equality of \texttt{colorClasses}.  Note this is
vacuously true when $G$ has no $k$-colouring at all; every use site supplies
colourability separately.
\end{definition}

n22060.title: $s$ is a maximal independent set of $G$ within $t$
n22060.content:
\begin{definition}[$s$ is a maximal independent set of $G$ within $t$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsMaximalIndepSetIn}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsMaximalIndepSetIn}
\leanok
$s$ is independent, lies inside $t$, and cannot be enlarged *within
$t$* without losing independence.

The book only ever says "maximal independent set of $G - X$"
for various $X$.  Rather than form the deleted graph, this relativises: $t$ is the
ambient set, and maximality is tested against subsets of $t$.  Taking
\texttt{t = Set.univ} recovers the plain notion.  This is the shape
\texttt{IsCanonicalColouring} needs, where each colour class must be maximal in what
remains after the earlier classes are removed.
\end{definition}

n22061.title: A canonical colouring, as a list of colour classes
n22061.content:
\begin{definition}[A canonical colouring, as a list of colour classes]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsCanonicalColouring}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsCanonicalColouring}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsMaximalIndepSetIn}
Build the colour classes greedily, each time taking as large an
independent set as possible from what remains.  Exercise 8.6.3 shows this costs
nothing, so enumerating canonical colourings suffices to find $\chi(G)$ --- the basis
of the \S{}8.6 procedure for the storage problem, which the book concedes *is not
very efficient for large graphs*.

Stated as a \emph{static} condition on a list of classes, not as a
procedure: $L[i]$ is required to be maximal-independent in the complement of
$L[0] \cup \dots \cup L[i-1]$, which is what "maximal independent set of
$G - (V_{1} \cup \dots \cup V_{i-1})$" means.  The last two conjuncts say $L$ really is a
partition --- the classes cover $V$ and are pairwise disjoint.  A \texttt{List} rather than
a \texttt{Fin k $\to$ Set V} because the book's condition is inherently ordered, and because
exercise 8.6.3 concludes with \texttt{L.length $\le$ k} rather than $= k$ (a canonical
colouring may use fewer colours, which is precisely why the procedure finds $\chi$
rather than merely confirming $k$).
\end{definition}

n22062.title: The Mycielski tower $G_{2} = K_{2}, G_{3}, G_{4}, \dots$
n22062.content:
\begin{definition}[The Mycielski tower $G_{2} = K_{2}, G_{3}, G_{4}, \dots$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.mycielskiTower}
\label{SimpleGraph.mycielskiTower}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.mycielskian}
Iterate Mycielski's construction from a single edge.  The book
records the first few: $G_{2} = K_{2}$, $G_{3}$ is the 5-cycle, $G_{4}$ is the Gr\"otzsch graph
of figure 8.2.  Exercise 8.5.1 strengthens theorem 8.7 for this particular tower:
each $G_k$ is not merely $k$-chromatic but $k$-\emph{critical}.

Each $G_k$ lives on a different carrier (\texttt{V $\oplus$ V $\oplus$ Unit} of the
previous one), so the recursion must be \texttt{Sigma}-valued: it returns a carrier
\emph{together with} a graph on it.  The book's tower starts at $k = 2$; the clauses
$0$ and $1$ are padding so the function is total, and every statement about the
tower carries the hypothesis $2 \le k$.  This def is the reason \texttt{mycielskian} must
exist as a standalone operation rather than being inlined into theorem 8.7.
\end{definition}

n22063.title: exists\_isKCritical\_subgraph

n22064.title: connected
n22064.content:
\begin{theorem}[connected]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsCritical.connected}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsCritical.connected}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsCritical}
If a graph were disconnected, its chromatic number would be the
maximum of those of its components --- colour each component independently.  So one
component already achieves $\chi(G)$, and that component is a proper subgraph with
the same chromatic number, contradicting criticality.  Corollary 8.2 strengthens
this considerably: every critical graph is not merely connected but a \emph{block},
having no cut vertex at all.

Step 3 is the whole content and is reusable: the same
"components colour independently" lemma is exercise 8.4.6 in its counting form
($\pi_k$ multiplies over components).  Worth proving once in a shared form.
\end{theorem}

n22065.title: minDegree\_ge
n22065.content:
\begin{theorem}[minDegree\_ge]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsKCritical.minDegree_ge}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsKCritical.minDegree_ge}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsKCritical}
A vertex of small degree is never an obstacle to colouring, since
some colour is always free for it.  So a graph that genuinely needs $k$ colours,
\emph{minimally}, cannot contain such a vertex --- criticality is what turns "$v$ is easy
to colour" into a contradiction rather than merely an observation.

$k - 1$ is $\mathbb{N}$-subtraction, but the statement is a lower bound,
so truncation is harmless: at $k = 0$ it reads \texttt{0 $\le$ minDegree}.  Step 4 is where
the strict inequality $\delta < k - 1$ is spent, so it needs $k \ge 1$ to know
\texttt{Fin (k-1)} is the right palette --- available from $h.1$ as in step 1.
\end{theorem}

n22066.title: card\_filter\_degree\_ge\_of\_chromaticNumber
n22066.content:
\begin{theorem}[card\_filter\_degree\_ge\_of\_chromaticNumber]
\lean{SimpleGraph.card_filter_degree_ge_of_chromaticNumber}
\label{SimpleGraph.card_filter_degree_ge_of_chromaticNumber}
\leanok
Needing $k$ colours is not a global accident --- it forces $k$ distinct
vertices each locally rich enough (degree $\ge k - 1$) to be part of the obstruction.
The critical subgraph is what localises the difficulty; without it, "$G$ needs $k$
colours" says nothing about any individual vertex.

Step 3 is stated about \texttt{G.degree}, not \texttt{H.coe.degree}, which is
why the filter in the goal mentions only $G$ --- the critical subgraph is existential
and does not appear in the statement.
\end{theorem}

n22067.title: chromaticNumber\_le\_maxDegree\_add\_one
n22067.content:
\begin{theorem}[chromaticNumber\_le\_maxDegree\_add\_one]
\lean{SimpleGraph.chromaticNumber_le_maxDegree_add_one}
\label{SimpleGraph.chromaticNumber_le_maxDegree_add_one}
\leanok
Colour the vertices one at a time in any order: when a vertex's turn
comes it has at most $\Delta$ neighbours, so at most $\Delta$ colours are forbidden and one
of $\Delta + 1$ is always free.  The book observes the bound *is sometimes very much
greater than the actual value* --- bipartite graphs are 2-chromatic with arbitrarily
large $\Delta$ --- making it weaker than Vizing's edge analogue (theorem 6.2) in one
sense; and weaker in a second sense too, since \emph{many} graphs satisfy $\chi' = \Delta + 1$
whereas Brooks' theorem 8.4 shows only two families satisfy $\chi = \Delta + 1$.

The book's route is recorded because it is the book's, but the
direct route is preferred: it avoids depending on \texttt{exists\_isKCritical\_subgraph}
and \texttt{IsKCritical.minDegree\_ge}, both of which are substantially harder than this
corollary.  This is the cheapest genuine win in the file --- a good first fill.
\end{theorem}

n22068.title: not\_isClique\_of\_isVertexCut
n22068.content:
\begin{theorem}[not\_isClique\_of\_isVertexCut]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsCritical.not_isClique_of_isVertexCut}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsCritical.not_isClique_of_isVertexCut}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsCritical, SimpleGraph.IsVertexCut}
A clique cut is too rigid to cause trouble: its vertices are forced
to take distinct colours anyway, and distinct colours can always be permuted into
agreement, so the pieces reconcile and the graph never needed the extra colour.
Step 4 is the entire content --- for a general cut the restrictions to $S$ need not
be related by a permutation, and exercise 8.1.8 identifies the exact weakening
(uniquely $(k-1)$-colourable) under which the argument still runs.

\texttt{hconn : G.Connected} is load-bearing and is \emph{not} redundant
given \texttt{hcrit}: although \texttt{IsCritical.connected} proves connectivity from
criticality, it needs \texttt{[Nonempty V]}, which this statement does not assume.
Passing \texttt{hconn} explicitly keeps the two results independent and avoids a
dependency cycle.  Note also that the book's $S$-components are defined only for a
\emph{connected} $G$, so step 2 genuinely needs it.
\end{theorem}

n22069.title: connected\_and\_no\_cut\_vertex
n22069.content:
\begin{theorem}[connected\_and\_no\_cut\_vertex]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsCritical.connected_and_no_cut_vertex}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsCritical.connected_and_no_cut_vertex}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsCritical, SimpleGraph.IsVertexCut}
Criticality forces the graph to hold together tightly: it can have no
single point of failure.  Theorem 8.3 goes one step further and analyses the
2-vertex cuts that remain possible --- and finds they too are heavily constrained.

There is no \texttt{IsBlock} in Mathlib or this repo, so "is a block"
is unfolded into the book's own definition, connected + no cut vertex.  A cut
vertex is spelled as a one-element vertex cut, matching \texttt{IsVertexCut} above.  The
\texttt{Connected} conjunct is not merely decoration: without it the statement would be
satisfied by the empty graph.
\end{theorem}

n22070.title: not\_adj\_of\_isVertexCut\_pair
n22070.content:
\begin{theorem}[not\_adj\_of\_isVertexCut\_pair]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsCritical.not_adj_of_isVertexCut_pair}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsCritical.not_adj_of_isVertexCut_pair}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsCritical, SimpleGraph.IsVertexCut}
This is what makes the type 1 / type 2 dichotomy meaningful.  Since
$u$ and $v$ are \emph{not} joined by an edge, a $(k-1)$-colouring of a
${u,v}$-component is free to give them the same colour or different colours; which
it is \emph{forced} to do is exactly the component's type.  Were $uv$ an edge, every
component would be trivially of type 2 and theorem 8.3 would say nothing.

Stated for \texttt{IsCritical} rather than \texttt{IsKCritical}: the book
says "$k$-critical", but $k$ plays no role in the argument, so the hypothesis is
weakened to plain criticality.  \texttt{huv : u $\ne$ v} is needed to know ${u, v}$ really has
two elements.
\end{theorem}

n22071.title: chromaticNumber\_ge\_of\_card\_edges
n22071.content:
\begin{theorem}[chromaticNumber\_ge\_of\_card\_edges]
\lean{SimpleGraph.chromaticNumber_ge_of_card_edges}
\label{SimpleGraph.chromaticNumber_ge_of_card_edges}
\leanok
Many edges force many colours: each colour class is edge-free, so
large classes leave too little room for edges.  Equality holds exactly for
balanced complete multipartite graphs, where every non-edge is inside a class and
all classes have the same size.

Stated multiplicatively over $\mathbb{R}$ --- $\nu^{2}/(\nu^{2} - 2\varepsilon)$ would need
division and a proof that the denominator is nonzero.  (It always is: $G$ simple
gives $2\varepsilon \le \nu(\nu-1) < \nu^{2}$, so $\nu^{2} - 2\varepsilon \ge \nu > 0$ whenever $V$ is nonempty, whence
the \texttt{[Nonempty V]} hypothesis.)  $\chi$ is replaced by an arbitrary $k$ with
\texttt{G.Colorable k}, dodging $\mathbb{N}\infty$; this is equivalent to the book's statement, since
the right-hand side is monotone in $k$ and $\chi$ is the least colourable $k$.
\end{theorem}

n22072.title: chromaticNumber\_le\_five\_of\_odd\_cycles\_meet
n22072.content:
\begin{theorem}[chromaticNumber\_le\_five\_of\_odd\_cycles\_meet]
\lean{SimpleGraph.chromaticNumber_le_five_of_odd_cycles_meet}
\label{SimpleGraph.chromaticNumber_le_five_of_odd_cycles_meet}
\leanok
Odd cycles are the sole obstruction to 2-colourability, so if they
all pile up on one shortest cycle, only a bounded amount of extra colour is needed
to handle them.  Minimality in step 2 is what makes the cycle \emph{induced}, and hence
3-colourable rather than merely small.

The hypothesis quantifies over all pairs of closed walks that
are cycles of odd length, and asks for a common \emph{support} vertex.  Note $h$ is
also applied with $p = q$ in step 2's minimality argument, where it is vacuous ---
the content is only in the disjointness contradiction of step 4.
\end{theorem}

n22073.title: welsh\_powell
n22073.content:
\begin{theorem}[welsh\_powell]
\lean{SimpleGraph.welsh_powell}
\label{SimpleGraph.welsh_powell}
\leanok
Colour greedily in order of decreasing degree.  When the $i$-th
vertex's turn comes, two things bound the colours forbidden to it: it has $d_{i}$
neighbours, so at most $d_{i}$ colours are blocked; and only $i - 1$ vertices are
coloured so far, so at most $i - 1$ colours exist.  Hence \texttt{min\{d$_{i}$ + 1, i\}} colours
suffice at step $i$, and the worst case over $i$ bounds $\chi$.  This genuinely
improves $\chi \le \Delta + 1$ (corollary 8.1.2): high-degree vertices are handled while few
colours exist, low-degree ones later when the count $i$ no longer binds.
Exercise 8.1.4 derives two further bounds from it.

The sorted degree sequence is presented as an equivalence
\texttt{$\sigma$ : Fin (card V) $\simeq$ V} together with $h\sigma$, which says \texttt{i $\mapsto$ deg ($\sigma$ i)} is antitone ---
i.e. $\sigma$ enumerates the vertices in nonincreasing degree order, so
\texttt{G.degree ($\sigma$ i)} \emph{is} the book's $d_{i}$.  $i + 1$ rather than $i$ because \texttt{Fin} is
0-indexed and the book is 1-indexed.

Worth knowing while filling: \textbf{$h\sigma$ is not needed for the proof}, only for the
statement.  Steps 1--4 bound $\chi$ by that \texttt{sup} for \emph{any} enumeration $\sigma$; what $h\sigma$
buys is that the \texttt{sup} is then the book's \texttt{max$_{i}$ min\{d$_{i}$ + 1, i\}} for the sorted
sequence, which is the small quantity worth having.  So do not go looking for a
place to use $h\sigma$ --- there isn't one.
\end{theorem}

n22074.title: chromaticNumber\_le\_ceil\_sqrt\_two\_mul\_card\_edges
n22074.content:
\begin{theorem}[chromaticNumber\_le\_ceil\_sqrt\_two\_mul\_card\_edges]
\lean{SimpleGraph.chromaticNumber_le_ceil_sqrt_two_mul_card_edges}
\label{SimpleGraph.chromaticNumber_le_ceil_sqrt_two_mul_card_edges}
\leanok
Needing many colours forces many edges: a $\chi$-chromatic graph carries
at least as many edges as $K_\chi$.  So a sparse graph cannot have a large chromatic
number.

The book's ${x}$ denotes the \textbf{ceiling}, rendered as $\lceil\cdot\rceil_{+}$
(\texttt{Nat.ceil}), which is the correct choice here since the quantity is nonnegative.
\texttt{Real.sqrt} needs a real argument, hence the cast on $2 * \varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}

n22075.title: nordhaus\_gaddum
n22075.content:
\begin{theorem}[nordhaus\_gaddum]
\lean{SimpleGraph.nordhaus_gaddum}
\label{SimpleGraph.nordhaus_gaddum}
\leanok
A graph and its complement cannot both be hard to colour: an edge
missing from $G$ is present in $G^{c}$, so the two compete for the same $\nu - 1$
adjacencies at each vertex.  Equality holds for complete graphs, where
$\chi(K_{n}) = n$ and $\chi(K_{n}^{c}) = 1$.  This is the archetypal Nordhaus--Gaddum inequality,
of which many analogues are known for other graph parameters.

The addition is in $\mathbb{N}\infty$, where subtraction is badly behaved ---
hence step 1, which moves the whole argument into $\mathbb{N}$ before any arithmetic.  Step
3's index gymnastics (reverse, then complement) is the fiddliest part and is worth
isolating as its own lemma about the two sorted sequences.
\end{theorem}

n22076.title: szekeres\_wilf
n22076.content:
\begin{theorem}[szekeres\_wilf]
\lean{SimpleGraph.szekeres_wilf}
\label{SimpleGraph.szekeres_wilf}
\leanok
$D$ is the \textbf{degeneracy} of $G$.  Strip off a vertex of degree at
most $D$, repeatedly, recording the order; then colour the vertices back in reverse
order --- when a vertex is restored it has at most $D$ neighbours already present, so
one of $D + 1$ colours is free.  This refines $\chi \le \Delta + 1$ (corollary 8.1.2), since
$D \le \Delta$ always and often $D$ is far smaller: a tree has $D = 1$, giving $\chi \le 2$ no
matter how large $\Delta$ is.

"Induced subgraph" is indexed by \texttt{Finset V} (a vertex subset)
rather than by a \texttt{Subgraph}, since the book's maximum is over \emph{induced} subgraphs
only.  The \texttt{sup} includes $s = \emptyset$, whose \texttt{minDegree} is $0$ by Mathlib's
convention; this can only make $D$ larger and so weakens the bound harmlessly.
Note the induction in step 2 is the formal content of "repeatedly strip off" --- as
usual, the informal repetition becomes an induction on the size of what remains.
\end{theorem}

n22077.title: gallai\_two\_per\_class
n22077.content:
\begin{theorem}[gallai\_two\_per\_class]
\lean{SimpleGraph.gallai_two_per_class}
\label{SimpleGraph.gallai_two_per_class}
\leanok
The hypothesis provides \emph{some} colouring, possibly using far more
than $k$ colours, in which no colour class is a singleton.  The claim is that this
feature survives optimisation down to $k$ colours.  The difficulty is that the two
requirements pull against each other: merging classes reduces the colour count but
tends to empty classes out, and the whole point is that it can be arranged never to
leave one vertex stranded.

The hypothesis is existential in the number of colours $n$, so
the given colouring is \texttt{C : G.Coloring (Fin n)} for an unknown $n$ --- step 1's
strengthening is what makes that usable.  \texttt{Set.ncard} is used rather than a
\texttt{Finset} card so the statement needs no decidability on colour classes.
\end{theorem}

n22078.title: isKCritical\_three\_iff\_odd\_cycle
n22078.content:
\begin{theorem}[isKCritical\_three\_iff\_odd\_cycle]
\lean{SimpleGraph.isKCritical_three_iff_odd_cycle}
\label{SimpleGraph.isKCritical_three_iff_odd_cycle}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsKCritical}
An odd cycle is 3-chromatic and minimally so --- delete any edge or
vertex and it unrolls into a path, which is 2-colourable.  Conversely a 3-critical
graph cannot contain an odd cycle properly, and it must contain one, so it \emph{is}
one.  This classification is exactly what Brooks' theorem 8.4 consumes: its proof
observes that *since 1-critical and 2-critical graphs are complete and 3-critical
graphs are odd cycles, we have $k \ge 4$*.

"The only 3-critical graphs are the odd cycles" is up to
isomorphism, hence \texttt{Nonempty (G $\simeq$g cycleGraph n)} rather than an equality.  Steps
3--5 are the same three moves used in \texttt{isKCritical\_two\_iff} (with an edge in place
of an odd cycle); factoring out "a subgraph attaining $\chi(G)$ must be $\top$" as a
lemma about \texttt{IsCritical} pays for itself across all three cases of 8.1.7.
\end{theorem}

n22079.title: isKCritical\_one\_iff
n22079.content:
\begin{theorem}[isKCritical\_one\_iff]
\lean{SimpleGraph.isKCritical_one_iff}
\label{SimpleGraph.isKCritical_one_iff}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsKCritical}
A 1-chromatic graph has no edges and at least one vertex.
Criticality forces exactly one --- with two or more vertices, deleting one leaves a
graph still needing one colour, so the chromatic number would not drop.

\texttt{$\top$ : SimpleGraph (Fin 1)} is $K_{1}$; on a single vertex the
complete and empty graphs coincide, which is what makes step 3 go through despite
$G$ being edgeless.  Note that without the \texttt{Subgraph}-lattice definition of
\texttt{IsCritical}, step 2 would fail: the edge-only order has no proper subgraph of $\bot$
to test, and every edgeless graph would count as 1-critical.
\end{theorem}

n22080.title: isKCritical\_two\_iff

n22081.title: not\_uniquelyColorable\_of\_isVertexCut
n22081.content:
\begin{theorem}[not\_uniquelyColorable\_of\_isVertexCut]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsKCritical.not_uniquelyColorable_of_isVertexCut}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsKCritical.not_uniquelyColorable_of_isVertexCut}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsKCritical, SimpleGraph.IsVertexCut, SimpleGraph.UniquelyColorable}
This generalises theorem 8.2 from clique cuts to uniquely colourable
ones, and isolates what theorem 8.2 was really using.  A clique cut forces the
vertices of $S$ to take distinct colours; what the gluing actually needs is only
that the \emph{partition} of $S$ is forced, so that the pieces can be reconciled by
renaming colours.  Complete graphs are uniquely colourable, so theorem 8.2 is the
special case.

The shared machinery worth extracting once: (i) an
$S$-component family indexed by \texttt{ConnectedComponent}, (ii) "every edge of $G$ lies
in some $S$-component", and (iii) the gluing lemma turning agreement on $S$ into a
colouring of $G$.  With those, theorem 8.2 and this exercise differ only in step 4.
$k - 1$ is $\mathbb{N}$-subtraction; \texttt{hG.1} supplies $k \ge 1$.
\end{theorem}

n22082.title: neighborSet\_not\_subset

n22083.title: no\_isKCritical\_card\_eq\_succ

n22084.title: chromaticNumber\_join
n22084.content:
\begin{theorem}[chromaticNumber\_join]
\lean{SimpleGraph.chromaticNumber_join}
\label{SimpleGraph.chromaticNumber_join}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.join}
No colour can be used on both sides of a join, so the two palettes are
forced to be disjoint and the chromatic numbers simply add.  This makes joins a
convenient way to build graphs of prescribed chromatic number, and is why the wheel
$C_n \lor K_{1}$ needs $\chi(C_n) + 1$ colours.

Addition is in $\mathbb{N}\infty$; both summands are finite here (finite
carriers), so it is ordinary addition, but the casts still need care --- extracting
$a$, $b$ as naturals up front, as in step 1, keeps the arithmetic in $\mathbb{N}$.
\texttt{[Nonempty $\alpha$]}, \texttt{[Nonempty $\beta$]} ensure both sides genuinely contribute.
\end{theorem}

n22085.title: join\_isCritical\_iff
n22085.content:
\begin{theorem}[join\_isCritical\_iff]
\lean{SimpleGraph.join_isCritical_iff}
\label{SimpleGraph.join_isCritical_iff}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsCritical, SimpleGraph.join}
By part (a) the join's chromatic number is the sum, so a drop on one
side is a drop for the join.  This yields a construction for critical graphs of
large chromatic number: join known critical graphs.  For instance $K_{1} \lor C_{5}$ is
4-critical, $C_{5}$ being 3-critical (exercise 8.1.7) --- this is exactly the family
exercise 8.1.12 asks for.

Step 4 is the one that would be missed by reasoning only about
"remove a vertex or a within-side edge"; the subgraph lattice of a join contains
subgraphs that are not themselves joins, and they must be handled.
\end{theorem}

n22086.title: hajos\_construction
n22086.content:
\begin{theorem}[hajos\_construction]
\lean{SimpleGraph.hajos_construction}
\label{SimpleGraph.hajos_construction}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsKCritical}
Glue two $k$-critical graphs at a single vertex $v$, delete one edge
at $v$ from each, and join the two orphaned endpoints $v_{1}$, $v_{2}$ by a new edge; the
result is again $k$-critical.  Step 1 is the heart: the new edge forces $v_{1}$ and
$v_{2}$ apart, so $v$ must agree with one of them, and that agreement is exactly what
repairs the deleted edge on that side.  The \textbf{Haj\'os construction} matters because,
iterated from $K_k$, it generates \emph{every} graph with chromatic number at least $k$
--- a complete but impractical characterisation.

The outline's binder $\{k\ v\ v_{1}\ v_{2} : \_\}$ cannot elaborate
(heterogeneous types under one hole), so the statement uses explicit
${k : \mathbb{N}} {v v_{1} v_{2} : V}$.  Both graphs live on \textbf{one} carrier $V$; "exactly one
vertex in common" is \texttt{hmeet : G$_{1}$.support $\cap$ G$_{2}$.support = \{v\}}, and each $G_{i}$'s real
content is \texttt{G$_{i}$.induce G$_{i}$.support}, which is why the hypotheses are stated about the
induced graphs rather than about $G_{1}$, $G_{2}$ directly.  Edge deletion is \texttt{\textbackslash\{\} edge}
and edge addition is \texttt{$\sqcup$ edge}.
\end{theorem}

n22087.title: exists\_isKCritical\_four
n22087.content:
\begin{theorem}[exists\_isKCritical\_four]
\lean{SimpleGraph.exists_isKCritical_four}
\label{SimpleGraph.exists_isKCritical_four}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsKCritical}
The excluded case $n = 5$ is exactly exercise 8.1.9(b): no
$k$-critical graph has $k + 1$ vertices, so no 4-critical graph has five.  The
book's figure 8.2 (the Gr\"otzsch graph) is another witness, for $n = 11$.

The carrier is pinned to \texttt{Fin n}, so each construction must be
transported along an explicit equivalence --- \texttt{Fin 1 $\oplus$ Fin (n-1) $\simeq$ Fin n} for case 2,
and the Haj\'os single-carrier encoding of exercise 8.1.11 for case 3.  That
transport, rather than the graph theory, is most of the Lean work here; a reusable
"\texttt{IsKCritical} transfers along \texttt{$\simeq$g}" lemma is worth having first.
\end{theorem}

n22088.title: kainen
n22088.content:
\begin{theorem}[kainen]
\lean{SimpleGraph.kainen}
\label{SimpleGraph.kainen}
\leanok
Colour each side separately; the two colourings may clash across the
cut, but there are at most $n - 1$ cut edges and $n!$ ways to relabel one side's
palette --- far more freedom than there are constraints to violate.  A thin cut
therefore cannot force an extra colour.  Note how sharp the count is: $n$ cut edges
would give $n \cdot (n-1)! = n!$, exactly enough to rule out every permutation.

\texttt{hcut} is stated as \texttt{\#cross + 1 $\le$ n} rather than
\texttt{\#cross $\le$ n - 1} to avoid $\mathbb{N}$-subtraction, and it carries $n \ge 1$ as a side benefit.
The partition $(X, Y)$ is $X$ and its complement, so $Y$ never appears by name.
Step 4 needs \texttt{Fintype.card (Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) = n !} and the factorial identity
$n ! = n * (n-1)!$.
\end{theorem}

n22089.title: edgeConnectivity\_ge
n22089.content:
\begin{theorem}[edgeConnectivity\_ge]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsKCritical.edgeConnectivity_ge}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsKCritical.edgeConnectivity_ge}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsKCritical, SimpleGraph.edgeConnectivity}
Criticality forces robust connectivity: a graph that \emph{minimally} needs
$k$ colours cannot be pulled apart by fewer than $k - 1$ edge deletions.  This sits
alongside theorem 8.1, which gives the corresponding degree bound $\delta \ge k - 1$, and
corollary 8.2, which rules out cut vertices --- three different senses in which a
critical graph is tightly held together.

The conclusion \texttt{k - 1 $\le$ edgeConnectivity} \emph{is} the definition of
$(k-1)$-edge-connected (B\&M \S{}3.1: $G$ is $k$-edge-connected if $\kappa' \ge k$), so no
separate predicate is needed.  Step 1 relies on \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0} being harmless: if $G$
has no edge cut at all the bound must still be proved, and there step 2 has nothing
to work with --- dispatch that case by noting a graph with no edge cut is complete or
trivial.
\end{theorem}

n22090.title: brooks\_chromaticNumber\_le\_maxDegree
n22090.content:
\begin{theorem}[brooks\_chromaticNumber\_le\_maxDegree]
\lean{SimpleGraph.brooks_chromaticNumber_le_maxDegree}
\label{SimpleGraph.brooks_chromaticNumber_le_maxDegree}
\leanok
Corollary 8.1.2 gives $\chi \le \Delta + 1$ for every graph; Brooks says only
\emph{two families} attain it --- odd cycles ($\chi = 3 = \Delta + 1$) and complete graphs
($\chi = n = \Delta + 1$).  Everything else needs only $\Delta$ colours.  The book contrasts
this with Vizing's theorem 6.2, where \emph{many} graphs satisfy $\chi' = \Delta + 1$.  The
trick of the proof is the ordering: by ending at a vertex two of whose neighbours
were forced to share a colour, the greedy algorithm is given one unit of slack
exactly where it would otherwise run out.

0 hits in Mathlib --- this is a genuine build.  \texttt{hnotcycle} is
stated as \texttt{$\forall$ n, Odd n $\to$ IsEmpty (G $\simeq$g cycleGraph n)}, i.e. $G$ is isomorphic to no
odd cycle; \texttt{hnotcomplete} as $G \ne \top$.  Both are consumed only in step 2.  Step 1's
caveat is worth taking seriously before starting: the reduction to the critical
subgraph is stated casually by the book but is not free in Lean.
\end{theorem}

n22091.title: brooks\_iff\_edge\_bound

n22092.title: chromaticIndex\_le\_four\_of\_maxDegree\_three
n22092.content:
\begin{theorem}[chromaticIndex\_le\_four\_of\_maxDegree\_three]
\lean{SimpleGraph.chromaticIndex_le_four_of_maxDegree_three}
\label{SimpleGraph.chromaticIndex_le_four_of_maxDegree_three}
\leanok
The edge chromatic number $\chi'(G)$ is the chromatic number of the line
graph $L(G)$, whose vertices are the edges of $G$ with adjacency "shares an end".
So Brooks' \emph{vertex}-colouring theorem yields an \emph{edge}-colouring bound, recovering
for cubic graphs what Vizing's theorem 6.2 gives in general.

Two departures from the book, both weakenings.  (i) $\chi'$ is
spelled as \texttt{$\chi$(lineGraph)}; there is no separate \texttt{chromaticIndex} here.  (ii) The
book says \emph{loopless}, which in B\&M permits parallel edges; \texttt{SimpleGraph} has none,
so this is the simple-graph case only.  With multiplicities the degree count in
step 1 is unchanged, but \texttt{lineGraph} would have to be redefined, so the weakening
is deliberate.  Note also that the exercise is stated with $\Delta = 3$ exactly, not
$\Delta \le 3$; only $\le$ is used.
\end{theorem}

n22093.title: kCritical\_two\_vertex\_cut\_structure
n22093.content:
\begin{theorem}[kCritical\_two\_vertex\_cut\_structure]
\lean{SimpleGraph.kCritical_two_vertex_cut_structure}
\label{SimpleGraph.kCritical_two_vertex_cut_structure}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsKCritical, SimpleGraph.IsVertexCut, SimpleGraph.Subgraph.IsType1, SimpleGraph.Subgraph.IsType2, SimpleGraph.contractEdge, SimpleGraph.uvComponent}
At a 2-vertex cut a critical graph splits into exactly two pieces with
\emph{opposite} demands on $u$ and $v$ --- one insisting they agree, the other that they
differ.  That is why the cut cannot be repaired, and it is the structural fact that
both Brooks' theorem (via corollary 8.3) and theorem 8.5 exploit.

Worth proving first, and reused in step 6: \textbf{for $k \ge 2$,
criticality can be checked on single-edge deletions alone.}  Any $H < \top$ is
contained in some \texttt{$\top$ \textbackslash\{\} edge e}, and $\chi$ is monotone, so \texttt{$\chi$(H.coe) $\le$ $\chi$($\top$ \textbackslash\{\} edge e)};
vertex deletions are subsumed because a critical graph has $\delta \ge k - 1 \ge 1$
(theorem 8.1), so every vertex carries an edge.  This closes the gap between the
book's edge-only check and the \texttt{Subgraph}-lattice definition of \texttt{IsCritical}.

The \texttt{(by simp [uvComponent])} arguments in the statement are the membership proofs
\texttt{u, v $\in$ (uvComponent \dots).verts}, discharged by unfolding --- the ${u, v}$ is glued
onto every component by construction.
\end{theorem}

n22094.title: kCritical\_two\_vertex\_cut\_degree\_sum
n22094.content:
\begin{theorem}[kCritical\_two\_vertex\_cut\_degree\_sum]
\lean{SimpleGraph.kCritical_two_vertex_cut_degree_sum}
\label{SimpleGraph.kCritical_two_vertex_cut_degree_sum}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsKCritical, SimpleGraph.IsVertexCut}
This inequality is precisely what Brooks' theorem uses to dispose of
the 2-vertex-cut case: combined with $d(u), d(v) \le \Delta$ it forces $2\Delta \ge 3k - 5$,
which for $k \ge 4$ already gives $k \le \Delta$.

Stated additively as $3k \le d(u) + d(v) + 5$ rather than
$d(u) + d(v) \ge 3k - 5$, because $\mathbb{N}$-subtraction would truncate $3k - 5$ to $0$ for
$k \le 1$ and make the statement vacuous exactly where it should be informative.
Step 5 deserves care: if $u$ and $v$ had a common neighbour in $G_{2}$, contracting
would merge two edges into one and the degree identity would fail --- establish that
they do not, or weaken the identity to the inequality actually needed.
\end{theorem}

n22095.title: fourChromatic\_hasK4Subdivision

n22096.title: hasK4Subdivision\_of\_few\_low\_degree

n22097.title: hasK4Subdivision\_of\_card\_edges
n22097.content:
\begin{theorem}[hasK4Subdivision\_of\_card\_edges]
\lean{SimpleGraph.hasK4Subdivision_of_card_edges}
\label{SimpleGraph.hasK4Subdivision_of_card_edges}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.HasK4Subdivision}
Enough edges relative to vertices force the graph to be locally rich
enough to contain four branch vertices and six connecting paths.  The invariant in
step 2 is the whole trick: deleting a low-degree vertex is "free" with respect to
the quantity $2\nu - \varepsilon$, so the stripping can be run to completion without ever
losing the hypothesis.  Part (b) shows $2\nu - 2$ is exactly the right threshold.

Restated additively as $2\nu \le \varepsilon + 2$ rather than $\varepsilon \ge 2\nu - 2$, to
keep $\mathbb{N}$-subtraction out.  Step 2's bookkeeping is the $\mathbb{N}$-arithmetic core and is worth
isolating: \texttt{(G.induce \{v\}$^{c}$).edgeFinset.card + G.degree v = G.edgeFinset.card}.
\end{theorem}

n22098.title: numColorings\_add\_contract
n22098.content:
\begin{theorem}[numColorings\_add\_contract]
\lean{SimpleGraph.numColorings_add_contract}
\label{SimpleGraph.numColorings_add_contract}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.contractEdge, SimpleGraph.numColorings}
Classify the $k$-colourings of $G - e$ by whether they give $u$ and
$v$ the same colour: the "same" ones are the colourings of $G \cdot e$, the "different"
ones are the colourings of $G$.  The book notes the recursion *bears a close
resemblance to the recursion formula for $\tau(G)$* in theorem 2.8, and that it can be
run in either direction --- reducing to empty graphs (efficient for sparse $G$) or to
complete graphs (efficient for dense $G$), as illustrated in figure 8.9.

Stated additively, $\pi_k(G) + \pi_k(G\cdot e) = \pi_k(G-e)$, to stay in
$\mathbb{N}$ --- the book's headline form has a subtraction.  Happily this \emph{is} how B\&M's own
proof ends, so the Lean statement is the more faithful of the two.  Steps 2 and 3
are the only real work; step 1 is bookkeeping and step 4 is $rw$.
\end{theorem}

n22099.title: exists\_chromaticPolynomial
n22099.content:
\begin{theorem}[exists\_chromaticPolynomial]
\lean{SimpleGraph.exists_chromaticPolynomial}
\label{SimpleGraph.exists_chromaticPolynomial}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.numColorings}
This is what justifies calling $\pi_k(G)$ the \textbf{chromatic polynomial}.
The book notes that \emph{no one has yet discovered which polynomials are chromatic}:
Read (1968) conjectured the coefficients must first rise then fall in absolute
value, but even that plus this corollary is not sufficient --- $k^{4} - 3k^{3} + 3k^{2}$
satisfies all of them yet is no graph's chromatic polynomial (exercise 8.4.2(b)).

\texttt{[Nonempty V]} is load-bearing, as step 2 shows: for $\nu = 0$ the
empty graph has $\pi_k = 1$, whose constant term is $1$, not $0$.  The alternation is
encoded as \texttt{$\forall$ i, 0 $\le$ (-1)\^{}($\nu$ - i) * p.coeff i} rather than as an explicit sum with
non-negative $a_{i}$, which is equivalent and much easier to carry through step 5.
\end{theorem}

n22100.title: chromaticPolynomial\_coeff\_card\_sub\_one
n22100.content:
\begin{theorem}[chromaticPolynomial\_coeff\_card\_sub\_one]
\lean{SimpleGraph.chromaticPolynomial_coeff_card_sub_one}
\label{SimpleGraph.chromaticPolynomial_coeff_card_sub_one}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.numColorings}
The second coefficient of the chromatic polynomial simply counts the
edges.  The mechanism is that each deletion--contraction step peels off exactly one
copy of the contracted graph's leading term, and the contracted graph has degree
one less --- so the $k^{\nu-1}$ coefficient decrements once per edge.  This is a first
small step toward the general question of which polynomials are chromatic, and it
is what makes exercise 8.4.2(b) possible.

$p$ is a hypothesis rather than a construction, which is why
step 1 is needed at all --- without uniqueness there is no link between the $p$ given
here and the one corollary 8.6 builds.  That uniqueness lemma is worth stating once
and reusing in exercises 8.4.2(b) and 8.4.8.
\end{theorem}

n22101.title: numColorings\_of\_isTree
n22101.content:
\begin{theorem}[numColorings\_of\_isTree]
\lean{SimpleGraph.numColorings_of_isTree}
\label{SimpleGraph.numColorings_of_isTree}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.numColorings}
Root the tree anywhere and colour outward: the root takes any of the
$k$ colours, and every other vertex is reached across exactly one edge from its
already-coloured parent, so it avoids just that one colour.  The formula reflects
the structure exactly --- $\nu - 1$ edges, each imposing precisely one constraint, with
no cycles to make the constraints interact.

$(k - 1)$ is $\mathbb{N}$-subtraction, harmless because at $k = 0$ both
sides are $0$ for a nonempty tree.  Consumed by exercises 8.4.3(b) (as the spanning
tree bound) and 8.4.4 (as the deleted-edge case of the cycle).
\end{theorem}

n22102.title: numColorings\_le\_of\_connected

n22103.title: numColorings\_cycleGraph
n22103.content:
\begin{theorem}[numColorings\_cycleGraph]
\lean{SimpleGraph.numColorings_cycleGraph}
\label{SimpleGraph.numColorings_cycleGraph}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.numColorings}
Sanity checks: at $k = 2$ the formula gives $1 + (-1)^{n}$, which is $2$
for even $n$ and $0$ for odd $n$ --- matching that even cycles are bipartite (two
2-colourings) and odd cycles are not (none).  The $(-1)^{n}$ term is precisely where
the parity of the cycle enters, and it is what makes odd cycles the exceptional
family throughout this chapter.

Stated over $\mathbb{Z}$ with a cast on the left, because
$(k-1)^{n} + (-1)^{n}(k-1)$ is not a natural number expression --- the $(-1)^{n}$ term is
genuinely negative for odd $n$.  The base case is $n = 3$ rather than $n = 0$
because \texttt{cycleGraph n} is only a cycle for $n \ge 3$, and because contracting an edge
of $C_{3}$ would leave a multi-edge, which \texttt{contractEdge} silently simplifies.
\end{theorem}

n22104.title: numColorings\_join\_singleton
n22104.content:
\begin{theorem}[numColorings\_join\_singleton]
\lean{SimpleGraph.numColorings_join_singleton}
\label{SimpleGraph.numColorings_join_singleton}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.join, SimpleGraph.numColorings}
Choose the apex's colour first --- $k$ ways --- and then $G$ must be
coloured with the remaining $k - 1$ colours.  This is the chromatic-polynomial
counterpart of $\chi(G \lor K_{1}) = \chi(G) + 1$, the $K_{1}$ case of exercise 8.1.10(a).

$hk : 1 \le k$ keeps $k - 1$ from truncating in step 3, where the
equivalence \texttt{\{c : Fin k // c $\ne$ j\} $\simeq$ Fin (k-1)} genuinely needs $k \ge 1$.  The
\emph{statement} happens to hold at $k = 0$ as well --- both sides are then $0$, the join
being nonempty --- so $hk$ is a convenience for the proof rather than a correction to
the claim.
\end{theorem}

n22105.title: numColorings\_wheel

n22106.title: numColorings\_eq\_prod\_components
n22106.content:
\begin{theorem}[numColorings\_eq\_prod\_components]
\lean{SimpleGraph.numColorings_eq_prod_components}
\label{SimpleGraph.numColorings_eq_prod_components}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.numColorings}
No edge joins different components, so their colourings are entirely
independent: a colouring of $G$ is precisely a choice of colouring for each
component, and the count multiplies.  This is the chromatic-polynomial version of
\texttt{$\chi$(G) = max $\chi$(G$_{i}$)}, and one of the formulae the book lists as *facilitating the
calculation of chromatic polynomials*.

Step 2 is the same "components are independent" equivalence used
by \texttt{IsCritical.connected} (in its \texttt{sup} form) --- worth building once in a shared
place and specialising twice, since the counting and the $\chi$ versions differ only
in what is applied to the resulting family.
\end{theorem}

n22107.title: numColorings\_union\_mul\_inter

n22108.title: chromaticPolynomial\_no\_root\_gt\_card
n22108.content:
\begin{theorem}[chromaticPolynomial\_no\_root\_gt\_card]
\lean{SimpleGraph.chromaticPolynomial_no_root_gt_card}
\label{SimpleGraph.chromaticPolynomial_no_root_gt_card}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.numColorings}
$\pi_k(G)$ counts colourings, so it is positive at every integer
$k \ge \chi(G)$, and $\chi(G) \le \nu$ always.  The exercise strengthens this from integers to
all reals: beyond $\nu$ the polynomial has no zero whatsoever.  The book notes that
the roots of chromatic polynomials \emph{exhibit an unexpected regularity} for planar
graphs, citing Tutte (1970) on their connection with the golden ratio.

Over $\mathbb{R}$ here (not $\mathbb{Z}$ as in corollary 8.6), since the claim is
about real roots; $hp$ ties $p$ to the integer-valued counting function at naturals
only, which is exactly what step 1 needs.  Step 2 is the substantial piece and is of
independent interest --- it is the standard proof that $\pi_k$ is a polynomial at all,
and an alternative to corollary 8.6's induction.
\end{theorem}

n22109.title: exists\_triangleFree\_chromaticNumber\_eq
n22109.content:
\begin{theorem}[exists\_triangleFree\_chromaticNumber\_eq]
\lean{SimpleGraph.exists_triangleFree_chromaticNumber_eq}
\label{SimpleGraph.exists_triangleFree_chromaticNumber_eq}
\leanok
One might expect a graph needing many colours to contain a large
clique --- after all, a clique's vertices must all differ.  This theorem says the
converse fails badly: chromatic number can be arbitrarily high with no triangle at
all.  Starting from $K_{2}$, the construction gives a triangle-free $k$-chromatic graph
on $3\cdot 2^{k-2} - 1$ vertices --- the 5-cycle for $k = 3$, the Gr\"otzsch graph for
$k = 4$.  The book adds that Erd\H{o}s (1961) proved by the probabilistic method that
for any $k, l \ge 2$ there is a graph of girth $k$ and chromatic number $l$, and that
Descartes' construction (exercise 8.5.2) already achieves girth $6$.

Self-contained: everything needed is the local \texttt{mycielskian}
def, and step 5's recolouring is the only delicate part.  The carrier is
existentially quantified, so each induction step may change it --- which is exactly
what \texttt{mycielskian} does (\texttt{W $\mapsto$ W $\oplus$ W $\oplus$ Unit}).  Note the "without loss of
generality" in the book's step 5 is a genuine permutation of the palette and must
be performed explicitly.
\end{theorem}

n22110.title: mycielskiTower\_isKCritical
n22110.content:
\begin{theorem}[mycielskiTower\_isKCritical]
\lean{SimpleGraph.mycielskiTower_isKCritical}
\label{SimpleGraph.mycielskiTower_isKCritical}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsKCritical, SimpleGraph.mycielskiTower}
Theorem 8.7 already shows $G_k$ is $k$-chromatic; the exercise asks
for the stronger fact that it is \emph{minimally} so --- the shadows and apex are arranged
so tightly that every element of the graph is load-bearing.  So the Mycielski tower
produces not just triangle-free graphs of high chromatic number but triangle-free
\emph{critical} ones.  For $k = 3$ it gives the 5-cycle (3-critical by exercise 8.1.7)
and for $k = 4$ the Gr\"otzsch graph, which the book displays in figure 8.2 precisely
as its example of a 4-critical graph.

\texttt{mycielskiTower} is \texttt{Sigma}-valued, so \texttt{(mycielskiTower k).2} is
the graph and \texttt{(mycielskiTower k).1} its carrier; the induction in step 1 must
therefore be stated over the \texttt{Sigma}, not over a fixed carrier.  The definitional
unfolding \texttt{mycielskiTower (k+1) = ⟨\_, (mycielskiTower k).2.mycielskian⟩} is what
makes step 2 usable.
\end{theorem}

n22111.title: descartes\_construction

n22112.title: exists\_chromaticNumber\_ge\_girth\_six
n22112.content:
\begin{theorem}[exists\_chromaticNumber\_ge\_girth\_six]
\lean{SimpleGraph.exists_chromaticNumber_ge_girth_six}
\label{SimpleGraph.exists_chromaticNumber_ge_girth_six}
\leanok
High chromatic number is compatible not merely with triangle-freeness
(theorem 8.7) but with the complete absence of short cycles.  Locally such a graph
looks like a tree --- every small neighbourhood is acyclic and trivially
2-colourable --- yet globally it resists any bounded number of colours.  Chromatic
number is a genuinely global invariant.

The conclusion is the honest $\ge$ form ($k \le \chi$, \texttt{6 $\le$ girth})
rather than the book's "$k$-chromatic of girth six".  Two reasons: part (a) delivers
only a lower bound on $\chi$, and \texttt{girth = 6} exactly would additionally require
exhibiting a 6-cycle, which the construction does not obviously do.  Step 3's
instantiation at $m$ rather than $k$ is the small manoeuvre that lets the $\ge$
induction feed part (a)'s $=$ hypothesis.
\end{theorem}

n22113.title: exists\_isCanonicalColouring
n22113.content:
\begin{theorem}[exists\_isCanonicalColouring]
\lean{SimpleGraph.exists_isCanonicalColouring}
\label{SimpleGraph.exists_isCanonicalColouring}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsCanonicalColouring}
Greedily enlarge the first colour class to a maximal independent set,
absorbing whatever later classes will give up; repeat on what remains.  Nothing is
lost: the result is canonical and uses no more colours than before.

\emph{Why this matters (\S{}8.6).}  The storage problem asks for the fewest warehouse
compartments so that incompatible chemicals are separated --- which is the chromatic
number of the incompatibility graph.  No good algorithm is known, so the book gives
an enumerative procedure: list the minimal coverings (equivalently, by theorem 7.1,
the maximal independent sets), then search over canonical colourings.  \textbf{This
exercise is what makes that search complete} --- restricting attention to canonical
colourings loses nothing.  The book's example (figure 8.11) has minimal coverings
${a,c,e,g}$, ${b,c,d,e,g}$, ${b,d,e,f}$, ${b,c,d,f}$, hence maximal independent sets
${b,d,f}$, ${a,f}$, ${a,c,g}$, ${a,e,g}$, and $\chi = 3$ via the canonical colouring
$({b,d,f}, {a,e,g}, {c})$.

\texttt{L.length $\le$ k}, not $= k$: a canonical colouring may use fewer
colours than the one it was built from, and that is precisely the point --- the least
length over canonical colourings \emph{is} $\chi(G)$, which is what the \S{}8.6 procedure
computes.  Step 1's strengthening is essential: the statement as given is not
directly inductive, because the recursive call is about a \emph{deleted} graph.
\end{theorem}

n22267.name: Bonami.b_reasonable_anticon_zero
n22267.type_full:
∀ {Ω : Type u_2} [inst : MeasurableSpace Ω] {P : MeasureTheory.Measure Ω} [MeasureTheory.IsProbabilityMeasure P]
  {X : Ω → Real} {B : Real},
  Bonami.IsBReasonable X P B →
    Measurable X →
      MeasureTheory.Integrable (fun ω => HPow.hPow (X ω) 2) P →
        MeasureTheory.Integrable (fun ω => HPow.hPow (X ω) 4) P →
          LT.lt 0 (ProbabilityTheory.moment X 2 P) →
            ∀ {t : Real},
              LE.le 0 t →
                LE.le t 1 →
                  LE.le (HDiv.hDiv (HPow.hPow (HSub.hSub 1 (HPow.hPow t 2)) 2) B)
                    (P
                        (setOf fun ω =>
                          LT.lt (HMul.hMul (HPow.hPow t 2) (ProbabilityTheory.moment X 2 P))
                            (HPow.hPow (X ω) 2))).toReal

n22268.name: Bonami.b_reasonable_tail_bound
n22268.type_full:

  {X : Ω → Real} {B : Real},
  Bonami.IsBReasonable X P B →
    ∀ (t : Real),
      LT.lt 0 t →
        LT.lt 0 (ProbabilityTheory.moment X 2 P) →
          MeasureTheory.Integrable (fun ω => HPow.hPow (X ω) 4) P →
            LE.le
              (P
                  (setOf fun ω =>
                    GE.ge (HPow.hPow (X ω) 4)
                      (HMul.hMul (HPow.hPow t 4) (HPow.hPow (ProbabilityTheory.moment X 2 P) 2)))).toReal
              (HDiv.hDiv B (HPow.hPow t 4))

n22389.name: LMN.one_step_dtDepth_bound
n22389.type_full:
∀ {n s₂ : Nat} (gates : Fin s₂ → DNF n) (w l : Nat),
  (∀ (i : Fin s₂), LE.le (gates i).width w) →
    LT.lt 0 w →
      (∀ (i : Fin s₂) (t : Term n),
          Membership.mem (gates i) t →
            ∀ (l₁ : Literal n),
              Membership.mem t l₁ → ∀ (l₂ : Literal n), Membership.mem t l₂ → Eq l₁.var l₂.var → Eq l₁ l₂) →
        (∀ (i : Fin s₂) (t : Term n), Membership.mem (gates i) t → List.Nodup t) →
          LT.lt 0 n →
            ∀ (p : Real),
              LT.lt 0 p →
                LE.le p (HDiv.hDiv 1 (HMul.hMul 40 ↑w)) →
                  LE.le p 1 →
                    GE.ge
                      (SwitchingLemma2.bernoulliRestrProb p fun ρ =>
                        ∀ (i : Fin s₂), LE.le (dtDepth (SwitchingLemma2.restrictFn (gates i).eval ρ)) l)
                      (HSub.hSub 1
                        (HMul.hMul (↑s₂)
                          (HAdd.hAdd (HPow.hPow (1 / 2) l) (Real.exp (Neg.neg (HDiv.hDiv (HMul.hMul (↑n) p) 3))))))

  (∀ (j : Fin cs.length),

                    (∀ (x : Fin n → Bool),
                      Eq ((cs.get j).eval fun i => gates i x) (c_j.eval fun k => (g_j k).eval x)))))) →
    Exists fun M =>
      Exists fun merged =>
        Exists fun new_cs =>
          And (∀ (k : Fin M), LE.le (merged k).width l)
            (And
              (∀ (k : Fin M) (t : Term n),

n22465.name: LMN.layer2_composed_bound_base
n22465.type_full:
∀ {n : Nat} (data : LMN.Layer2Data n) (c_top : BoolCircuit.Circuit data.numGates) (s_rem l t : Nat),
  LT.lt 0 l →
    LT.lt 0 n →
      LE.le (HAdd.hAdd c_top.depth 2) 2 →
        LE.le c_top.size s_rem →
          LE.le data.width l →
            LT.lt 0 s_rem →
              LE.le
                (SwitchingLemma2.bernoulliRestrProb (LMN.composedDelta l (↑l) 2) fun ρ =>
                  GT.gt (dtDepth (SwitchingLemma2.restrictFn (fun x => c_top.eval fun i => (data.gates i).eval x) ρ)) t)
                (HAdd.hAdd
                  (HAdd.hAdd (HAdd.hAdd (HMul.hMul (↑s_rem) (HPow.hPow (1 / 2) l)) (HPow.hPow (1 / 2) t))
                    (HMul.hMul (↑s_rem) (Real.exp (Neg.neg (HDiv.hDiv (↑n) (HMul.hMul 120 ↑l))))))
                  (Real.exp (Neg.neg (HDiv.hDiv (↑n) (HMul.hMul 120 ↑l)))))

n23891.name: SimpleGraph.konig_matrix
n23891.type_full:
∀ {m n : Nat} (A : Matrix (Fin m) (Fin n) Bool) {c : Nat},
  IsLeast
      (setOf fun k =>
        Exists fun R =>
          Exists fun C =>
            And (Eq (HAdd.hAdd R.card C.card) k)
              (∀ (i : Fin m) (j : Fin n), Eq (A i j) true → Or (Membership.mem R i) (Membership.mem C j)))
      c →
    ∀ {d : Nat},
      IsGreatest
          (setOf fun k =>
            Exists fun S =>
              And (Eq S.card k)
                (And (∀ (p : Prod (Fin m) (Fin n)), Membership.mem S p → Eq (A p.1 p.2) true)
                  (And (Set.InjOn Prod.fst ↑S) (Set.InjOn Prod.snd ↑S))))
          d →
        Eq c d

    Iff (Networks.IsOrientable G m n)

                    ↑(Networks.edgeBoundaryCard G S))
                  (LE.le (Neg.neg ↑(Networks.edgeBoundaryCard G S))

        ∀ {v₁ v₂ v₃ : V},

                    And (Membership.mem (sdiff (G.bridgeOf c.toSubgraph e).verts c.toSubgraph.verts) v₀)
                      (Exists fun P₁ =>
                        Exists fun P₂ =>
                          Exists fun P₃ =>
                            And P₁.IsPath
                              (And P₂.IsPath
                                (And P₃.IsPath
                                  (And (∀ (x : V), Membership.mem P₁.support x → Membership.mem P₂.support x → Eq x v₀)
                                    (And
                                      (∀ (x : V), Membership.mem P₁.support x → Membership.mem P₃.support x → Eq x v₀)

n24463.name: wm_combined_potential_bound
n24463.type_full:
∀ (n : Nat),
  LT.lt 0 n →
    ∀ (β : Real),
      LT.lt 0 β →
        LT.lt β 1 →
          ∀ (M_star M_WM : Nat),
            LE.le (HPow.hPow β M_star) (HMul.hMul (↑n) (HPow.hPow (HDiv.hDiv (HAdd.hAdd 1 β) 2) M_WM)) →
              LE.le (Real.log (HPow.hPow β M_star))
                (Real.log (HMul.hMul (↑n) (HPow.hPow (HDiv.hDiv (HAdd.hAdd 1 β) 2) M_WM)))

n24465.name: wm_weight_shrinkage
n24465.type_full:
∀ (β : Real),
  LT.lt 0 β →
    LT.lt β 1 →
      ∀ (M : Nat) (W : Nat → Real),
        (∀ (k : Nat), LT.lt 0 (W k)) →
          (∀ (k : Nat), LT.lt k M → LE.le (W (HAdd.hAdd k 1)) (HMul.hMul (W k) (HDiv.hDiv (HAdd.hAdd 1 β) 2))) →
            LE.le (W M) (HMul.hMul (W 0) (HPow.hPow (HDiv.hDiv (HAdd.hAdd 1 β) 2) M))

n24466.name: wm_weight_upper_bound
n24466.type_full:
∀ (n : Nat),
  LT.lt 0 n →
    ∀ (β : Real),
      LT.lt 0 β →
        LT.lt β 1 →
          ∀ (M : Nat) (W : Nat → Real),
            Eq (W 0) ↑n →
              (∀ (k : Nat), LT.lt 0 (W k)) →
                (∀ (k : Nat), LT.lt k M → LE.le (W (HAdd.hAdd k 1)) (HMul.hMul (W k) (HDiv.hDiv (HAdd.hAdd 1 β) 2))) →
                  LE.le (W M) (HMul.hMul (↑n) (HPow.hPow (HDiv.hDiv (HAdd.hAdd 1 β) 2) M))
